title: Coastal Brew
sub: Why is a growing coffee chain making less money?
skills: Reading a P&L · unit economics · cannibalisation
prompt: Our client, Coastal Brew, runs 120 coffee shops across the south of England. Over the last two years revenue has grown slightly, from $96M to $98M, but operating profit has fallen from $12M to $4.5M. The CEO has asked us to find out why profits are falling and what to do about it.

clarify.a: Company-owned cafés (no franchising). Sells hot drinks, cold drinks and food. Since 2024 it has also sold through two delivery apps.
Get back to at least $10M operating profit within two years.
Competitors report flat to slightly lower margins, nothing like a 60% drop. This is mostly a Coastal Brew problem.
No. 120 stores throughout, no openings or closures.

structure.root: Why has profit fallen $7.5M?

hypothesis: Revenue is roughly flat, so the problem is on the cost side, probably a new or fast-growing cost line. The delivery channel launched in this period, so that's where I'd look first.

questions.q: Here is the P&L. Where is the profit going?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Coastal Brew P&L
exhibit.note: Delivery orders were 5% of revenue in 2024 and 25% in 2026.

questions.answer:
Revenue added $2.0M, but costs rose by $9.5M. Two lines explain almost all of it:

  • App commissions: +$6.0M (from 1.5% to 7.6% of revenue). Delivery went from 5% to 25% of sales, and the apps charge ~30% commission.
  • Ingredients & packaging: +$2.5M, rising faster than revenue (25.0% → 27.0%), which points to delivery packaging.

Staff and rent are flat as a % of revenue. So-what: the delivery channel is eating the margin. Next I'd like to compare the profit on a delivery order with an in-store order.
questions.note: A strong candidate converts the cost lines into % of revenue without being asked.

questions.q: Compare the economics of an in-store order and a delivery order. Is delivery adding profit?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 2 · Order economics
exhibit.note: Customer research: 60% of delivery customers say they would otherwise have visited the café.

questions.answer:
Contribution per order (before staff, rent and overheads):

  • In-store: $6.00 − $1.50 = $4.50 (75%)
  • Delivery: $9.00 − $2.25 − $0.90 − $2.70 = $3.15 (35%)

But 60% of delivery orders replace an in-store visit. The true gain per delivery order = $3.15 − 0.6 × $4.50 = $3.15 − $2.70 = $0.45.

So-what: each delivery order looks bigger, but it adds only about $0.45 of profit because most of it replaces a high-margin café visit. The growth of delivery has mostly moved customers to a worse channel.
questions.note: Push weaker candidates: 'Is the $3.15 all new profit?' The cannibalisation step is what this case tests.

questions.q: What could Coastal Brew do to restore profit? Brainstorm.
questions.answer:
Make delivery orders more profitable

  • Charge higher menu prices on the apps (common practice)
  • Negotiate commission down in return for volume or exclusivity
  • A delivery-only menu built around high-margin items; cheaper packaging

Shift customers to cheaper channels

  • Own app with click-and-collect (no commission), with loyalty points to make the switch worth it
  • In-store offers aimed at customers who used to visit

Fix the base

  • Check staff scheduling against the lower in-store footfall

questions.q: The CEO likes the idea of raising delivery prices by 15%. The apps estimate we'd lose 10% of delivery orders. What's the impact? (We sell about 2.7M delivery orders a year.)
questions.answer:
New ticket $10.35; commission 30% = $3.11; ingredients $2.25 (same food); packaging $0.90.
New contribution = $10.35 − $3.11 − $2.25 − $0.90 ≈ $4.10 (up from $3.15).

Before: 2.7M × $3.15 ≈ $8.5M. After: 2.43M × $4.10 ≈ $9.95M. Gain ≈ $1.45M a year.

Sanity check: +$0.95 per order on 2.4M orders ≈ $2.3M, minus ~270k lost orders × $3.15 ≈ $0.85M, so ≈ $1.45M. ✓
Bonus point: some lost delivery customers may come back to the café, which makes the move even better.

reco: Coastal Brew's profit has fallen $7.5M because delivery has grown from 5% to 25% of sales, and a delivery order adds only ~$0.45 of real profit once you account for café visits it replaces. I recommend three moves: (1) raise app menu prices ~15%, worth about $1.45M a year; (2) launch click-and-collect in the Coastal Brew app to move customers off the commission channels; (3) renegotiate commissions with the threat of lower volume. Risk: the apps may rank us lower in search. The price rise closes about $1.45M of the $5.5M gap to the $10M target; the rest has to come from moving orders to click-and-collect and lower commissions, which we should size next. Next step: test the price increase in 10 stores for 4 weeks before rolling it out.
great: Converts the P&L into % of revenue straight away
Spots cannibalisation without a hint
Sanity-checks the ~$1.45M a second way
Recommendation opens with the answer and the number, not a recap

title: Nordwind E-Bikes
sub: Should a Danish premium e-bike maker enter the US?
skills: Market sizing · breakeven · entry mode
prompt: Nordwind makes premium e-bikes in Denmark and sells them through 600 bike shops across Europe (revenue $150M). European growth is slowing, so the founders are considering the United States. Their goal: $44M of US revenue (measured at Nordwind's selling price to shops) within five years, and an operating profit in the US by year 3. Should they enter, and if so, how?

clarify.a: Premium city and trekking e-bikes, average retail price about $4,000.
Through independent bike shops. Nordwind sells to shops at 60% of retail price.

clarify.q: How is the revenue goal measured?
clarify.a: At Nordwind's selling price to shops, not at retail prices.
None today. A few US shops import small volumes informally.

structure.root: Should Nordwind enter the US, and how?

branches.head: How to enter?
items: Distributor vs own network vs acquisition

hypothesis: The US market is big enough. The real question is whether Nordwind can reach enough shops fast enough, so I expect the entry mode to decide the case.

questions.q: Here is some market data. What market share would Nordwind need to hit its goal in year 5?
questions.answer:
Year-5 market = 1.0M × 1.1⁴ ≈ 1.46M units → premium = 15% ≈ 220k units.

Units needed = $44M ÷ $2,400 ≈ 18,300 bikes → share of premium ≈ 18.3k ÷ 220k ≈ 8%.

So-what: 8% would make Nordwind roughly the #4 premium brand within five years. That's ambitious but not crazy in a fragmented segment. Next I'd look at the competition.

questions.q: Here are the premium competitors. What does this tell you?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 2 · US premium e-bike share of units, %

questions.answer: The market is fragmented: the top four hold 55% and a long tail holds 45%. A European brand (B) already holds 15%, so US buyers clearly accept European premium bikes. To reach 8%, Nordwind needs to match Brand D. So-what: the share target is realistic if Nordwind gets its bikes into enough shops. That makes the route to market the key decision.

questions.q: Nordwind is choosing between two ways to enter. Which is better?

rows: Variable cost per bike (make, ship, duty)
exhibit.title: Exhibit 3 · Entry options

questions.answer:
Contribution per bike: A = $2,400 × 85% − $1,500 = $540; B = $2,400 − $1,500 = $900.

Annual profit is the same when 540V − 1.5M = 900V − 6M → 360V = 4.5M → V = 12,500 bikes/year.

Below 12,500 bikes a year the distributor is better; above it, the own network wins. At year-5 volume (~18,300): A ≈ $8.4M, B ≈ $10.5M.

Own-network breakeven = $6M ÷ $900 ≈ 6,700 bikes/year. If volumes ramp 3k → 7k → 11k → 15k → 18.3k, B makes a small profit in year 2, but recovering the $12M upfront takes until year 5.
questions.note: Let the candidate set up the indifference equation. Good candidates realise the answer is 'distributor first, then switch'.

questions.q: What risks should the founders weigh?
questions.answer:
• Tariffs and trade policy on EU-made goods can wipe out the $900 margin overnight. Consider US final assembly.
  • Distributor lock-in: a 5-year exclusive contract would block the switch to an own network.
  • Brand awareness: no US brand recognition, so early volumes may be slower.
  • Service: e-bikes need repairs and spare parts; shops need training.

reco: Yes, enter the US, but through a distributor first. Hitting $44M needs about 8% of the premium segment, which is achievable in a fragmented market. A distributor is more profitable until volumes pass ~12,500 bikes a year and needs no $12M upfront, so it also meets the 'profitable by year 3' goal more safely. The contract should be 3 years or less, with the right to take over distribution once that volume is reached. Main risk: tariffs. As a next step, model US assembly and start in 2-3 bike-friendly states.
great: States the 8% share and judges whether it's realistic
Sets up the 12,500-bike crossover clearly
Recommends a sequence (distributor → own network), not just one option
Raises tariffs without prompting

title: Meridian Hospitals
sub: How can a hospital chain double its revenue in five years?
skills: Revenue trees · sizing growth levers · capital constraints
prompt: Meridian runs 12 private multi-specialty hospitals in South India with revenue of $300M a year. The board wants to double revenue to $600M within five years without hurting quality. How should Meridian get there?

clarify.a: Inpatient 65%, outpatient consultations 20%, pharmacy 10%, diagnostics 5%.
2,400 beds. Average bed occupancy 62%; well-run peers in the region reach 75%.
EBITDA margin 18% (~$54M). Moderate debt; the board is open to raising more.
Mostly large cities (Bengaluru, Chennai, Hyderabad). No presence yet in smaller (tier-2) cities.

structure.root: +$300M revenue in 5 years: where from?

hypothesis: Existing hospitals can deliver maybe a third of the growth through occupancy. The rest needs new beds, and given the 5-year time frame, buying hospitals may beat building them.

questions.q: Occupancy varies a lot by hospital. What do you see?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Bed occupancy by hospital, %
exhibit.note: H10-H12 opened in the last 3 years in newer parts of the cities.

questions.answer: Nine hospitals sit between 60% and 78%. Three newer ones (H10-H12) are around 40% and drag the average down to 62%. So-what: the occupancy problem is concentrated. Typical causes for new hospitals: not enough well-known doctors, and few referrals from local GPs. Fixing these three is the fastest growth lever available.

questions.q: How much revenue would Meridian gain by raising average occupancy from 62% to 75%?
questions.answer:
Inpatient revenue = 65% × $300M = $195M. Assuming revenue grows in line with occupied beds: $195M × 75/62 ≈ $236M → +$41M.

If the other streams (outpatient, pharmacy, diagnostics: $105M) grow ~10% a year organically: $105M × 1.1⁵ ≈ $169M → +$64M.

Existing hospitals ≈ +$105M. Gap still to fill ≈ $195M. So-what: around two-thirds of the target needs new capacity.

Note: a 75% average means every hospital at the peer benchmark. Lifting only H10-H12 to 75% takes the average to about 70% (about +$26M); the nine established hospitals (about 69%) must also rise.

questions.q: Here are two ways to add capacity. How would you fill the remaining $195M?
questions.answer:
A hospital built in year 1 only matures in year 5, so building alone is too slow: ~5-6 new hospitals ($200-240M) all opened in year 1.

Buying gives revenue straight away: about 4 acquisitions at ~$35M each after upgrade ≈ $140M for ~$150M. Add 2 new builds in big cities for ≈ $55-70M by year 5 → total ≈ $195-210M.

Funding: ~$230M over 5 years, plus upgrade capex for the acquired hospitals (ask the interviewer), against ~$54M+ a year of EBITDA. Doable with some debt, but tight. Look at asset-light options (management contracts) to reduce the capital needed.

reco: Meridian can reach $600M, but it can't build its way there in five years. I recommend three steps: (1) lift occupancy across all 12 hospitals to the 75% peer benchmark, starting with the three under-filled ones (+~$40M; fixing only those three gives about +$26M), alongside organic growth in outpatient, pharmacy and diagnostics (+~$65M); (2) buy about four hospitals in tier-2 cities (+~$140M), which also opens new markets; (3) build two flagship hospitals in big cities (+~$60M by year 5). Total investment is about $230M. The biggest risk is keeping quality consistent across acquired hospitals, so next steps are a clinical-quality checklist for acquisitions and a shortlist of targets.
great: Sizes each lever, adds them up, and names the remaining gap
Notices that new builds take 4 years to mature
Checks whether the plan can be funded
Mentions quality, the client's own constraint

title: PackRight
sub: Should a packaging maker buy a plastics recycler?
skills: Valuation with multiples · synergies · avoiding double counting
prompt: PackRight makes plastic packaging for food and drink brands across Europe: revenue $800M, EBITDA $120M. New rules will require packaging to contain at least 30% recycled plastic by 2030. PackRight is considering buying RePlast, a recycler with revenue of $120M and EBITDA of $12M. The owners are asking $180M. Should PackRight buy?

clarify.q: Why buy, not buy on the market?
clarify.a: PackRight worries it won't be able to buy enough recycled plastic at a reasonable price.
Uses 400,000 tonnes of plastic a year → needs 120,000 tonnes recycled by 2030.
80,000 tonnes a year, sold at market price (~$1,500/tonne) to many buyers.
Recyclers usually sell for 9-11× EBITDA. Use 10×.

structure.root: Is RePlast worth more than $180M to PackRight?

branches.head: Deal
items: Alternatives: long-term contracts, build our own plant

hypothesis: At 15× EBITDA the asking price is high for a recycler. I expect the deal to make sense only if the supply-security benefit is real and large.

questions.q: Is there really a supply problem? Look at this market outlook.

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · European recycled plastic, million tonnes (case data)

questions.answer: Supply exceeds demand until 2027. From 2028 demand overtakes supply, and by 2030 the gap is 1.9Mt (−20%). So-what: recycled plastic will be scarce just as PackRight legally needs it. Expect prices to rise, and some buyers to get no supply at all. Securing supply is valuable.

questions.q: A colleague says: 'RePlast's plastic costs $1,200/tonne to make and sells for $1,500. If we own it, we save $300 × 80,000 = $24M a year. That's a huge synergy.' Do you agree?
questions.answer:
No, that's double counting. RePlast already earns that $300/tonne margin. It's part of the $12M EBITDA we're paying for. Moving the profit from RePlast to PackRight doesn't create new profit for the group.

The real value is access: in a shortage, owning RePlast guarantees 80k of the 120k tonnes needed, and protects PackRight against price spikes and lost contracts.
questions.note: This is the key test of the case. Don't hint unless the candidate is completely stuck.

questions.q: Now value the deal. Real synergies: $5M a year of cost savings (logistics, overheads), and brands will pay a 3% premium for guaranteed-recycled packaging on $200M of PackRight sales, about $6M of extra EBITDA. Integration costs $15M one-off.
questions.answer:
RePlast standalone: 12 × 10$120M
Cost synergies: 5 × 10$50M
Revenue synergies: 6 × 10$60M
Integration cost−$15M
Maximum value to PackRight$215M

$215M > $180M asking → $35M of value created. But without the revenue synergy: 120 + 50 − 15 = $155M < $180M.

So-what: the whole decision depends on whether customers really pay the green premium, which is the least certain synergy.

questions.q: How would you protect PackRight in the deal?
questions.answer:
• Negotiate the upfront price towards ~$155-165M (what's justified without the revenue synergy)
  • Pay an earn-out (extra payment later) only if green-premium contracts are signed
  • Before signing, get letters of intent from 2-3 major brands for the premium packaging
  • Check RePlast's technology can produce food-grade recycled plastic

reco: PackRight should buy RePlast, but not at a flat $180M. Recycled plastic will be scarce from 2028, and RePlast covers two-thirds of what PackRight legally needs by 2030. With all synergies, RePlast is worth about $215M to PackRight. Without the uncertain green premium, it's worth only $155M. So I'd offer around $160M upfront plus an earn-out of up to $20M tied to signed premium contracts. Key risk: integration and food-grade quality. Next steps: technical due diligence and talks with three anchor customers.
great: Catches the $24M double count
Separates certain synergies from uncertain ones
Structures the price (earn-out) instead of giving a plain yes or no
Connects the regulation deadline to the shortage

title: FitHub Gyms
sub: Should a private equity fund buy a budget gym chain?
skills: LBO-style returns maths · value creation plan · exit
prompt: Summit Capital, a mid-sized private equity fund, has been offered FitHub, a chain of 80 budget gyms in the UK. FitHub makes $25M EBITDA and the seller is asking 8× EBITDA ($200M). Summit needs to make 2.5× its money within five years. Should Summit invest?

clarify.a: 50% debt, 50% fund equity: $100M debt, $100M equity.
Sell in year 5 at the same 8× multiple. Debt expected to fall to $60M by then from cash flow.
~4,000 members per gym, $25/month, no contract. Gyms are leased.
UK budget gyms growing ~5% a year; two large competitors.

structure.root: Can Summit make 2.5× on FitHub?

hypothesis: Work backwards: figure out the EBITDA FitHub needs in year 5, then check whether the plan gets there.

questions.q: What EBITDA does FitHub need in year 5 for Summit to make 2.5×?
questions.answer:
Equity needed at exit = 2.5 × $100M = $250M. Add remaining debt $60M → enterprise value $310M.

At 8× → EBITDA needed = $310M ÷ 8 ≈ $38.75M, i.e. +$13.75M (+55%) from today's $25M.

questions.q: Management's plan has three parts. How much EBITDA does it add?

rows: Open 20 gyms by year 4; each makes $0.4M EBITDA when mature; costs $2M each to fit out
$25 → $27/month across all gyms; expect to lose 5% of members
LED lighting and solar panels: $2M a year saved
exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Management value creation plan

questions.q: What concerns would you raise with the investment committee?
questions.answer:
• Cash tension: the plan spends $40M on new gyms (20 × $2M) but also assumes debt falls by $40M from cash flow. Both need the same cash, so check it's possible to do both.
  • Exit multiple: if it drops to 7×: EV = 7 × 38.1 ≈ $267M → equity $207M → ~2.1×.
  • Price rise: budget customers are price-sensitive; competitors may not follow.
  • New gyms take time to fill; year-4 openings may not be mature by the exit.
questions.note: Candidates who spot the cash tension without being prompted are at offer level.

reco: At $200M, FitHub returns about 2.45× in our base case, just short of the 2.5× target, with real downside if exit multiples fall or the cash plan doesn't hold together. I'd recommend Summit bids, but at around $190M (7.6×). Keeping $100M of debt, Summit's equity falls to $90M, and the same plan returns ~2.7× if we still exit at 8× ($245M ÷ $90M), or ~2.55× even if the exit multiple only matches our 7.6× entry. The conditions: a funded capex plan for the new gyms and a price test in 10 gyms before the rise goes everywhere. If the seller won't move, walk away.
great: Works backwards from the return to the EBITDA needed
Gives returns as a multiple and checks them
Spots the capex vs debt-paydown cash conflict
Recommends a price, not just yes or no

title: CloudLedger
sub: How should a software company price its new AI add-on?
skills: Value-based pricing · price-volume trade-off · portfolio effects
prompt: CloudLedger sells online accounting software to 200,000 small businesses at $50 a month. It has built an AI add-on that does routine bookkeeping automatically. The product team wants to know what to charge for it.

clarify.a: Maximise profit from the add-on, but the CEO also cares about keeping core customers.
About $15 per customer per month (mostly AI computing).
A standalone AI bookkeeping tool costs $99/month. A part-time bookkeeper costs ~$40/hour.
Optional add-on on top of the $50 plan.

structure.root: What price for the AI add-on?

hypothesis: The value to customers is far above the cost, so the price will sit between the competitor's $99 and a much lower adoption-friendly price. The trade-off between margin and adoption is the real question.

questions.q: What is the add-on worth to a typical customer?
questions.answer: The add-on saves about 6 hours of bookkeeping a month (from pilot data). 6 × $40 = $240/month of value. Cost to serve is $15, and the competitor charges $99. So-what: the sensible range is roughly $30-$100. Pricing at the full $240 value isn't realistic: customers expect to keep some of the saving.
questions.note: Give the '6 hours' figure if the candidate asks how much time it saves.

questions.q: A customer survey shows how many would buy at each price. Which price maximises add-on profit?
questions.answer:
Annual profit = 200,000 × adoption × (price − $15) × 12

$2980k × $14 × 12 = $13.4M
$4960k × $34 × 12 = $24.5M
$7936k × $64 × 12 = $27.6M
$9920k × $84 × 12 = $20.2M

$79 maximises add-on profit (~$27.6M a year).

questions.q: New data: customers who use the add-on are far less likely to cancel CloudLedger. Each adopter is worth an extra $200 a year of core-product profit. Does this change your answer?
questions.answer:
Add $200 × adopters to each option:

$2913.4 + 16.0 = $29.4M
$4924.5 + 12.0 = $36.5M
$7927.6 + 7.2 = $34.8M
$9920.2 + 4.0 = $24.2M

$49 now wins. Looking at the whole customer, not just the add-on, changes the answer. So-what: price for adoption, because the add-on's biggest value is keeping core customers.

reco: Launch the AI add-on at $49 a month. On its own the add-on would make the most at $79, but each adopter is also much less likely to cancel, which makes $49 about $1.6M a year better overall (≈$36.5M vs $34.8M). Consider a 'Pro' tier at ~$89 later for heavier users. Risk: AI computing costs could rise with usage. Next step: A/B test $49 vs $59 with new customers.
great: Uses all three pricing lenses before the survey
Calculates profit, not revenue
Changes the answer when new data arrives, and says why

title: FreshMart
sub: A hard discounter is coming. How should a regional grocer respond?
skills: Sizing the threat · comparing responses to doing nothing
prompt: FreshMart operates 60 supermarkets in the US Midwest. A European hard discounter (small stores, ~1,500 products, prices 20-30% below supermarkets) has announced 25 new stores in FreshMart's region over the next three years. FreshMart's CEO wants a plan to respond.

clarify.a: Average store sells $20M a year; EBIT margin 4%. Contribution on each lost dollar of sales ≈ 25%.
30 of FreshMart's 60 stores are within 3 miles of a planned discounter store.
In other regions, supermarkets near a new discounter lost ~12% of sales in year 1 and ~8% for good.
Strong fresh food, local brand, good service; prices ~10% above market average.

structure.root: How should FreshMart respond?

hypothesis: The threat is concentrated in half the stores, so a targeted response probably beats a chain-wide price cut.

questions.q: How much profit is at risk if FreshMart does nothing?
questions.answer:
Sales lost for good = 30 stores × $20M × 8% = $48M/year. Profit lost = $48M × 25% = $12M/year.

Total EBIT = 60 × $20M × 4% = $48M → doing nothing costs a quarter of FreshMart's profit.

questions.q: Which customers leave? Look at this exhibit.

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Sales lost by category at supermarkets near a discounter (other regions)

questions.answer: Losses concentrate in packaged groceries and household goods (13-14%), where products are identical and price wins. Fresh categories barely move (2-3%). So-what: fight on price only for packaged staples, and lean into fresh, where FreshMart is stronger.

questions.q: Option A: match the discounter's prices on 300 key packaged items in the 30 exposed stores. That gives up 3 margin points on 20% of their sales, and halves the sustained sales loss (8% → 4%). Worth it?
questions.answer:
Cost = 30 × $20M × 20% × 3% = $3.6M/year. Benefit = sales loss falls by 4% → 30 × $20M × 4% × 25% = $6.0M/year saved.

Net +$2.4M vs doing nothing. Remaining damage ≈ −12 + 6 − 3.6 = −$9.6M. Price matching helps, but it isn't enough on its own.

questions.q: What else should FreshMart do?
questions.answer:
• Private label on packaged staples: discounter-level prices at better margins
  • Double down on fresh: bigger produce and deli counters in exposed stores; the discounter's range is thin here
  • Loyalty programme with personalised offers to keep high-value families
  • Don't cut prices chain-wide: 30 unaffected stores would give away margin for nothing

reco: Doing nothing puts $12M a year at risk, about a quarter of FreshMart's profit. Respond in the 30 exposed stores only: match prices on ~300 packaged staples (net +$2.4M), launch a private-label range in the same categories, and invest in fresh food, where the discounter is weak and customers don't leave. Avoid a chain-wide price war. Next step: pilot the full package in the first 5 stores the discounter targets, and track weekly sales by category.
great: Compares every option against doing nothing
Uses the category chart to decide where to fight
Keeps the response limited to the stores that are actually exposed

title: Desert Dairy
sub: Should a dairy company build a new plant?
skills: Demand vs capacity · timing · cheaper alternatives first
prompt: Desert Dairy is a leading dairy producer in Saudi Arabia. Its one plant can produce 500 million litres a year and is running at 460M litres. Demand is growing ~7% a year. The board is considering a new $150M plant that would add 200M litres of capacity. Should they build it?

clarify.a: Contribution ≈ $0.30 per litre.
About 3 years from decision to production.
Engineers say $20M of upgrades could squeeze 60M more litres from the existing plant within a year.
Two competitors have also announced expansions.

structure.root: Build a new plant?

hypothesis: They will need more capacity, but the cheap upgrade should come first. The real question is when to commit to the new plant, given the 3-year build.

questions.q: When does Desert Dairy run out of capacity?
questions.answer:
Year012345
Demand (M litres, +7%/yr)460492527564603645

Current plant (500M) runs out in year 2. With the $20M upgrade (560M) it's enough until year 3, when demand reaches 564M. A new plant takes 3 years, so the decision has to be made now to have capacity by year 3-4.

questions.q: Is the $20M upgrade worth it?
questions.answer: Extra volume sold: year 2 ≈ 27M litres (527 − 500) → $8M; year 3 onwards the full 60M litres → $18M/yr. Payback ≈ 2.5–3 years from today ($0 in year 1, $8M in year 2, $18M in year 3), even if the new plant later takes over this volume. Easily worth it, and it buys time.

questions.q: Here is the industry picture. Does this change anything?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Saudi dairy capacity vs demand, billion litres (case data)
exhibit.note: Includes competitors' announced expansions, but not Desert Dairy's new plant.

questions.answer: Industry capacity grows 25% while demand grows ~23%. Utilisation is ~87% today and stays ~85% in three years even before our plant. Adding 0.2bn more would push it to ~81%. So-what: more capacity → pressure on prices. Model a lower contribution (e.g. $0.25/litre) for the new plant's volume, and consider building it in phases.

reco: Do the $20M upgrade immediately: it pays back in under 3 years and covers demand until year 3. Approve the new plant now because of the 3-year build, but in two phases (e.g. 100M litres first), because competitors are also expanding and prices may come under pressure. Use co-packers to cover any short-term peaks. Next steps: firm up raw-milk supply contracts, and rerun the plant economics at $0.25/litre.
great: Builds the demand table year by year
Spots that the 3-year build forces the decision now
Tries the cheaper option first
Considers competitor supply and prices, not only our own demand

title: SkyLine MRO
sub: Why do aircraft spend so long in maintenance?
skills: Process mapping · finding waiting time · cost-benefit
prompt: SkyLine is a mid-sized airline with 40 narrow-body aircraft. Every two years each aircraft goes through a 'heavy check', a major maintenance overhaul done in SkyLine's own hangar. A heavy check takes 28 days, versus 20 days at the best airlines. The COO wants to know why, and what it's worth to fix.

clarify.a: An aircraft in the hangar can't fly. Each lost day costs about $60,000 of contribution.
40 aircraft, each checked every 2 years → 20 heavy checks a year.
No. Safety and quality are fine; it's only about time.

structure.root: Why 28 days, and what's it worth?

branches.head: Size the prize
items: Days lost × checks × cost per day

hypothesis: The repair work itself is probably similar to the best airlines; the extra days are likely waiting time.

questions.q: What is the prize if SkyLine matches the best airlines?
questions.answer: 8 days × 20 checks × $60k = $9.6M a year.

questions.q: Here's where the 28 days go. What do you see?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Days per stage of a heavy check

questions.answer: Repair time is the same (10 days). The gap is all waiting: parts (9 vs 2 days) and approvals (3 vs 1). SkyLine spends 12 of its 28 days (43%) waiting. (Best airlines spend one extra day on testing.) So-what: this is a planning problem, not a skills problem. Fix parts first: it's 7 of the 8 days.

questions.q: The team proposes: (1) order parts in advance based on past checks, holding $5M of extra stock (cost of holding stock: 20% a year); (2) digital sign-off software at $0.5M a year. Parts waiting falls to 4 days and approvals to 1. Is it worth it?
questions.answer:
Days saved = (9 − 4) + (3 − 1) = 7 days → 7 × 20 × $60k = $8.4M/year.

Costs = $5M × 20% + $0.5M = $1.5M/year. Net ≈ +$6.9M/year. Clearly worth it.

reco: SkyLine's heavy checks take 8 days longer than the best airlines because aircraft wait for parts and approvals, not because repairs are slow. Pre-ordering parts and digital sign-off cut 7 days per check, worth $8.4M a year for $1.5M of cost (net ~$6.9M). Start with the next 5 checks, then tackle the 2 extra days still spent waiting for parts (4 vs 2); testing needs no work, as SkyLine is already a day faster than its peers there. Risk: holding parts that don't get used, so review the parts list every quarter.
great: Sizes the prize first
Separates working time from waiting time
Nets off the cost of holding stock

title: Visit Al Noor
sub: How can a Gulf state double its international tourists?
skills: Growth maths · capacity constraints · stakeholders
prompt: The tourism authority of Al Noor, a (fictional) Gulf state, receives 5 million international visitors a year. As part of its plan to diversify the economy away from oil, the government wants 10 million visitors a year by 2033 (7 years from now). The minister has asked us what it would take.

clarify.a: Jobs for nationals, foreign currency, less dependence on oil revenue.
GCC neighbours 40%, Europe 25%, South Asia 20%, others 15%.
35,000 hotel rooms, ~70% occupancy. 80% of visitors stay in hotels for 4 nights on average, 1.8 guests per room.
12,000 rooms under construction or approved.

structure.root: What does it take to reach 10M visitors?

hypothesis: Doubling in 7 years needs ~10% growth a year. That's hard but doable. I suspect hotel capacity and flights, not demand, will be the bottleneck.

questions.q: What annual growth rate is needed?
questions.answer: (10 ÷ 5)^(1/7) − 1 ≈ 10.4% a year. Rule of 72 check: 72 ÷ 10.4 ≈ 7 years to double. ✓

questions.q: How many hotel rooms will Al Noor need for 10M visitors? Assume a healthy target occupancy of 75%.
questions.answer:
Guest-nights = 10M × 80% × 4 = 32M → room-nights = 32M ÷ 1.8 ≈ 17.8M.

Rooms = 17.8M ÷ (365 × 75%) ≈ 65,000 rooms. Today 35,000 + 12,000 pipeline = 47,000 → shortfall ≈ 18,000 rooms.

Sanity check on today: 5M × 0.8 × 4 ÷ 1.8 ≈ 8.9M room-nights ÷ (35,000 × 365) ≈ 70% occupancy. ✓ matches the data.

questions.q: Air capacity is the other constraint. What do you conclude?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Visitors by source market, millions
exhibit.note: Growth potential = analyst estimate of extra visitors by 2033 with better flights and visas. Most GCC visitors arrive by road; Europe, South Asia and others arrive by air.

questions.answer: Potential growth totals ~5.0M, just enough for the 10M target, with Europe and South Asia making up ~70% of it. These are long-haul and flight-dependent: new routes and airline deals are critical. GCC visitors mostly drive, so they don't need flights.

questions.q: What should the government do, and what should it leave to the private sector?
questions.answer:
• Government: e-visa / visa on arrival for priority markets; incentives for airlines on new routes; airport capacity; an events calendar; training nationals for hospitality jobs
  • Private sector: build the 18,000 extra rooms (land or tax incentives to attract them); attractions; tour operators
  • Both: sustainability standards (water, energy) and protecting the culture that attracts visitors

reco: Reaching 10 million visitors by 2033 needs ~10% growth a year, and the binding constraints are capacity, not demand. Al Noor needs ~65,000 hotel rooms, about 18,000 beyond today's pipeline, and new flight routes from Europe and South Asia, which offer ~70% of the growth. I recommend that government focuses on visas, airline route deals, events and a national workforce programme, and uses land and tax incentives to bring in private hotel investment. Next step: a joint plan with the national airline for 10 new routes.
great: Converts visitors into rooms correctly
Checks the model against today's 70% occupancy
Separates public and private roles
Links tourism to the government's real goal (jobs, diversification)

title: Plugged In
sub: How big is the UK market for home EV chargers?
skills: Top-down sizing · segmentation · sanity checks
prompt: A private equity fund is looking at a company that installs electric-vehicle chargers in people's homes. Before going further, they want a quick estimate: how many home chargers are installed in the UK each year, and what is that worth?

clarify.a: Home chargers only (not public or workplace). Units per year and $ value including installation.
None given. The candidate should make sensible assumptions and say them out loud.

structure.root: Home chargers installed per year

branches.head: Used EV buyers
items: Used EVs bought by first-time EV owners

hypothesis: I'd guess a few hundred thousand units a year, worth a few hundred million dollars.

questions.q: Walk me through your estimate.
questions.answer:
These are illustrative assumptions a candidate might use. They're there to show the method, not to be quoted as facts.

New cars sold in the UK per year~1.9M
× share that are fully electric~25% → ~475k
× have a driveway or garage~60% → ~285k
× install a charger~80% → ~230k
+ first-time EV owners buying used (~200k × 60% × 50%)~60k
+ replacements (early market)small
Total units per year~290k
× ~$1,000 installed≈ $290M

questions.q: How would you sanity-check this?
questions.answer:
• Supply side: number of installers × jobs per installer per year
  • Cross-check from the stock side: EVs on the road × share with a home charger, change year on year; or chargers sold as reported by the makers
  • Ask for the limiting factor: in many cities, off-street parking (not demand) limits the market

reco: Roughly 290,000 home chargers a year, worth about $290M, driven mainly by new EV sales and limited by how many people have off-street parking. For the fund the growth story matters more than the level: the market grows in line with EV adoption, and the biggest upside is the ~40% of households without driveways, if kerbside solutions emerge.
great: States a guess before calculating
Segments new vs used buyers
Names the limiting factor (parking)
Rounds sensibly and gives one clear number

title: SnackCo Protein Bar
sub: Should a snack maker launch a protein bar?
skills: Breakeven · cannibalisation · launch risk
prompt: SnackCo is a mid-sized snack company best known for its granola bars. Its marketing team wants to launch a high-protein bar for gym-goers. Launch costs are $12M in the first year. Should SnackCo launch?

clarify.a: Sells to retailers at $1.50 per bar; variable cost $0.70.
$8M marketing + $4M production line, all in year 1.
Break even in year 1, or at least show a clear path to it.

structure.root: Launch the protein bar?

hypothesis: The margin per bar is healthy. The risk is volume: whether SnackCo can sell enough bars in year 1 to cover $12M.

questions.q: How many bars does SnackCo need to sell to break even in year 1?
questions.answer: Contribution = $1.50 − $0.70 = $0.80. Breakeven = $12M ÷ $0.80 = 15M bars.

questions.q: Research says 20% of protein-bar buyers would otherwise have bought a SnackCo granola bar (contribution $0.50). Does that change the answer?
questions.answer: Effective contribution = $0.80 − 20% × $0.50 = $0.70. Breakeven = $12M ÷ $0.70 ≈ 17.1M bars.

questions.q: Is 17M bars achievable? Here is the market data.

rows: Regular buyers in SnackCo's retail channels
Bars bought per buyer per week
Realistic year-1 share for a new brand
exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Market data (case data)

questions.answer:
Market = 2M × 1.5 × 52 = 156M bars/year. At 10% share → 15.6M bars.

That just covers the 15M breakeven, but falls short of the 17.1M needed once cannibalisation is included → year-1 loss ≈ (17.1 − 15.6) × $0.70 ≈ $1M.

So-what: close to breakeven. The launch is attractive if year 2 continues without the $4M line cost, but year 1 is borderline.

reco: Launch, but test before committing the full $8M marketing budget. Once granola-bar cannibalisation is counted, SnackCo needs ~17M bars to break even in year 1, and a realistic 10% share gives ~15.6M, a small loss of about $1M. Year 2 is profitable since the $4M line is a one-off. Start in two regions with gym and fitness-retail partners, measure repeat purchase, then scale. Risk: big protein brands discounting to defend shelf space.
great: Includes cannibalisation in the breakeven
Converts a share into bars and compares with breakeven
Notices the one-off cost makes year 2 different

title: Vertex Mobile
sub: Why is a telecom operator's revenue falling?
skills: Isolating the problem · segmenting · flanker brands
prompt: Vertex is the second-largest mobile operator in its country. Revenue has fallen 6% in a year, from about $2.12B to $1.99B, while costs are flat. The CEO wants to know what's going on and what to do.

clarify.a: Postpaid (monthly contracts) and prepaid (pay-as-you-go). No big enterprise or fixed-line business.
Market revenue is flat overall, so Vertex is losing share.
A competitor launched 'Zap', a digital-only prepaid brand: unlimited data for $15/month, sold only via an app.

structure.root: Why is revenue down ~$127M?

hypothesis: The new $15 digital brand is the obvious suspect. I'd expect the loss to be in prepaid, among young, data-heavy users.

questions.q: Here's revenue by stream. Where is the drop?
questions.answer: Postpaid is flat. All of the drop is prepaid (−$127M, −18%): subscribers −14% (5.0M → 4.3M) and revenue per user −4%. Losing customers matters about three times more than lower revenue per user.

questions.q: Which prepaid customers are leaving?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 2 · Prepaid churn (% of customers leaving per month) by age

questions.answer: Churn among 18-25s jumped from 3% to 8% a month; other ages barely moved. Young, digital, data-hungry users are leaving, almost certainly for Zap. So-what: this is a targeted competitive attack, not a general problem with Vertex.

questions.q: Vertex could launch its own digital brand at $15. It expects to win back 400,000 subscribers, but ~2% of its 3.3M postpaid customers (paying $35/month) might switch down to it. Net effect?
questions.answer:
Gain = 400k × $15 × 12 = +$72M/year. Loss = 2% × 3.3M = 66k × ($35 − $15) × 12 ≈ −$16M/year.

Net ≈ +$56M/year, recovering ~45% of the lost revenue. A digital brand is also cheaper to run (no shops).

reco: Vertex's revenue drop is entirely in prepaid, driven by 18-25 year-olds leaving for a competitor's $15 digital brand. I recommend launching Vertex's own digital-only brand at a similar price. It recovers ~$56M a year net of postpaid customers switching down. Keep it clearly separate from postpaid (app-only, no handset deals) to limit switching. Next steps: a 3-month launch plan, and a retention offer for young prepaid users whose contracts are ending.
great: Isolates the stream before diagnosing
Splits subscribers vs revenue per user
Includes postpaid customers switching down in the maths

title: RideNow Drivers
sub: Design a feature to keep ride-hailing drivers on the platform
skills: Two-sided platforms · user segmentation · prioritisation · metrics
prompt: You're a product manager at RideNow, a ride-hailing app. Many new drivers quit within their first 90 days, which forces RideNow to keep spending on recruiting. Design a product feature to improve driver retention.

clarify.a: About 50% of new drivers stop driving within 90 days.
Your choice. Pick one and say why.
Must be live in one quarter. Can't simply raise pay across the board.

structure.root: A feature to keep new drivers

branches.head: Goal & users
items: Segments: full-time, part-time, students, new arrivals

hypothesis: New part-time drivers quit because they can't predict what they'll earn. A feature that shows them when and where to drive will have the biggest impact.

questions.q: Which driver segment would you focus on, and why?
questions.answer: New part-time drivers (drive <20 hours/week). They're the biggest group of quitters and the most flexible about when they drive. Full-timers already learn the patterns. Remember that RideNow is a two-sided platform: riders benefit too when more drivers stay at peak times.

questions.q: List the pain points and pick a solution.
questions.answer:
Pain pointSolutionImpact / effort
Don't know when to drive to earn wellWeekly 'earnings planner' showing best hours and expected $/hourHigh / Medium
Long empty time between ridesLive demand heatmapMedium / Low
One bad rating early hurts a lotRating protection for the first 20 tripsMedium / Low
No one to askMentor matching with experienced driversMedium / High

Pick: the earnings planner. It goes straight at the main reason people quit (uncertain earnings) and can be built from data RideNow already has.

questions.q: How would you measure success?
questions.answer:
• North star: % of new drivers still active at day 90
  • Inputs: % of new drivers using the planner weekly; hours driven in planned peak slots; earnings per hour in weeks 1-4
  • Guardrails: rider waiting times (if all drivers chase the same peaks, other times suffer); earnings of existing drivers

reco: Build a weekly earnings planner for new part-time drivers: it shows the best hours and areas to drive, with expected earnings per hour. It tackles the main reason drivers quit, unpredictable earnings, and uses data RideNow already has. Measure success by 90-day driver retention, with rider waiting times as a guardrail. Launch to half of new drivers in one city as an A/B test, then expand.
great: Lays out the plan of the answer up front
Segments drivers and picks one group with a reason
Remembers the platform has two sides
Gives a north star, inputs and a guardrail, not a list of ten metrics

title: LinguaLeap
sub: Weekly users of a language app fell 8%. Why?
skills: Root cause · segmenting before guessing
prompt: You're a product manager at LinguaLeap, a language-learning app. This morning the dashboard shows weekly active users (WAU) down 8% compared with last week. Your boss asks you to find out why.

clarify.a: Users who complete at least one lesson in 7 days. Definition unchanged.
Sudden: WAU was stable for months, then dropped over 4-5 days.
No holiday this week; last year the same week was flat.

structure.root: Why did WAU fall 8%?

hypothesis: A sudden drop with no season to explain it usually means something we changed. I'd segment by platform and check recent releases first.

questions.q: Here's WAU by platform. What's going on?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · WAU index by platform (Week −4 = 100)
exhibit.note: Android app version 5.2 was released at the start of this week. Android = ~45% of users. Index values: iOS stays at 100–101; Android is 99–100 until this week, then 82.

questions.answer: iOS is flat. Android fell ~18% (45% of users × 18% ≈ 8% overall ✓). It started the same week as Android release 5.2. So-what: almost certainly caused by the release, not by users or competitors.

questions.q: What would you check next?
questions.answer:
• Crash rate and app-start success on 5.2
  • Push notification delivery: lesson reminders bring back many users; a change in permissions could silently stop them
  • Funnel: open app → start lesson → finish lesson, to see where Android users drop

Interviewer reveals: reminder notifications delivered on Android fell from 92% to 15% after 5.2, because a new permission prompt is declined by most users.

questions.q: What do you do now?
questions.answer:
• Now: hotfix that asks for the permission at a better moment, with a clear explanation (e.g. after the user's first lesson streak)
  • Recover: email/in-app message to affected users to switch reminders back on
  • Prevent: add 'notifications delivered' to release checklists and alerts

reco: The 8% drop is an Android problem caused by release 5.2: a new notification permission is being declined, so reminders no longer reach most users and fewer come back for lessons. Ship a hotfix that asks for the permission at a better moment, win back affected users by email, and add notification delivery to the release checklist so it can't happen silently again.
great: Checks data and definitions first
Segments before guessing
Confirms the size (45% × 18% ≈ 8%)
Fixes now and prevents it happening again

title: Northline Air
sub: Why did a profitable regional airline start losing money?
skills: Route economics · load factor · break-even
prompt: Our client, Northline Air, is a regional airline flying 180-seat jets between Norwegian cities. Two years ago it made a healthy profit. Last year it lost money for the first time, even though passenger numbers rose. The CEO wants to know why, and what to do.

clarify.a: Eighteen months ago Northline opened two new routes in the north: Bergen–Tromsø and Stavanger–Bodø.
One aircraft type, 180 seats, all leased. No new aircraft were added; the new routes use spare capacity.
A larger rival also flies Bergen–Tromsø, three times a day. Competitors' margins on the old routes are stable.
Return to profit next year.

structure.root: Why has Northline gone from profit to loss?

branches.head: Cost by route
items: Cost per flight: fuel, crew, airport fees, leasing
Longer northern sectors cost more per flight

hypothesis: Passenger numbers grew, so volume isn't the problem. I suspect the two new routes: they're longer (higher cost per flight) and face a strong competitor, so they may be flying half empty.

questions.q: Here is profit by route last year. What's going on?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Profit by route, last year
exhibit.note: All aircraft have 180 seats. Revenue = flights × 180 × load factor × fare.

questions.answer:
The three original routes earn $26.4M together, comfortably covering the $8M of overheads. The two new routes lose $22.5M, which turns the airline into a loss of $4.1M.

The cause is the load factor: about 50% on the new routes against ~80% on the old ones, while each new flight costs about 52% more (longer sectors). Higher fares don't make up for it.

So-what: the core business is healthy. This is a new-route problem, so the next question is whether those routes can ever break even.
questions.note: Strong candidates check one revenue figure: 4,200 × 180 × 82% × $110 ≈ $68M.

questions.q: What load factor would Bergen–Tromsø need to break even at today's fare and cost?
questions.answer:
Break-even passengers per flight = cost per flight ÷ fare = $21,000 ÷ $140 = 150 passengers.

Out of 180 seats that is a load factor of 83%. Today it flies about 94 passengers (52%).

So-what: the route needs ~56 more passengers on every flight, a 60% increase in demand. With a rival flying the same route three times a day, that is very unlikely through marketing alone.

Careful: this is the full-cost break-even. To decide whether to close the route, compare revenue per flight (about $13,104) with the costs that would disappear (fuel, crew, airport fees), not the aircraft leases, which Northline pays anyway unless the aircraft can be used or sub-leased elsewhere.

questions.q: What options does Northline have for the two new routes?
questions.answer:
Fix the economics

  • Cut frequency (e.g. from about two return flights a day to one) so each flight fills up
  • Raise fares only if demand is business-heavy and price-insensitive (unlikely against a rival)
  • Codeshare with the rival to share passengers

Redeploy the aircraft

  • Add frequencies on the profitable core routes if they are full at peak times
  • Charter or lease out the spare aircraft in the summer

Exit

  • Close a route only if its revenue doesn't cover the costs that would disappear, or its aircraft can earn more elsewhere; check first whether the government subsidises any northern routes

reco: Northline is losing money because its two new northern routes fly about half empty while costing ~52% more per flight; they lose $22.5M, turning a healthy core network into a $4.1M loss. Bergen–Tromsø would need to fill 83% of its seats to break even, against 52% today. I recommend cutting frequency on both routes now, exploring a codeshare or a route subsidy, and closing any route that still doesn't cover its avoidable costs (fuel, crew, airport fees) after one season, unless its aircraft can be sub-leased or redeployed more profitably. Move the spare aircraft to peak times on the core routes. Risk: leaving the north may weaken the brand there. Next step: check peak-hour demand on the core routes.
great: Splits the network into old vs new routes straight away
Turns break-even into a load factor, not just a number of passengers
Sees that a rival flying three times a day makes this demand jump unrealistic
Recommends frequency cuts before full exit

title: Kettle & Crumb
sub: A bakery chain added products and lost profit
skills: Complexity cost · waste · product rationalisation
prompt: Kettle & Crumb runs 140 bakery cafés across England. Over two years sales grew a little, but operating profit almost halved, from $7.4M to $3.9M. The founder wants to understand why and fix it.

clarify.a: It more than doubled its range, from 40 products to 90, to give customers more choice.
Everything is baked fresh each morning in the café. Unsold items are thrown away at closing.
Prices rose in line with inflation, and so did wages. Neither explains the drop.
Back to at least $6M operating profit next year.

structure.root: Why has profit fallen by $3.5M?

hypothesis: The range more than doubled while sales barely moved. More products with the same demand means smaller, less predictable batches, so I expect waste is rising.

questions.q: Here is the trend. What stands out?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Kettle & Crumb, three-year view
exhibit.note: Ingredients cost about 30% of the sales value of a product.

questions.answer:
Sales are up only 5% while the range is up 125%. Waste has gone from 6% to 13% of sales. At ingredient cost (30% of sales value), the cost of waste rose from $1.12M to $2.54M: about $1.42M of the $3.5M fall.

The rest probably comes from the same cause: more staff hours to bake 90 products in small batches.

So-what: the extra products add cost but not sales. Let's see which products are wasted most.

questions.q: Here is the 2025 range split into three tiers. Bakers spend about one hour a day per café on the bottom 30 products (staff cost $13 an hour, 140 cafés, open 360 days a year). What happens if we remove the bottom 30?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 2 · Range by tier, 2025
exhibit.note: Overall waste: about 13% of sales value.

questions.answer:
The bottom 30 products bring only $3.25M of sales (5%) but waste worth 42% of their sales (about 30% of what's baked is thrown away).

Assume 80% of their customers buy another product instead:

  • Lost sales: 20% × $3.25M = $0.65M, losing 70% gross margin = −$0.45M
  • Waste saved: 42% × $3.25M = $1.37M of sales value, which costs 30% to make = +$0.41M
  • Baking time saved: 140 × 360 × $13 × 1 hour = +$0.66M

Net: about +$0.61M a year. On ingredients alone it's roughly neutral (−$0.05M); the gain is in labour.

So-what: the range cut is worth doing, but mainly because it simplifies the morning bake, not because of waste. The 80% switching assumption matters a lot: test it.
questions.note: The trap is to count the full sales of the bottom 30 as profit saved, or to forget that most of their customers will buy something else.

questions.q: What else would you do besides cutting the range?
questions.answer:
• Bake to demand: use till data to set batch sizes per café and day of week
  • Bake twice a day for best-sellers, so the morning batch can be smaller
  • Sell before waste: half-price after 4pm or an app for surplus food
  • Rotate seasonal products instead of keeping all of them all year
  • Check labour: staff hours per café before and after the range grew

reco: Kettle & Crumb's profit fell because the range grew from 40 to 90 products without adding sales, pushing waste from 6% to 13% of sales and adding baking hours. I recommend cutting the bottom 30 products, which make 5% of sales but waste product worth 42% of their sales value, worth about $0.6M a year mostly through baking time saved, and baking to demand using till data. Risk: some loyal customers lose a favourite, so keep a short seasonal slot. The range cut closes only part of the $2.1M gap to the $6M target; bringing waste back towards its old 6% would add about $1.4M at ingredient cost, so baking to demand is the bigger lever. Next step: pilot the shorter range in 15 cafés for six weeks.
great: Links the range growth to waste before seeing the data
Values waste at ingredient cost, not sales value
Accounts for customers who switch to another product
Points to labour as the bigger hidden cost

title: PrintWell
sub: A printer maker's ink profits are disappearing
skills: Razor-and-blade model · lifetime value · subscription maths
prompt: PrintWell makes home printers sold across Europe. Its operating profit has fallen from $546M to $366M in three years even though it sells as many printers as before. The CEO wants to know why and how to stop the decline.

clarify.a: Printers are sold below cost. Profit comes from ink cartridges, which customers buy over the life of the printer.
Cheaper third-party cartridges that fit PrintWell printers are now sold widely online.
About 10 million PrintWell printers are in use; each lasts about five years.
Stop the decline and find a model that holds up against third-party ink.

structure.root: Why is profit falling while printer sales are flat?

hypothesis: Profit lives in ink. If printer sales are flat, the likely cause is PrintWell selling fewer cartridges per printer: third-party ink taking share.

questions.q: Use this data to explain the profit fall.
questions.answer:
Ink profit = printers in use × cartridges per printer × PrintWell's share × margin.

  • Then: 10M × 4 × 80% × $18 = $576M
  • Now: 10M × 4 × 55% × $18 = $396M

Hardware loses the same $30M a year in both periods. So profit fell from $546M to $366M, a drop of $180M, all from share of cartridges.

So-what: the business model depends on owning the ink. It has lost 25 percentage points of cartridge share (80% → 55%), almost a third of its share, to cheaper copies.

questions.q: What is a customer worth over the life of a printer, then and now?
questions.answer:
Lifetime value = −$15 on the printer + 5 years × 4 cartridges × share × $18.

  • Then: −15 + 20 × 80% × 18 = $273
  • Now: −15 + 20 × 55% × 18 = $183

So-what: each customer is worth about a third less. The printer is still worth subsidising, but the ink needs protecting.

questions.q: PrintWell is considering an ink subscription: $6 a month, cartridges delivered automatically. Each cartridge costs PrintWell $7 to make and ship. A typical home uses 4 a year. Is it attractive?
questions.answer:
Per subscriber per year: revenue $72, cost 4 × $7 = $28, so margin $44.

A typical non-subscriber today gives PrintWell 4 × 55% × $18 = $39.6 a year.

So a subscriber is worth about $4.4 more a year than the average customer today, even though PrintWell earns less per cartridge, because a subscriber buys all of their ink from PrintWell, not 55% of it.

But the average hides a split. A home that already buys only PrintWell ink earns it 4 × $18 = $72 a year, and would be worth $28 less on the subscription. The subscription only adds value for homes buying less than $44 ÷ $72 ≈ 61% of their ink from PrintWell.

So-what: worth launching, but aimed at new printer buyers and customers who have drifted to third-party ink, not loyal buyers. Track take-up by segment, and use page limits per plan so heavy users don't make the flat fee unprofitable.

reco: PrintWell's profit fell $180M because its share of ink cartridges dropped from 80% to 55% as third-party ink spread; printers still sell, but each customer is now worth about $183 instead of $273. I recommend launching an ink subscription with page-based plans, which earns ~$44 a year per home (vs $39.6 for the average customer today) and locks in the ink. Bundle it with new printers and target homes that have drifted to third-party ink: it only adds value for homes buying less than about 61% of their ink from PrintWell. Risk: heavy users could make a flat fee unprofitable, so tie plans to pages printed. Next step: pilot in one country with new printer buyers.
great: Writes ink profit as a formula before calculating
Sees the printer loss as an investment in a customer
Spots that loyal buyers would be worth less on the subscription
Flags heavy users as the risk in a flat fee

title: Sunrise Mobile
sub: More subscribers, less money: a mobile operator's shrinking revenue
skills: ARPU · revenue mix · bundling
prompt: Sunrise Mobile is Kenya's third-largest mobile network. It added subscribers every year, yet revenue has fallen two years in a row. The board wants to know why and how to grow revenue again.

clarify.a: Mostly prepaid customers who top up small amounts. 12.6 million subscribers today.
Sunrise matched a rival's price cut on calls two years ago. Data prices are unchanged.
Across Kenya, people are switching from calls to messaging and video calls on apps, which use data.
Grow revenue by at least 5% a year.

structure.root: Why is revenue falling while subscribers grow?

branches.head: Market
items: Shift from calls to apps (over data)

hypothesis: Subscribers are up, so revenue per subscriber must be falling. With calls moving to apps and a price cut on calls, voice ARPU is my first suspect.

questions.q: Here is revenue per subscriber per month (ARPU) broken down. What's happening?
questions.answer:
Total revenue = subscribers × ARPU × 12: $605M → $514M, down 15%.

ARPU fell $0.80 a month. Voice fell $0.80, other fell $0.15, and data grew only $0.15. Customers are moving calls onto apps, and the price cut made the remaining calls cheaper.

So-what: data is where usage is going, but Sunrise isn't capturing it: data ARPU grew just 10% while voice shrank 38%.

questions.q: Why might data revenue be growing so slowly when data usage is rising fast?
questions.answer:
• Price per GB falling as customers buy larger, cheaper bundles
  • Free Wi-Fi at home, work and malls handles much of the app traffic
  • Network quality: if Sunrise's 4G is weaker than rivals', heavy data users keep a second SIM for data
  • No bundles: rivals sell daily bundles of calls, data and social media; Sunrise sells them separately

Good next question: what share of Sunrise customers carry a rival's SIM for data?

questions.q: Sunrise could launch a daily bundle. Research suggests 25% of subscribers would take it, adding $1.20 a month each after cannibalisation, at a cost of $0.30 a month each. What's the annual impact?
questions.answer:
Buyers: 25% × 12.6M = 3.15M. Net gain each: $1.20 − $0.30 = $0.90 a month.

Annual: 3.15M × $0.90 × 12 = $34M, about 6.6% of today's revenue.

So-what: it adds 6.6% of today's revenue, but revenue is falling about 9% a year ($565M → $514M), so the bundle alone would slow the decline rather than deliver 5% growth. To reach +5%, Sunrise also has to stop the voice decline and win back data-SIM users through network investment.

reco: Sunrise's revenue is falling because voice revenue per customer dropped 38% as calls moved to apps and prices were cut, while data revenue barely grew. I recommend launching daily bundles of data and social media, worth about $34M a year (6.6% of revenue, not enough on its own to offset the ~9% yearly decline), and investing in 4G where customers carry a rival's SIM for data. Stop competing on voice price. Risk: rivals cut bundle prices in response. Next step: test bundle prices in two regions.
great: Recognises ARPU, not subscribers, as the driver
Separates voice, data and other
Explains why data revenue lags data usage
Sizes the bundle and compares it with the target

title: Maple Cinemas
sub: Fewer visitors and smaller snack spend at a cinema chain
skills: Fixed-cost leverage · per-visitor economics · payback
prompt: Maple Cinemas runs 300 screens across Canada. Two years ago it made $29M of operating profit; this year it expects a loss of about $24M. The CEO wants to understand what happened and how to get back to profit.

clarify.a: Ticket revenue is shared with film studios (Maple keeps 45%). Food and drink (concessions) have an 80% margin and Maple keeps all of it.
Ticket prices are flat at about $13. Snack prices rose slightly.
Cinema attendance across Canada is down ~15%. Streaming windows are shorter.
Return to at least $20M operating profit.

structure.root: Why has profit gone from $29M to a loss?

hypothesis: A cinema is mostly fixed cost, so a fall in visitors hits profit hard. Concessions carry a far higher margin rate than tickets, so I'd also check spend per visitor.

questions.q: Calculate operating profit two years ago and today.
questions.answer:
Profit = visitors × (ticket × 45% + snack spend × 80%) − fixed costs.

  • Two years ago: 16M × (13 × 0.45 + 6.5 × 0.8) − 148 = 16 × (5.85 + 5.20) − 148 = $29M
  • Today: 13M × (5.85 + 4.00) − 152 = −$24M

Two things: 3M fewer visitors (−19%), and each visitor spends $1.50 less on snacks, which cuts margin per head by $1.20.

So-what: lost visitors cost about $33M (3M × $11.05 of margin each), lower snack spend about $16M (13M × $1.20), and fixed costs rose $4M: about $53M of swing in total. Concessions carry a much higher margin rate (80% vs 45%), so each dollar of snack spend lost hurts profit almost twice as much as a dollar of ticket revenue. Spend per head dropped 23%, and that is partly within Maple's control.

questions.q: Why might snack spend per visitor have fallen?
questions.answer:
• Price rises pushed customers past a threshold ($10 for a popcorn and drink)
  • Long queues at peak times, so people skip the counter
  • Mix shift: fewer family films and more adult dramas
  • Customers bringing their own snacks

Quick fixes: order-ahead in the app, combo pricing below a round number, self-service drinks.

questions.q: Maple could convert 40 screens to premium (reclining seats, better sound) for $1.2M each. Premium tickets cost $6 more, Maple keeps all of the premium, and attendance on those screens rises 15%. How long is the payback?
questions.answer:
Visitors per screen today: 13M ÷ 300 ≈ 43,333. On 40 screens: 1,733,333 visitors, plus 15% = 260,000 extra.

  • Premium fee: 1,993,333 × $6 = $11.96M
  • Extra visitors' tickets: 260,000 × 13 × 45% = $1.52M
  • Extra visitors' snacks: 260,000 × 5 × 80% = $1.04M

Total: $14.5M a year on a $48M investment: payback in 3.3 years.

So-what: attractive. Premium screens also cut seats, so check they don't sell out on weekends. And check how much of the extra 15% comes from Maple's own standard screens: if all of it did, the gain would be the premium fee alone (about $12.0M) and payback about 4.0 years.

reco: Maple slipped to a loss because visitors fell 19% with the market and snack spend per visitor fell 23%, and with mostly fixed costs that wiped out profit. I recommend (1) fixing concessions with app ordering and combo pricing, and (2) converting 40 screens to premium, which pays back in about 3.3 years and adds $14.5M a year. Risk: premium screens have fewer seats, so blockbuster weekends could sell out. Next step: pilot premium in five busy sites.
great: Builds profit per visitor before totals
Spots that concessions earn a far higher margin per dollar than tickets
Counts extra visitors' snack spend in the premium payback
Flags lost seats on premium screens

title: Brookhollow Water
sub: A bottled-water company sells more but earns less
skills: Route economics · cost to serve · incentives
prompt: Brookhollow Water sells bottled water in Mexico through small corner shops (tienditas). Over two years it grew from 9,000 to 15,000 shops, but sales volume barely moved and profit fell. The CEO asks why.

clarify.a: Its own trucks visit each shop once a week. A truck and crew cost about $300 a day.
The sales team is paid a bonus for each new shop signed.
Unchanged. Gross margin before delivery is about $0.70 a case.
Restore profit without losing volume.

structure.root: Why is profit falling as distribution grows?

hypothesis: Volume is flat but there are two-thirds more shops, so each delivery must be much smaller. Delivery cost per case is probably the problem.

questions.q: Use this data to compare delivery cost per case two years ago and now.

rows: Truck and crew cost per day ($)
exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Distribution data

questions.answer:
Cases per shop per week: then 40M ÷ 9,000 ÷ 52 ≈ 85.5; now 41M ÷ 15,000 ÷ 52 ≈ 52.6.

Cost per stop: then $300 ÷ 25 = $12.00; now $300 ÷ 22 ≈ $13.64 (shops are more spread out).

Cost per case: then $12.00 ÷ 85.5 ≈ $0.14; now $13.64 ÷ 52.6 ≈ $0.26.

So-what: delivery cost per case is up 85%. The new shops each buy very little, so every truck stop moves fewer cases.

questions.q: Analysis shows about 6,000 of the shops buy only 8 cases a week, and a truck can only reach 20 of them a day. Are they profitable?
questions.answer:
Cost per stop: $300 ÷ 20 = $15. Per case: $15 ÷ 8 = $1.88.

Gross margin before delivery is $0.70 a case, so each case to these shops loses $1.18.

So-what: the sales bonus rewards adding shops that cost more to serve than they earn.

questions.q: What should Brookhollow Water do?
questions.answer:
• Visit small shops every two weeks with bigger drops (check they have storage space)
  • Use distributors or shared delivery for low-volume areas
  • Minimum order per delivery, or a delivery fee below it
  • Change the sales bonus from shops signed to profitable volume
  • Re-plan routes to cluster stops

reco: Brookhollow Water's profit fell because it spread the same volume across two-thirds more shops: delivery cost per case rose 85%, and 6,000 small shops lose about $1.18 on every case. I recommend moving those shops to fortnightly delivery or a distributor, setting a minimum order, and paying the sales team on profitable volume rather than new shops. Risk: some small shops switch to a rival brand. Next step: re-route one region with fortnightly visits for two months.
great: Converts the data to cases per stop
Finds that the new shops lose money on every case
Links the problem to the sales incentive
Proposes cheaper service, not just dropping shops

title: Lumen Bank
sub: A digital bank grows fast but its losses grow faster
skills: Lifetime value · acquisition cost · churn
prompt: Lumen is a UK app-only bank. It signed up 320,000 new customers last year, 60% more than the year before, but its losses doubled. Investors want a path to profit within two years.

clarify.a: Interest margin on deposits plus card fees: about $45 a year from an average active customer.
Advertising, comparison-site fees, and recently a $100 bonus for switching your salary account.
Customers who stop using the account, measured as annual churn.
Mostly fixed (technology, compliance). Assume flat.

structure.root: Why are losses growing as Lumen grows?

branches.head: Cost to acquire
items: Cost per new customer by channel

hypothesis: If fixed costs are flat, losses grow only if each new customer costs more than they're worth. I'd compare acquisition cost with lifetime value by channel.

questions.q: Compare last year with the year before. What's happening to customer economics?

rows: Margin per active customer per year ($)
exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Customer acquisition

questions.answer:
Lifetime value ≈ annual margin ÷ churn (ignoring discounting).

  • Year before: $45 ÷ 15% = $300 vs acquisition cost $60: ratio 5.0×
  • Last year: $45 ÷ 29% = $155 vs acquisition cost $140: ratio 1.1×

Marketing spend rose from $12.0M to $44.8M.

So-what: new customers now cost about as much as they will ever earn. Growth is no longer creating value.

questions.q: Here is last year's split by channel. What do you see?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 2 · Acquisition by channel, last year

questions.answer:
Lifetime value ÷ acquisition cost by channel:

  • Organic & referral: $375 on $40: 9.4×
  • Comparison sites: $180 on $160: 1.1×
  • Switching bonus: $82 on $250: 0.33×, losing money on every customer

The switching bonus attracts people who take the $100 and leave: 55% churn.

So-what: one channel drives most of the loss. Cut it and lean on referrals.
questions.note: Blended cost per customer checks out: (120×40 + 110×160 + 90×250) ÷ 320 ≈ $140.

questions.q: How could Lumen lower churn, so each customer is worth more?
questions.answer:
• Pay the bonus in stages: $25 a month for four months while the salary keeps arriving
  • Make it the main account: bill-splitting, savings pots, salary-day features
  • Onboarding nudges in the first 30 days, when most churn happens
  • Referral rewards for both sides (the cheapest, stickiest channel)

reco: Lumen's losses doubled because it bought growth with a $100 switching bonus that brings customers worth about $82 for $250 each; overall, a new customer now costs about what they earn over their life. I recommend stopping the upfront bonus (pay it in instalments tied to salary deposits), doubling down on referrals, and capping comparison-site spend at a 2× value-to-cost ratio. Growth will slow, but every customer added will make money. Risk: slower growth may disappoint investors. Next step: test the staged bonus on half of new sign-ups.
great: Uses lifetime value vs acquisition cost, not just totals
Breaks results down by channel
Explains why the bonus brings high churn
Accepts slower growth in exchange for profitable growth

title: Meadowlane Grocers
sub: Sales are up, profit has halved. Why?
skills: Profit bridge · price vs volume vs cost
prompt: Meadowlane is a family-owned grocer with three large stores in Yorkshire. Sales rose 3% this year to $47.8M, but operating profit fell by half, from $5.4M to $2.7M. The owners want to know what happened and what to do about it.

clarify.q: What do we mean by profit?
clarify.a: Operating profit: sales minus cost of goods, minus store costs (staff, rent, energy).

clarify.q: Has anything changed in the market?
clarify.a: A discount supermarket opened two miles from the largest store last spring.
Yes. Suppliers raised prices sharply, especially for fresh food, and Meadowlane passed the increases on.
Get back to last year's profit within two years.

structure.root: Why did profit halve while sales grew?

branches.head: Revenue
items: By store: is it the store near the discounter?

hypothesis: Sales grew because prices rose, not because more people shopped. I suspect two things: fewer baskets after the discounter opened, and higher store costs such as wages and energy.

questions.q: Here are Meadowlane's numbers for the last two years. Build a profit bridge: how much did each driver add or take away?
questions.answer:
Profit per basket is spend minus cost of goods: $9 last year, $9 this year. Unchanged.

  • Price: +$2 × 1.99M baskets = +$3.98M
  • Cost of goods: −$2 × 1.99M = −$3.98M (the two cancel out: supplier inflation was passed on in full)
  • Volume: −0.11M baskets × $9 = −$0.99M
  • Fixed costs: $13.5M → $15.2M = −$1.70M

Total: −$2.69M, matching the fall from $5.4M to $2.7M.

So-what: the supplier inflation everyone talks about is not the problem; it went straight into prices. Profit fell because store costs rose $1.7M and Meadowlane lost 110k baskets (−5%).
questions.note: Many candidates stop at 'costs went up'. Push for the bridge: it shows that cost of goods is a red herring.

questions.q: Here is what drove the rise in store costs; the wage rise follows the higher legal minimum wage. Could winning back baskets alone restore last year's profit?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 2 · Increase in store costs this year ($M)

questions.answer:
Wages ($0.95M) and energy ($0.50M) explain 85% of the increase. The wage rise is driven by the legal minimum wage, so it won't reverse.

To earn $5.4M again at today's $9 per basket and $15.2M of store costs, Meadowlane needs ($5.4M + $15.2M) ÷ $9 = 2.29M baskets, 15% more than today and more than it ever had.

So-what: volume alone won't fix this. Meadowlane needs to win back some baskets and run its stores more efficiently.

questions.q: What would you recommend to the owners?
questions.answer:
Win back shoppers near the discounter

  • Price-match 100 everyday staples; keep margin on fresh, local and deli
  • A loyalty scheme so Meadowlane knows who has stopped coming

Lower store costs

  • Self-checkouts and staff rotas matched to footfall by hour
  • Energy: LED lighting and doors on fridges (often a 1 to 2 year payback)

Find out first: is the basket loss all at the store near the discounter? If so, it's a local problem, not a brand problem.

reco: Profit halved because store costs rose $1.7M (mostly wages and energy) and Meadowlane lost 5% of its baskets after a discounter opened; supplier inflation was passed on in full, so it isn't the cause. Volume alone can't fix it: getting back to $5.4M would need 15% more baskets. I recommend price-matching everyday staples at the affected store, plus self-checkouts, footfall-based rotas and an energy programme. Risk: price-matching erodes margin if it spreads beyond staples. Next step: check basket trends store by store.
great: Builds a bridge instead of listing causes
Notices price and cost of goods cancel out
Turns 'win back volume' into a number and sees it isn't enough
Asks whether the loss is local to one store

title: Selva Ceramics
sub: A busy tile factory with collapsing margins
skills: Complexity cost · changeovers · cost to serve
prompt: Selva Ceramics makes porcelain floor and wall tiles in Castellón, Spain. It sold a record 8.4 million m² this year (8.0M the year before) and the factory has never been busier, yet operating profit fell from $5.2M to $1.26M. The CEO asks you to find out why.

clarify.a: Flat at about $7.00 per m² at the factory gate.
The gas price Selva pays fell slightly last year.
Selva started accepting small custom orders from architects and designers: special colours and sizes.
Restore profit to at least $4M without losing the design customers.

structure.root: Why did profit fall when volume grew?

hypothesis: Price is flat and volume is up, so cost per m² must have risen. With gas prices falling, I'd look at how much energy each m² uses, which depends on how the kilns are run.

questions.q: Here is cost per m² by component. Where did profit go?
questions.answer:
Profit per m² fell from $2.90 to $2.40. Bridge:

  • Volume: +0.4M m² × $2.90 = +$1.16M
  • Variable cost: −$0.50 × 8.4M = −$4.20M
  • Fixed costs: −$0.90M

Kiln energy is +$0.45 of the $0.50 rise per m², 90% of it, even though gas got cheaper.

So-what: each m² now needs more energy. That points to how the kilns are used, not what energy costs.
questions.note: Volume: 8.0M m² last year, 8.4M m² this year. Fixed costs: $18.0M last year, $18.9M this year.

questions.q: Every time a kiln line changes colour or size it burns about $1,800 of gas heating up and running off rejects. Otherwise energy costs $1.15 per m². What does that tell you about average run length?
questions.answer:
Energy per m² = $1.15 + $1,800 ÷ run length.

  • Last year: $1.30 → $1,800 ÷ run = $0.15 → run ≈ 12,000 m²
  • This year: $1.75 → $1,800 ÷ run = $0.60 → run ≈ 3,000 m²

So-what: average runs are four times shorter. The custom orders fill the factory with changeovers: busy, but not productive.

questions.q: Selva could set a minimum run of 6,000 m² and batch custom orders weekly. What is that worth? How would you keep design customers?
questions.answer:
New energy per m² = $1.15 + $1,800 ÷ 6,000 = $1.45, saving $0.30 per m²: about $2.52M a year, before any lost orders. Profit would rise to about $3.8M.

To keep designers:

  • Small-run surcharge priced at the changeover cost ($1,800 per run), so small orders pay their way
  • Weekly custom slot: collect orders and run them together
  • Stock a curated range of popular "custom" colours
questions.note: Strong candidates price the surcharge from the changeover cost rather than inventing a number.

reco: Profit fell from $5.2M to $1.26M because small custom orders cut average kiln runs from about 12,000 to 3,000 m², raising energy per m² by 35% even as gas got cheaper. I recommend a 6,000 m² minimum run with weekly batching of custom work, worth about $2.5M a year and lifting profit to about $3.8M, plus a small-run surcharge that covers the changeover cost and should close the rest of the gap to the $4M target. Risk: some designers go elsewhere, so offer a stocked custom range. Next step: re-plan two months of orders to confirm the run lengths are achievable.
great: Finds that energy use, not energy price, is the issue
Back-solves run length from the cost formula
Prices the surcharge from the true changeover cost
Keeps the design customers rather than dropping them

title: Harborline Ferries
sub: Passengers held up. Profit didn't.
skills: Mix effects · route profitability · one-offs vs recurring
prompt: Harborline runs passenger and car ferries between islands on Norway's west coast. Passenger numbers rose slightly last year, to 1.57 million, but the company went from an operating profit of $7.5M to a loss of $1.1M. The CEO wants to understand why before the board meeting next month.

clarify.a: Yes. Harborline launched a new commuter route last year to support its bid for a large regional contract next year.
Fares on the existing routes didn't change. The new route has low commuter fares.
Fuel prices rose. One older vessel also needed a major refit.
Back to profit next year, without damaging the contract bid.

structure.root: Why has Harborline gone from profit to loss?
