hypothesis: Passengers are up, so this is about price per passenger and cost. I'd split the existing routes from the new one, which probably carries few passengers at low fares.

questions.q: Here is the company-wide picture. What's happened?
questions.answer:
Average fare fell from $40.00 to $38.09 and cost per passenger rose from $23.00 to $25.07: margin per passenger fell 23%, from $17.00 to $13.02. Fixed costs also rose $3.5M.

Fares didn't change on existing routes, so the lower average must come from the new route's mix.

questions.q: Here is this year by route. The new route also added $1.5M of terminal and berth costs; the refit added $2M. Break down the swing.

exhibit.title: Exhibit 2 · This year by route group

questions.answer:
New route: 0.12M × ($15 − $38) − $1.5M = −$4.26M. Each passenger costs $38 to carry and pays $15: the ferry sails mostly empty outside rush hour.

Without the new route Harborline would still be at $3.2M, versus $7.5M last year. The rest of the fall:

  • Fuel on existing routes: +$1 × 1.45M = $1.45M
  • Refit: $2M (one-off, should not repeat)
  • 50k fewer passengers on existing routes × $17 = $0.85M

Check: $4.26M + 1.45M + 2.00M + 0.85M = $8.56M, the full swing from $7.50M to −$1.06M.

So-what: the new route is the biggest single problem. Next year, profit recovers about $2M as the refit drops out, but stays well below last year unless the new route's economics change.

questions.q: The CEO says the new route is strategic for next year's regional contract. What would you do?
questions.answer:
• Cut sailings to commuter peaks (two each way morning and evening): most of the cost is sailing empty at midday
  • Use the smallest vessel on the route to lower fuel and crew cost per sailing
  • Ask the region for a service payment as part of the contract bid: public commuter routes are often subsidised in Norway
  • Set a decision date: if the contract is lost, close the route
  • On existing routes: a fuel surcharge, and plan refits for the off-season

reco: Harborline swung from $7.5M profit to a $1.1M loss mainly because the new commuter route loses $4.3M a year: it carries few passengers at low fares. A one-off $2M refit and higher fuel costs explain most of the rest. I recommend cutting the new route to peak-hour sailings on a smaller vessel and making a service payment part of the regional contract bid, with a clear exit if the bid fails; add a fuel surcharge on existing routes. Risk: fewer sailings could weaken the bid, so agree the timetable with the region. Next step: model peak-only sailings with the operations team.
great: Notices fares didn't change on existing routes, so the drop must be mix
Separates one-off costs (refit) from recurring ones
Quantifies the new route on its own
Respects the strategic reason but sets an exit trigger

title: Northstar Pet Nutrition
sub: The CEO blames freight. Is she right?
skills: Hypothesis testing · mix vs inflation · pricing
prompt: Northstar makes dry dog and cat food sold in Canadian pet stores and supermarkets. Volume grew 9% last year, but operating profit fell from $16.0M to $9.6M. The CEO believes the cause is freight: trucking rates rose sharply. She has asked you to confirm it and recommend a fix.

clarify.a: Two recipe families: Classic and Premium (grain-free, higher meat content). Both sell at the same shelf price, about $18 a bag.
Premium was launched at the Classic price two years ago to win shelf space quickly.
Trucking rates rose about 10% last year.
Recover last year's profit within 18 months.

structure.root: What explains the $6.4M profit fall?

hypothesis: Freight is a real increase, but it's usually a small share of cost per bag. With two recipes at one price, I suspect a mix shift towards Premium, which costs more to make.

questions.q: Here is cost per bag. Test the CEO's freight theory.
questions.answer:
Cost per bag rose $1.54. Freight is only +$0.15 of that, worth $0.65M on 4.35M bags: 10% of the $6.40M gap.

Ingredients rose $1.14 a bag, worth $4.96M: 77% of the gap.

Full bridge: more bags +$2.80M, higher cost per bag −$6.70M, higher fixed costs −$2.50M: −$6.40M in total. Volume growth roughly offsets the fixed-cost rise, so cost per bag is the story.

So-what: freight is real but minor. Ingredients are the story. Let's see why they rose.
questions.note: Both years: price $18 per bag. Bags: 4.00M → 4.35M. Fixed costs: $16.0M → $18.5M.

questions.q: Here is ingredient cost by recipe and the recipe mix. Split the ingredient increase into inflation and mix.

rows: Ingredient cost per bag, last year ($)
Ingredient cost per bag, this year ($)
exhibit.title: Exhibit 2 · Ingredients by recipe

questions.answer:
Mix effect (more Premium at last year's costs): (35% − 20%) × ($9.00 − 5.50) = $0.525 a bag.

Inflation (each recipe got dearer): 65% × $0.30 + 35% × $1.20 = $0.615 a bag.

Total $1.14 ✓. Mix and inflation are roughly half each.

So-what: Premium is succeeding with shoppers, but it earns $4.40 less per bag than Classic because it's sold at the same price. Northstar is growing its least profitable product.

questions.q: If Northstar raised only the Premium price, how much more per bag would it need to recover the full gap? Is that realistic?
questions.answer:
Premium bags: 35% × 4.35M = 1.52M. Needed: $6.40M ÷ 1.52M = $4.20 a bag, about 23% on $18, assuming volume holds.

Probably too much in one go. Premium recipes usually sell at a clear premium to standard ones, so some increase is justified, but a 23% jump risks losing shelf space.

Better: a $2 to $3 increase on Premium (it's still a better product), plus ingredient sourcing contracts, plus cutting trade promotions that rose $0.15 a bag.

questions.q: What would you tell the CEO in her board meeting?
questions.answer: Answer first: freight explains only about 10% of the fall. The real issue is that Premium, now 35% of volume, is priced like Classic while costing $4.40 more in ingredients. Then: the pricing fix, sourcing, and a test of price elasticity in one region.

reco: Freight is not the main problem: it explains about 10% of the $6.4M profit fall. Most of the gap comes from ingredients, split between inflation and a shift to Premium, which sells at the Classic price but costs $4.40 more a bag to make. I recommend repricing Premium by $2 to $3 a bag, locking in ingredient contracts, and trimming trade promotions. Risk: retailers resist a price rise, so lead with the stronger recipe story. Next step: test the new Premium price in one province for eight weeks.
great: Tests the client's hypothesis with numbers instead of accepting it
Splits ingredients into mix and inflation
Spots the pricing decision behind the mix problem
Sizes the price fix and judges whether it's realistic

title: BrightStep Tutoring
sub: How big is the market for paid maths tutoring?
skills: Segmented market sizing · sanity checks
prompt: BrightStep is a start-up offering live online maths lessons in small groups for secondary school pupils in England. Its investors want to know how big the paid maths tutoring market is, and whether BrightStep's target of $10M revenue in three years is realistic.

clarify.a: Secondary pupils, years 7 to 11 (ages 11 to 16), in England.
Money families pay for maths tutoring, online or in person. Leave out school-funded tutoring for now.
$12 per 60-minute small-group lesson. One-to-one tutors typically charge around $35 an hour.
Yes: the interviewer has pupil numbers and survey data on who pays for tutoring.

structure.root: Annual spend on paid maths tutoring

branches.head: Who pays
items: Share whose families pay for maths tutoring

branches.head: BrightStep's slice
items: Families who'd choose small groups over one-to-one

hypothesis: I'd expect a market in the hundreds of millions of dollars: a few hundred thousand tutored pupils, paying weekly through the school year.

questions.q: Here is the interviewer's data. Estimate the annual market.

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Share of pupils whose families pay for maths tutoring, by household income (%)

questions.answer:
Average share paying for maths tutoring = average of the five income groups = (6% + 8% + 11% + 15% + 20%) ÷ 5 = 12% (each group is one fifth of pupils).

Tutored pupils: 3.6M × 12% = 432k.

Spend: 432k × 30 sessions × $35 = $454M a year.

So-what: a market of roughly $450M, heavily skewed to higher-income families, who are the most likely to buy one-to-one tutors.
questions.note: Pupils in years 7 to 11 in England: about 3.6M. Tutored pupils have about 30 sessions a year at around $35. All figures are case assumptions.

questions.q: How many students does BrightStep need to reach $10M, and what share of tutored pupils is that?
questions.answer:
Revenue per student: 30 lessons × $12 = $360 a year.

Students needed: $10M ÷ $360 ≈ 27.8k, which is 6.4% of today's 432k tutored pupils.

So-what: ambitious but plausible, and BrightStep's low price could also attract families who don't pay for tutoring today, especially in the lower-income groups where only 6% to 8% currently pay.

questions.q: What would make you more or less confident in the $10M target?
questions.answer:
• More confident: schools buying lessons for whole groups (one sale, many pupils); strong retention from autumn to exam season; a low cost to win each family
  • Less confident: most tutoring is bought just before exams (fewer than 30 sessions); one-to-one tutors cutting prices online; families seeing small groups as "not real tutoring"
  • Test: retention from September to May and the cost of winning each paying family

reco: Paid maths tutoring for secondary pupils in England is worth roughly $454M a year: about 432k pupils, 30 sessions each at around $35. BrightStep's $10M target needs about 27.8k students, 6.4% of today's tutored pupils, which is achievable if its $12 price brings in families who can't afford one-to-one tutors. I'd back the plan subject to two checks: retention through the school year, and the cost of acquiring each family. Next step: run a term-long pilot with two schools to measure both.
great: Uses the income split to get the average, not a guess
Keeps units clear: pupils, sessions, price
Compares the target with the size of the market
Sees the low price could expand the market

title: Fontaro Filters
sub: Sizing a water-filter subscription in Mexico City
skills: Market sizing · value to customer · adoption
prompt: Fontaro sells under-sink water filters on a subscription in Monterrey: $15 a month covers the unit, installation and replacement cartridges. It wants to launch in Mexico City and asks: how many households could realistically subscribe, and what revenue could that bring?

clarify.a: Very few. Most households buy 20-litre jugs of purified water (garrafones), delivered or from a shop.
Owners, or renters whose landlord allows it. The filter needs mains water pressure and a kitchen sink.
Start with higher- and middle-income households. Lower-income households are a later, cheaper product.
A market big enough to justify a Mexico City warehouse and installation team.

structure.root: How many Mexico City households could subscribe?

hypothesis: The pitch is savings versus buying jugs. If a household spends more on jugs than $15 a month, the market could be several hundred thousand households.

questions.q: Here is the interviewer's data on Mexico City households. How many households are in the target market?
questions.answer:
Target = higher- and middle-income households that can install:

  • Higher income: 6.0M × 15% × 80% = 720k
  • Middle income: 6.0M × 35% × 60% = 1,260k

Total: 1.98M households, about 33% of the metro area.

questions.q: A typical target household buys 3 jugs a week at $2.25. Is the subscription a good deal for them?
questions.answer:
Jugs: 3 × $2.25 × 52 = $351 a year. Subscription: $15 × 12 = $180.

The household saves about $171 a year (49%), and stops carrying heavy jugs.

So-what: a strong value proposition for jug-buying households. The barrier isn't price; it's trust in tap water and the hassle of installation.

questions.q: If 10% of target households subscribe within three years, what annual revenue is that? Would you go?
questions.answer:
Subscribers: 1.98M × 10% = 198k. Revenue: 198k × $180 = $36M a year.

Is 10% reasonable? The savings case is strong, but water quality fears are deep-rooted. I'd want proof from Monterrey: what share of target households subscribed after three years there?

Go, in stages: start in neighbourhoods with many owner-occupiers, offer free water-quality testing at installation to build trust, and partner with landlords of new apartment buildings.

reco: Mexico City has about 2.0M higher- and middle-income households that could install a filter. Each would save about $171 a year versus buying jugs, so the offer is strong. At 10% take-up, Fontaro would have about 198k subscribers and $36M of annual revenue. I recommend launching, starting in owner-occupied neighbourhoods with free water testing to overcome distrust of tap water. Risk: take-up could be far lower if trust doesn't shift. Next step: compare with Monterrey's three-year take-up by neighbourhood.
great: Segments by income and ability to install, not just population
Turns the value proposition into a number (savings per year)
Questions the take-up assumption and looks for evidence
Identifies trust, not price, as the barrier

title: CloudPatch Security
sub: Is there room for another SMB security product?
skills: Market sizing · channel economics · B2B buying
prompt: CloudPatch has built a tool that continuously scans a small business's systems for security weaknesses and tells staff what to fix, for $250 a month. It wants to raise money to sell across the US. The board asks: how big is the market today, and how should CloudPatch reach it?

clarify.a: US businesses with 10 to 249 employees. Smaller ones rarely pay for security tools; larger ones have their own security teams.

clarify.q: How do small businesses buy IT?
clarify.a: Many outsource IT to a managed service provider (MSP), which chooses and resells tools to them.
Several scanning tools exist; some are bundled into broader security packages.
Size today's market and choose a route to market.

structure.root: How big is the market, and how do we reach it?

branches.head: Route to market
items: Through MSPs: cost to acquire, margin, lifetime

hypothesis: Regulated firms are under pressure to prove they're secure, so I expect most of today's spending is there. And if most small firms buy through MSPs, the channel may matter more than the product.

questions.q: Here is the interviewer's data. Size the market today.

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · US firms with 10 to 249 employees: 1,100k
exhibit.note: Price: about $3,000 per firm per year. Case assumptions.

questions.answer:
• Regulated: 1.1M × 30% × 45% = 149k firms
  • Other: 1.1M × 70% × 12% = 92k firms

Buying firms: 241k. At $3,000 a year: $0.72bn.

Regulated firms are 30% of firms but 62% of buyers.

So-what: a market of about $0.7bn today; the 88% of "other" firms that don't buy yet are the bigger long-term opportunity.

questions.q: 60% of these firms buy security through an MSP. Compare the value of a customer won directly vs through an MSP.
questions.answer:
Value over a 4-year life = price × gross margin × 4 − cost to acquire.

  • Direct: $3,000 × 80% × 4 − $4,500 = $5,100
  • Through MSP: $3,000 × 55% × 4 − $1,200 = $5,400

Despite the lower margin, an MSP customer is worth $300 more, because it costs $3,300 less to win. And direct sales can only reach the 40% of firms (96k of today's buyers) that don't use an MSP, while each MSP brings dozens of client firms at once.

So-what: MSPs should be the main channel: better value per customer and access to 60% of the market.

questions.q: What would make MSPs choose CloudPatch over the tools they already resell?
questions.answer:
• Multi-client dashboard: one screen for all their clients, saving technician time
  • Compliance reports ready for regulated clients' auditors and insurers
  • Margin at least as good as competing tools, with volume tiers
  • Automation that fixes common issues, not just flags them

Test with 10 MSPs serving healthcare and finance clients before scaling.

questions.q: The CEO wants to sell direct to keep margin. How do you respond?
questions.answer: The margin is higher direct, but the customer is worth less once acquisition cost is counted ($5,100 vs $5,400), and direct sales can't reach 60% of buyers. A hybrid works best: MSPs for reach, and a small direct team only for larger regulated firms that buy security themselves.

reco: Today's market is about $0.72bn: 241k firms, mostly in regulated industries, paying about $3,000 a year. I recommend selling mainly through MSPs: a customer won that way is worth about $5,400 versus $5,100 direct, and MSPs reach the 60% of firms that buy through them. Lead with compliance reporting for regulated clients. Risk: MSPs already resell bundled tools, so CloudPatch needs a clear time-saving edge. Next step: sign 10 pilot MSPs in healthcare and finance.
great: Segments by regulation, which drives buying
Values customers by channel instead of comparing margins only
Sees that channel reach outweighs margin
Handles the CEO's push-back with numbers

title: Circlebox Reuse
sub: Reusable takeaway boxes: big market, but does the model work?
skills: Market sizing · unit economics · sensitivity
prompt: Circlebox rents reusable takeaway boxes to restaurants in Paris. Customers return boxes to drop points; Circlebox collects, washes and redistributes them, and charges restaurants $0.25 each time a box is used. Investors ask: how big is the opportunity in the Paris region, and can Circlebox make money on each box?

clarify.q: What do restaurants pay for disposable packaging?
clarify.a: About $0.12 per container.
Customer demand for less waste, and expected regulation on single-use packaging.
A box costs $3.00 and lasts about 100 washes. Collection and washing cost $0.08 per use.
They're lost. Today about 90% of boxes come back after each use.

structure.root: Is this a big and profitable opportunity?

branches.head: Market size
items: Takeaway and delivery orders in the region

branches.head: Unit economics per use
items: Box cost spread over its life

hypothesis: The market is probably large, but I'd focus on the return rate: if boxes don't come back, each one is only used a few times and its $3 cost isn't covered.

questions.q: Estimate container uses per year in the Paris region. Assume 12M people, 0.5 takeaway or delivery orders per person per week, 1.5 containers per order.
questions.answer:
12M × 0.5 × 52 × 1.5 = 468M container uses a year.

At $0.25 per use, that's a theoretical market of $117M. At just 2% share, Circlebox would earn $2.3M.

So-what: the market is big enough. The real question is whether each use makes money.

questions.q: Here is the cost per use at different return rates. What do you conclude?
questions.answer:
A box that comes back with probability r is used on average 1 ÷ (1 − r) times before it's lost (capped by its 100-wash life).

At today's 90% return rate a box is used only 10 times: $3.00 ÷ 10 = $0.30 per use, plus $0.08 washing = $0.38, against a $0.25 fee. Circlebox loses about $0.13 on every use.

Break-even: the box must last $3.00 ÷ ($0.25 − $0.08) = 17.6 uses, which needs a return rate of 94.3%.

So-what: growth makes losses bigger at today's return rate. Fix returns before scaling.
questions.note: This is the key insight in the case: a small change in return rate changes box life dramatically.

questions.q: How could Circlebox raise the return rate above 95%?
questions.answer:
• Deposit of $2 to $3 refunded on return (the strongest lever)
  • More drop points: metro stations, offices, partner shops
  • Delivery riders collect empty boxes on their next order
  • App reminders and small rewards for quick returns
  • Charge restaurants for boxes their customers don't return, so they promote returns too

reco: The Paris region uses about 468M takeaway containers a year, so the market is large. But at today's 90% return rate each box is used only 10 times and Circlebox loses about $0.13 per use; it needs a 94.3% return rate just to break even. I recommend pausing expansion and introducing a refundable deposit plus more drop points, then scaling only once returns pass 96% in pilot areas. Risk: a deposit may put some customers off. Next step: test a $2 deposit in two arrondissements.
great: Sizes the market quickly, then moves to unit economics
Derives box life from the return rate
Finds the break-even return rate
Recommends fixing the model before scaling

title: Juniper Coffee
sub: Should we open a coffee kiosk at a busy station?
skills: Capacity at peak · break-even · payback
prompt: Juniper Coffee runs 12 coffee kiosks in the north of England. It has been offered a kiosk on the main concourse of a busy commuter station. The fit-out would cost $120k. The CEO wants to know whether to sign, and what profit to expect.

clarify.q: How does the station charge rent?
clarify.a: A share of sales: 12% of revenue, with no fixed rent.
Mostly commuters: demand is very concentrated between 7am and 9am on weekdays.
Pay back the fit-out within two years.
Two baristas during the morning peak, one for the rest of the day.

structure.root: Is the kiosk worth opening?

branches.head: Revenue
items: Customers per day: peak vs rest of day

branches.head: Capacity
items: Drinks a barista can make per hour

hypothesis: A station kiosk lives or dies on the morning peak. I'd check whether the kiosk can serve everyone who wants coffee between 7 and 9, not just how many people pass by.

questions.q: Juniper estimates 300 customers would want coffee in the 7-9am peak and about 90 across the rest of the day. A barista makes about 45 drinks an hour. How many customers can the kiosk actually serve each day?
questions.answer:
Peak capacity: 2 baristas × 45 drinks × 2 hours = 180 drinks. Demand is 300, so 120 customers a day walk away (or never join the queue).

Daily sales: 180 + 90 = 270 customers.

So-what: the kiosk is limited by how fast it can make coffee at peak, not by how many people pass by.

questions.q: Average spend is $3.80; the kiosk trades 360 days a year. Fixed costs are $110k staff and $15k other. Does it meet the two-year payback?
questions.answer:
Revenue: 270 × $3.80 × 360 = $369k.

Margin after coffee and station rent: 100% − 30% − 12% = 58%, so contribution = $214k.

Profit: $214k − $125k = $89k. Payback: $120k ÷ $89k = 1.3 years. It meets the hurdle.

Break-even: $125k ÷ ($3.80 × 58% × 360) ≈ 158 customers a day, versus 270 expected: a comfortable cushion.

questions.q: A third barista for the morning peak would cost about $15k a year. Worth it?
questions.answer:
Peak capacity rises to 3 × 45 × 2 = 270, still short of the 300 who want coffee, but +90 customers a day (30 are still turned away).

Extra profit: 90 × $3.80 × 58% × 360 − $15k = $56k a year.

So-what: yes, clearly. Also add app pre-ordering so regulars skip the queue, and check the kiosk layout can fit a third person and a second machine.

reco: Sign the lease. The kiosk should make about $89k a year and pay back the $120k fit-out in 1.3 years, with break-even at about 158 customers a day versus 270 expected. But the real constraint is the morning peak: with two baristas, 120 customers a day can't be served. Adding a third barista at peak adds about $56k a year. Risk: commuter numbers fall if hybrid working grows, so negotiate a break clause. Next step: confirm the kiosk can fit a second coffee machine.
great: Checks peak capacity before revenue
Treats station rent as a share of sales, not a fixed cost
Computes break-even and the safety margin
Sees that adding peak capacity is the biggest lever

title: Spoke & Sprocket
sub: A second bike shop: great summers, empty winters
skills: Seasonality · utilisation · payback
prompt: Spoke & Sprocket runs a busy bicycle repair shop in Amsterdam. The owners want to open a second shop near the university in Utrecht, which would cost $150k to fit out. They want to know if it would pay off, and how to deal with the quiet winter months.

clarify.a: Very: about 55 repairs a day from April to September, about 25 a day in winter.
Three technicians, needed to cope with summer. Each can do about 20 repairs a day.
Average repair $28; parts are 30% of that.
Assume about 300 a year: 150 from April to September and 150 from October to March.
Payback within three years.

structure.root: Will the Utrecht shop pay back within three years?

hypothesis: Summer is strong, but the shop pays for three technicians all year. Profit probably depends on filling winter capacity.

questions.q: Estimate annual profit and payback for the new shop.
questions.answer:
Repairs: 150 days × 55 + 150 days × 25 = 12,000.

Revenue: 12,000 × $28 = $336k. Contribution after parts (70%): $235k.

Profit: $235k − $171k = $64k a year. Payback: $150k ÷ $64k = 2.3 years.

So-what: it meets the three-year hurdle, but only just.
questions.note: Fixed costs per year: rent $36k, technicians $120k, other $15k.

questions.q: In winter, how much technician time is idle? The owners are considering a student plan: $9 a month for two services a year. They expect 800 sign-ups, and each service uses about $6 of parts. What is it worth?
questions.answer:
Winter idle capacity: 1 − 25 ÷ 60 = 58%.

Plan revenue: 800 × $9 × 12 = $86.4k. Services: 1,600 at about $6 of parts each = −$9.6k (labour is free: it uses idle winter time).

Cannibalisation: if 40% of subscribers would have paid for about 1.5 repairs a year anyway: −$9.4k of lost margin.

Net: +$67.4k a year, which would cut payback to about 1.1 years.

So-what: worth it, as long as services are booked into winter. Let subscribers book only from October to March.

questions.q: What else could fill winter capacity?
questions.answer:
• Fleet contracts: maintain bikes for delivery companies, hotels and bike-share operators
  • Winter service promotion: lights, brakes and tyres before the dark months
  • Refurbish and sell used bikes to students in September
  • Flex staff: a seasonal technician in summer instead of a third full-time one

reco: Open the Utrecht shop: it should make about $64k a year and pay back in 2.3 years, inside the three-year hurdle. Its weakness is winter, when 58% of technician time is idle. A student plan that books services into October to March adds about $67.4k a year and cuts payback to 1.1 years; fleet contracts could add more. Risk: a weak first summer while the shop builds awareness. Next step: talk to two local fleet operators before signing the lease.
great: Builds revenue by season, not with one average
Measures idle capacity
Counts cannibalisation in the subscription maths
Uses idle time as a near-free resource

title: Fillhaus Refill
sub: Whose footfall forecast do we believe?
skills: Break-even · forecast risk · negotiation
prompt: Fillhaus runs two zero-waste refill shops in Melbourne, where customers bring their own containers for dry food, oils and cleaning products. A shopping-centre landlord has offered a site in a new development and says it will bring about 90 customers a day. The fit-out costs $160k. Should Fillhaus open?

clarify.q: What do Fillhaus's existing shops do?
clarify.a: Around 55 customers a day each, after two years of trading.
Average basket $24; gross margin about 45%.
Rent $60k, two staff $130k, other $20k a year.
About 310 a year.
Payback within three years.

structure.root: Should Fillhaus open the new shop?

branches.head: Customers per day
items: Fillhaus's own shops as a benchmark

hypothesis: The landlord has an incentive to be optimistic. I'd test the decision against Fillhaus's own shops: if it only works at 90 customers a day, it's risky.

questions.q: Calculate annual profit using the landlord's forecast and using Fillhaus's own shops as a benchmark.
questions.answer:
Profit = customers × $24 × 310 days × 45% − $210k.

  • Landlord, 90 a day: $91k, payback 1.8 years
  • Benchmark, 55 a day: −$26k: a loss

Break-even: $210k ÷ ($24 × 310 × 45%) = 62.7 customers a day.

So-what: the decision depends entirely on whose forecast is right. On Fillhaus's own experience, the shop would lose money.

questions.q: At 55 customers a day, what basket size would Fillhaus need to break even? How could it get there?
questions.answer:
Basket needed: $210k ÷ (55 × 310 × 45%) = $27.37, 14% more than today.

  • Bundles of everyday staples (rice, oats, detergent) sold by the kilo
  • Click-and-collect refills prepared in advance (also saves staff time)
  • Workplace orders: offices refilling cleaning products monthly
  • Higher-margin own-brand products

questions.q: How would you negotiate with the landlord?
questions.answer:
• Turnover-based or stepped rent for the first two years, so the landlord shares the footfall risk
  • Fit-out contribution, common for anchor-style tenants in a new development
  • Break clause after 24 months if footfall targets aren't met
  • Ask for footfall data from the landlord's other centres to back up the 90 a day

reco: Don't sign on the current terms. The shop works only if the landlord's 90 customers a day is right ($91k profit); at the 55 a day Fillhaus's own shops achieve, it loses about $26k a year, with break-even at 63 customers. I recommend negotiating turnover-based rent and a fit-out contribution so the landlord shares the risk, and raising the basket towards $27 through bundles and workplace orders. Risk: a new development can take years to fill. Next step: request the landlord's footfall data from comparable centres.
great: Questions the source of the forecast
Uses the client's own shops as a benchmark
Finds break-even in customers and in basket size
Turns the analysis into a negotiation

title: Orbit Climbing
sub: A climbing gym that could become too popular
skills: Ramp-up · peak capacity · payback
prompt: Orbit wants to open an indoor climbing gym in a converted warehouse in Calgary. The fit-out (walls, flooring, safety systems) costs $2.2M. The plan assumes membership grows to 1,200 people by year three. The investors' hurdle is a payback within five years. Should they go ahead?

clarify.a: Memberships at $95 a month, plus day passes worth about $0.45M a year.
Rent $0.38M, staff $0.42M, other $0.15M a year. Variable costs (card fees, chalk, cleaning) about 5% of revenue.
Members: 600 in year one, 1,000 in year two, 1,200 in year three.
The gym can safely hold 120 climbers at once.

structure.root: Does the gym pay back within five years?

branches.head: Capacity
items: How many climbers are there at peak?

hypothesis: Gyms have high fixed costs, so the ramp-up matters. But the bigger risk may be the evening peak: if 1,200 members all want to climb after work, the gym may be too full to sell that many memberships.

questions.q: Calculate operating profit for years one to three and the payback.
questions.answer:
Profit = (members × $95 × 12 + $0.45M) × 95% − $0.95M.

  • Year 1: 600 members → $0.13M
  • Year 2: 1,000 members → $0.56M
  • Year 3: 1,200 members → $0.78M

Cumulative after three years: $1.46M of the $2.2M. At year-three profit, the remaining $0.74M takes another 0.9 years: payback ≈ 3.9 years, inside the five-year hurdle.

questions.q: Members climb 2.2 times a week; 40% of visits are in the weekday 6-9pm peak (15 hours a week); a session lasts 2 hours. How many people are in the gym at peak with 1,200 members? (Assume day-pass visitors climb mostly at weekends and off-peak, so ignore them for the evening peak.)
questions.answer:
Peak arrivals per hour: 1,200 × 2.2 × 40% ÷ 15 = 70.4.

Each stays 2 hours, so about 141 people are climbing at once, against a safe limit of 120.

Maximum members before peak overcrowding: 1,200 × 120 ÷ 141 ≈ 1,023.

So-what: the plan's year-three membership doesn't physically fit. Unless peak demand is shifted, membership caps at about 1,023.
questions.note: This is the crux of the case. Strong candidates spot the capacity question before being asked.

questions.q: What does the cap do to the investment case?
questions.answer:
At about 1,023 members, steady-state profit is $0.59M instead of $0.78M. Payback stretches: after year two the remaining $1.51M takes 2.6 more years: about 4.6 years, still inside five, but with little margin.

Fixes: off-peak memberships at a lower price (students, shift workers, parents), corporate memberships used at lunchtime, timed booking at peak, and a higher peak-access price.

questions.q: What would you recommend to the investors?
questions.answer: Go ahead, but redesign the membership model before opening: an off-peak tier priced ~30% lower, a peak tier priced higher, and pre-sold corporate memberships for daytime use. Track peak occupancy from day one.

reco: Go ahead, with a different membership model. On the plan's numbers the gym pays back in about 3.9 years, but at 1,200 members about 141 people would be climbing at peak against a safe limit of 120, so membership effectively caps at about 1,023 and payback stretches to about 4.6 years. I recommend launching with peak and off-peak tiers and pre-selling daytime corporate memberships to grow beyond the cap. Risk: if off-peak demand is weak, payback lands close to the hurdle. Next step: survey local climbers on when they would visit and at what price.
great: Models the ramp-up instead of using steady state from day one
Checks physical capacity at peak
Converts the capacity limit into a membership cap
Fixes the problem with pricing tiers, not just 'more marketing'

title: Paloma Streaming
sub: Should a niche streaming service raise its price?
skills: Price elasticity · break-even volume loss
prompt: Paloma is a Spanish streaming service for independent and classic cinema with 180,000 subscribers paying $6.99 a month. Content costs are rising and the CEO wants to raise the price to $8.49. She asks whether it's a good idea.

clarify.a: About $1.50 a month: streaming, payment fees and per-view royalties.

clarify.q: What happened last time prices rose?
clarify.a: Paloma raised the price two years ago, by a similar proportion (about 20%). The interviewer has the subscriber data.
The big streaming platforms cost more but have little classic or independent film.
Higher monthly profit, without damaging the brand.

structure.root: Does the price rise increase profit?

branches.head: Margin per subscriber
items: New price minus cost per subscriber

branches.head: Subscribers
items: How many cancel because of the rise

hypothesis: Paloma's subscribers are film enthusiasts with few alternatives, so I expect low price sensitivity. The rise likely pays off unless more than about a fifth of subscribers leave.

questions.q: Here is what happened to subscribers after the last price rise, announced in March. What do you take from it?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Subscribers around the last price rise (k)

questions.answer:
Subscribers fell about 8% over three months, from 152k to 140k, then recovered most of the loss within five months.

So-what: customers react, but the core audience stays. The real risk is the short-term dip, not a permanent loss.

questions.q: If 10% of subscribers cancel, does the rise pay off? How many could cancel before it stops paying?
questions.answer:
Monthly margin today: 180k × ($6.99 − $1.50) = $988k.

After: 162k × ($8.49 − $1.50) = $1,132k, +$144k a month (about $1.7M a year).

Break-even loss: 1 − 5.49 ÷ 6.99 = 21.5%. Paloma can lose about 1 in 5 subscribers and still be no worse off.

So-what: with last time's dip of about 8%, there's a wide safety margin.

questions.q: How would you roll it out?
questions.answer:
• Explain why: more films, restored classics, better subtitles
  • Annual plan at a modest discount (e.g. $89 a year, about 13% off 12 × $8.49, and still above today's $83.88) to lock in loyal subscribers
  • Keep existing subscribers at the old price for three months to soften the dip
  • Watch new sign-ups, not just cancellations: the higher price may slow growth

reco: Raise the price to $8.49. Even if 10% of subscribers cancel, monthly margin rises by about $144k, and the rise only stops paying if more than 21.5% leave; last time the dip was about 8% and mostly recovered. Pair it with an annual plan and a three-month grace period for existing subscribers. Risk: slower sign-ups from new viewers. Next step: track cancellations and sign-ups weekly for three months after launch.
great: Reads the chart for both the dip and the recovery
Computes break-even churn, not just one scenario
Thinks about sign-ups as well as cancellations
Proposes a rollout that softens the reaction

title: Forge Valves
sub: Material costs are up. How should a valve maker price?
skills: Value-based pricing · segmentation · cost pass-through
prompt: Forge makes industrial valves for chemical plants and water utilities, selling about 24,000 a year at an average $1,800. Steel and alloy costs have risen $60 per valve. The sales director wants an 11% price increase across the board. The CFO asks you to check whether that is the best approach.

clarify.a: Two groups: critical-service valves for chemical plants (30% of volume), and general-service valves for utilities and building systems (70%). Both groups average about $1,800 a valve today.

clarify.q: What does failure cost a chemical plant?
clarify.a: An unplanned shutdown costs a typical customer about $250,000.
In general service, several cheaper Asian and Eastern European competitors. In critical service, Forge has a strong reliability record.
$740 before the increase, $800 now.

structure.root: How should Forge price to protect profit?

branches.head: Volume response
items: Expected loss by segment at each price

hypothesis: A blanket increase treats very different customers the same. Critical-service customers value reliability far above the valve price, so they can take more; general-service customers will switch.

questions.q: What happens to annual contribution if Forge does nothing, and if it applies the 11% increase everywhere (sales expects 12% fewer valves)?
questions.answer:
Before the cost rise: 24k × ($1,800 − $740) = $25.4M. Absorbing the $60: 24k × $1,000 = $24.0M (−$1.44M).

+11% everywhere: price $1,998; 21.12k valves × ($1,998 − $800) = $25.30M.

So-what: the blanket rise beats absorbing the cost, but loses 12% of volume, most likely in general service, where competitors are cheaper.

questions.q: Now consider a segmented approach: +15% on critical service (expected volume loss 2%) and pass through only the $60 on general service (loss 3%).

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Three pricing options
exhibit.note: Cost per valve $800 in all options.

questions.answer:
• Critical: 7.06k × ($2,070 − $800) = $8.96M
  • General: 16.30k × ($1,860 − $800) = $17.27M

Total: $26.23M, versus $25.30M for the blanket rise: +$0.93M, while keeping almost all volume.

So-what: price to value where customers value reliability, and pass on cost where they shop on price.

questions.q: A critical-service valve now costs $2,070. How would you justify that to a chemical plant buyer?
questions.answer:
One unplanned shutdown costs about $250,000, more than 100 valves. If Forge's reliability avoids even one failure over the life of a plant's valves, the price difference pays for itself many times over.

  • Show field failure rates versus competitors
  • Offer a performance warranty or faster emergency replacement
  • Bundle inspection services

reco: Don't raise prices 11% across the board. Instead raise critical-service prices 15% and pass through only the $60 cost on general service: contribution of about $26.2M versus $25.3M for the blanket rise, with far less volume lost. Back the critical-service price with reliability data and a performance warranty. Risk: competitors improve reliability over time. Next step: brief the sales team on value-selling to the top 20 chemical-plant accounts.
great: Separates segments with different price sensitivity
Compares options on contribution, not revenue
Links price to the customer's cost of failure
Keeps the volume base in competitive segments

title: Cobalt Museums
sub: Raise income without turning visitors away
skills: Peak pricing · public sector objectives
prompt: Cobalt manages three city-owned museums in Bologna, with 900,000 paying visitors a year at a single $18 ticket (free first-Sunday visits for residents are extra). The city wants more income to fund restoration, but the museums' mission is broad public access, and weekend queues are already long. The director asks you to design a better price structure.

clarify.a: 60% of visits are at peak times (weekends, holidays); 40% off-peak (weekday mornings).
Total visitor numbers must not fall. Free first Sundays for residents must stay.
About $3: ticketing, cleaning, guides.
Peak tickets at $24, off-peak at $14, booked in time slots.

structure.root: Can a new price structure raise income and keep access?

branches.head: Mission
items: Access for residents and low-income groups

hypothesis: Peak visitors are mostly tourists with fixed plans, so they're less price-sensitive; cheaper weekday tickets can pull locals and students in. Income could rise and crowding fall at the same time.

questions.q: Research suggests peak visits fall 8% at $24 and off-peak visits rise 15% at $14. Calculate visitors and contribution, before and after.
questions.answer:
Today: 900k × ($18 − $3) = $13.50M.

After: peak 540k → 497k at $21 margin; off-peak 360k → 414k at $11 margin.

Contribution: $14.99M (+$1.49M, 11%). Visitors: 911k (+11k).

So-what: more income, slightly more visitors, and 43k fewer people in the weekend queues. It meets the city's conditions.

questions.q: Critics say $24 shuts out families. How would you protect access?
questions.answer:
• Keep free first Sundays for residents, with timed booking so they don't queue
  • Under-18s free and student tickets at the off-peak price at any time
  • A resident annual pass (e.g. $30) valid at any time
  • Publish the income raised and the restorations it pays for

questions.q: What would make you less confident in the forecast?
questions.answer:
• Off-peak growth may come mainly from people switching days, not new visitors: income still rises, but total visits might not
  • Tour groups may book elsewhere if they lose flexibility
  • Bad weather and events shift demand between slots

Test it for a summer season before making it permanent.

reco: Introduce peak and off-peak pricing: $24 at weekends and holidays, $14 on weekday mornings, in timed slots. On the research estimates, contribution rises from $13.5M to $15.0M, total visitors rise to about 911k and weekend crowding falls. Protect access with free first Sundays, free entry for under-18s and a low-cost resident pass. Risk: off-peak growth may be smaller if it's mostly people switching days. Next step: pilot for one summer season and measure visits by slot.
great: Respects the public mission as a constraint
Calculates both income and visitor numbers
Uses price to spread demand, not just raise income
Builds in protections for access

title: Solstice Ski School
sub: Raise lesson prices: everywhere, or only when it's full?
skills: Capacity-constrained pricing · demand curves · peak pricing
prompt: Solstice runs group ski lessons in a large Swiss resort. Over Christmas, New Year and February half-term, every class is full and many families are turned away; in other weeks classes are half-empty. Management proposes a 12% increase on all lessons from $95 to about $106. Is that the right move?

clarify.a: 80 instructors, each teaching two 8-person classes a day: 1,280 lesson places a day. More instructors can't be hired for the peak.
30 peak days and 90 regular days.
About $30 per lesson place (instructor pay per class, equipment); $1.2M fixed.
About 2,000 requests a day at peak and 800 in regular weeks at today's price.

structure.root: How should Solstice change prices?

branches.head: Peak weeks
items: Effect of a price rise on places sold

hypothesis: At peak, demand is far above capacity, so a higher price won't reduce lessons sold. In regular weeks it will. I suspect a peak-only increase beats a blanket one.

questions.q: Management expects the 12% rise to cut demand by 10% at peak and 17% in regular weeks. Compare profit with today.
questions.answer:
Today: peak 1,280 places (capped) × $65 × 30 days + regular 800 × $65 × 90 days − $1.2M = $5.98M.

Blanket +12% ($106.4): peak demand 1,800 is still above capacity, so 1,280 places sell as before; regular demand falls to 664.

Profit: $6.30M (+$0.32M). That is a gain of $0.44M at peak, where no lessons are lost, partly offset by −$0.11M in regular weeks, where families drop out.

So-what: the blanket rise helps, but only because of the peak. In regular weeks it destroys value.

questions.q: Here is estimated peak demand at different prices. What peak price maximises profit, with regular weeks left at $95?
questions.answer:
Profit per peak day = (price − $30) × places sold, where places sold is capped at 1,280:

At $140: 1,200 places × $110 = $132,000 a day, the highest in the table.

Season profit with peak at $140 and regular at $95: $7.44M, versus $5.98M today and $6.30M for the blanket rise.

So-what: raise peak prices sharply and leave regular weeks alone. Note that at $140 a few places go unfilled: at that point price, not capacity, limits sales.
questions.note: The trap: candidates who ignore the capacity cap overstate the gain at low prices.

questions.q: What about regular weeks? Could a lower price help?
questions.answer: There are 480 empty places a day in regular weeks. Each extra place sold adds $65 at today's price. Options: discounted multi-day packages, school and club groups, bundling with lift-pass or hotel partners. Test whether a cut brings genuinely new customers rather than discounting people who'd come anyway.

questions.q: Families complain that peak pricing is unfair. How do you handle it?
questions.answer:
• Early-booking prices for peak weeks, so planners pay less
  • Price by week, published in advance (no surge pricing on the day)
  • Keep a quota of places for local residents at the regular price

reco: Don't raise all prices by 12%: it adds only $0.32M, because the gain at peak is partly lost in regular weeks, where families drop out. Instead, raise peak-week lessons to about $140 and keep regular weeks at $95: profit rises from $5.98M to $7.44M, selling only 80 fewer places a day at peak. Fill regular weeks with packages and group deals. Risk: families see peak pricing as unfair, so publish prices early and offer early-booking rates. Next step: launch peak prices for next season's Christmas weeks.
great: Spots that capacity, not demand, limits peak sales
Applies the cap when reading the demand curve
Separates peak from regular weeks
Addresses fairness, not just profit

title: HelioVet
sub: Entering Poland: go direct or use a distributor?
skills: Entry mode · ramp-up · partner economics
prompt: HelioVet, a German company, sells software that stores and analyses X-ray images for veterinary clinics, at $150 per clinic per month. After success at home it wants to enter Poland. Localisation and certification would cost $400k up front. The CEO asks: is Poland worth entering, and should HelioVet build its own sales team or work through a distributor?

clarify.a: Only clinics with digital X-ray: about 35% of Poland's 4,800 clinics today, and rising.
Two specialist distributors sell equipment to most Polish clinics. One has offered to resell HelioVet for 25% of revenue.
Support costs about $30 per clinic per month. A direct team (sales, support, Polish-speaking staff) would cost $350k a year; with the distributor, $150k.
Recover the entry investment within four years.

structure.root: Should HelioVet enter Poland, and how?

branches.head: Entry mode
items: Direct: cost and speed of ramp-up
Distributor: margin given up vs reach

hypothesis: The market is small, so speed of adoption matters more than margin. A distributor that already visits most clinics could win customers much faster.

questions.q: How big is the addressable market today?
questions.answer:
Addressable: 4,800 × 35% = 1,680 clinics.

So-what: a small market, so any plan will need a large share of it, and the speed of winning clinics will matter.

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Clinics signed (cumulative)

questions.answer:
By year four the direct plan reaches 420 clinics (25% of today's addressable market); the distributor plan 500 (30%).

Profit per clinic per year: direct ($150 − $30) × 12 = $1,440; distributor ($150 × 75% − $30) × 12 = $990.

  • Direct: −$235k, −$62k, +$111k, +$255k → after investment −$331k
  • Distributor: −$2k, +$147k, +$266k, +$345k → after investment +$356k

So-what: the distributor gives up a quarter of revenue but wins clinics faster with a much lower fixed cost; it recovers the investment within four years. Going direct doesn't.

(Simplification: clinics count for the full year in which they're signed. Counting them only from mid-year, the distributor still ends positive and direct further behind.)

questions.q: What would you put in the distributor contract?
questions.answer:
• Minimum clinic targets each year, with HelioVet's right to go direct if they're missed
  • Customer data and contracts owned by HelioVet, so it keeps the relationships
  • Training and first-line support by the distributor; HelioVet handles software issues
  • Time limit (e.g. 3 to 5 years) on exclusivity

reco: Enter Poland through the distributor. Poland has about 1,680 clinics able to use HelioVet today; the distributor reaches them faster at a far lower fixed cost, delivering +$356k cumulative after the $400k investment over four years versus −$331k going direct. Protect the long term with minimum targets, HelioVet-owned customer contracts and time-limited exclusivity. Risk: dependence on one partner. Next step: negotiate terms with the distributor and pilot in Warsaw.
great: Sizes the addressable market from digital adoption
Compares entry modes over time, not at steady state
Sees that speed and fixed cost outweigh the margin given up
Protects the client in the partner contract

title: Rill Snacks
sub: Launching an organic snack brand in UAE supermarkets
skills: Price waterfall · retail economics · break-even velocity
prompt: Rill makes organic baked lentil snacks in Jordan. A UAE distributor can place it in 120 premium supermarkets in Dubai and Abu Dhabi, at a shelf price of $4.00 a pack. The founder wants to know how much Rill would actually earn per pack, and whether the launch can make money.

clarify.a: VAT is 5% (included in the shelf price). The retailer keeps 30% of the price before VAT; the distributor keeps 15% of what's left.
$1.12 per pack including production, freight and import duty.
About $270k in year one (listing fees and in-store sampling), then about $110k a year.
Similar premium snacks sell about 20 packs per store per week.

structure.root: Can Rill make money in the UAE?

branches.head: Unit economics
items: Net price minus cost per pack

hypothesis: A lot of the $4.00 goes to VAT, the retailer and the distributor; I'd expect Rill to keep about half. Whether that's enough depends on how fast packs sell in each store.

questions.q: Walk down from the $4.00 shelf price to what Rill receives per pack, and its margin.

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Where the $4.00 goes ($ per pack)

questions.answer:
• Remove VAT: $4.00 ÷ 1.05 = $3.81
  • Retailer keeps 30%: $2.67 left
  • Distributor keeps 15%: $2.27 to Rill (57% of the shelf price)
  • Minus $1.12 cost: $1.15 contribution per pack

questions.q: How many packs per store per week does Rill need to break even in year one and from year two? Compare with the benchmark of 20.
questions.answer:
Year one: $270k ÷ $1.15 ÷ 120 stores ÷ 52 = 37.7 packs per store per week.

From year two: $110k ÷ $1.15 ÷ 120 ÷ 52 = 15.4.

At the benchmark of 20: year one −$0.13M, year two +$0.03M.

So-what: expect a loss in year one, then a modest profit if Rill sells like its peers. The year-one loss takes about four more years of benchmark sales to earn back (cumulative break-even in year five), so Rill needs to beat the benchmark.

questions.q: How would you make the launch work?
questions.answer:
• Start with fewer stores (the 40 best) to cut listing fees and focus sampling
  • Negotiate listing fees against volume, or pay them in instalments
  • Sampling and eye-level shelf space in the first three months: trial drives repeat
  • Track packs per store per week monthly; agree with the distributor what happens below 10

reco: Launch, but plan for a year-one loss. Rill keeps $2.27 of the $4.00 shelf price and earns $1.15 per pack; it needs about 38 packs per store per week to break even in year one but only about 15 after that, against a benchmark of 20. At the benchmark, it loses about $127k in year one and earns about $33k a year after. I recommend starting in the best 40 stores, focusing sampling there, and expanding once sales pass the benchmark. Risk: slow sales in year one lead retailers to delist. Next step: agree store-level targets with the distributor.
great: Walks the price waterfall step by step, including VAT
Converts break-even into packs per store per week
Separates one-off launch costs from ongoing ones
Recommends a staged launch

title: Ferrow Pay
sub: Can a remittance app win the UAE–Philippines corridor?
skills: Unit economics · channel mix · break-even customers
prompt: Ferrow Pay is a money-transfer app. It wants to launch on the corridor from the United Arab Emirates to the Philippines, used by hundreds of thousands of Filipino workers who send money home each month. The board asks whether Ferrow Pay can build a profitable business on this corridor, and what it would take.

clarify.a: A flat $3 fee plus a 0.8% margin on the exchange rate. The average transfer is $400.
Today about 70% collect it as cash from agent shops; the other 30%, a growing share, receive it in a mobile wallet or bank account.
Payout partner: $1.50 for cash pickup, $0.40 to a wallet or bank. Compliance checks $0.50; card processing $0.60.
Licences, compliance team and operations: about $2.4M a year.

structure.root: Can Ferrow Pay be profitable on this corridor?

hypothesis: Remittance margins are thin, so the payout method may decide the case: cash pickup is expensive. If Ferrow Pay can move families onto mobile wallets, the economics improve sharply.

questions.q: Calculate contribution per transfer for each payout method.
questions.answer:
Revenue: $3 + 0.8% × $400 = $6.20.

  • Cash pickup: $6.20 − $1.50 − $1.10 = $3.60
  • Wallet or bank: $6.20 − $0.40 − $1.10 = $4.70

With 70% cash pickup, the blended contribution is $3.93.

So-what: a digital payout earns 31% more per transfer.

questions.q: Each customer sends 10 transfers a year. How many active customers does Ferrow Pay need to cover its $2.4M fixed costs today, and if cash pickup fell to 40%?
questions.answer:
Today: $2.4M ÷ ($3.93 × 10) = 61,069 customers.

At 40% cash: blended $4.26, so 56,338 customers, 8% fewer.

So-what: shifting payouts to wallets is worth as much as winning thousands of extra customers.

questions.q: It costs about $25 to win a customer, who stays about 2.5 years. Is acquisition affordable?
questions.answer:
Lifetime contribution: $3.93 × 10 × 2.5 = $98 versus $25: about 3.9× the acquisition cost.

So-what: affordable, with room to spend more on acquisition if it brings loyal senders.

questions.q: How would you win customers and move them to digital payouts?
questions.answer:
• Employer partnerships: sign up workers through companies that employ many Filipino staff
  • Cheaper fee for wallet payouts (e.g. $2 instead of $3): it still earns more than cash pickup
  • Community channels: churches, Filipino associations, word of mouth with referral bonuses
  • Speed and trust: instant delivery and clear exchange rates, since senders compare apps closely

Licensing and anti-money-laundering controls must be in place before launch: they're non-negotiable.

reco: Ferrow Pay can build a profitable corridor if it moves families to digital payouts. Each transfer earns $6.20; contribution is $3.60 on cash pickup but $4.70 to a wallet. At today's 70% cash mix it needs about 61,100 active senders to cover fixed costs; at 40% cash, about 56,300. Customers are worth about 4× their acquisition cost. I recommend launching with a lower fee for wallet payouts and employer partnerships to acquire senders. Risk: incumbents cut fees. Next step: secure licences and agree wallet payout partners in the Philippines.
great: Builds revenue from the fee and the FX margin
Compares payout methods per transfer
Turns the payout mix into a customers-needed number
Uses pricing to steer customers to the cheaper channel

title: Northcairn Recycling
sub: A battery recycling plant: is the market enough?
skills: Utilisation · break-even · supply contracts
prompt: Northcairn wants to build a lithium-ion battery recycling plant in northern Sweden that would recover lithium, nickel and cobalt from used batteries and factory scrap. The plant would cost $90M and process up to 20,000 tonnes a year. The board asks: should Northcairn build it?

clarify.a: Scrap from nearby battery factories today; end-of-life electric-car batteries later in the decade.
After variable processing costs, each tonne earns about $1,800 from recovered metals and gate fees. Fixed costs are $21M a year.
Signed supply agreements cover 45% of capacity.
Payback within eight years.

structure.root: Should Northcairn build the plant?

branches.head: Feedstock
items: Factory scrap now, car batteries later

hypothesis: Recycling plants have high fixed costs, so profit depends on running near capacity. Generic market growth doesn't matter if Northcairn can't secure the batteries.

questions.q: Calculate annual operating profit at 50%, 75% and 90% utilisation, and the break-even utilisation.

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Annual operating profit by utilisation ($M)

questions.answer:
Profit = 20kt × utilisation × $1,800 − $21M.

  • 50%: −$3.0M, payback —
  • 75%: +$6.0M, payback 15.0 years
  • 90%: +$11.4M, payback 7.9 years

Break-even utilisation: $21M ÷ (20kt × $1,800) = 58%.

To pay back in eight years the plant must earn $11.25M a year, which needs 90% utilisation.

So-what: only near-full running meets the hurdle; at 75% payback takes 15 years, and at 50% the plant loses money.

questions.q: Only 45% of capacity is contracted. What does that tell you, and what would you do?
questions.answer:
Contracted volume alone (45%) is below the 58% break-even: the plant would lose money on signed contracts only.

  • Sign more long-term supply contracts with battery factories and carmakers before committing the full $90M
  • Build in phases: a first line sized to contracted volume, then expand
  • Offer gate-fee discounts for multi-year commitments
  • Hedge metal prices partly, since lithium and nickel prices swing sharply

questions.q: What risks would you raise with the board?
questions.answer:
• Metal prices: a fall in lithium or nickel cuts the $1,800 margin per tonne
  • Battery chemistry: newer batteries use less cobalt and nickel, so they're worth less to recycle
  • Timing: car batteries reach end of life slowly, so the plant depends on factory scrap for years
  • Competition for scrap from other European recyclers

reco: Don't build the full plant yet. It needs 58% utilisation to break even and about 90% to pay back within eight years, yet only 45% of capacity is under contract; at 75% it would take 15 years to pay back. I recommend building in phases sized to contracted volume and signing long-term supply deals before adding capacity. Risk: metal price swings change the margin per tonne. Next step: approach the three largest battery factories in the Nordics for multi-year supply agreements.
great: Recognises utilisation drives profit in a fixed-cost plant
Compares contracted volume with break-even
Proposes phasing to reduce risk
Raises metal-price and chemistry risks

title: Elm Home Security
sub: Launching a premium plan: how much is really new money?
skills: Cannibalisation · incremental profit
prompt: Elm sells home security cameras and alarms with a $8-a-month app plan (self-monitoring). It wants to launch a premium plan at $18 a month that includes 24/7 professional monitoring, with a call-out if an alarm goes off. The marketing team forecasts strong demand. The CFO wants to know the true annual profit impact.

clarify.a: 160,000 on the $8 plan, costing about $2 a month each to serve.
About $7 a month per customer in total, including the app, the monitoring centre and call-outs (it replaces the $2 cost of the basic plan).
14% of existing customers upgrade; 30,000 new customers join for the premium plan.
$1.3M one-off; $0.94M a year minimum fee to the monitoring partner.

structure.root: What is the premium plan worth to Elm each year?

branches.head: Upgrading customers
items: Extra margin vs the plan they leave

hypothesis: The trap is counting upgraders as if they were new revenue. They already pay $8, so only the difference counts.

questions.q: Calculate the annual profit impact of the premium plan.
questions.answer:
Upgraders: 22.4k customers. Each moves from $6 to $11 margin a month: +$5. Annual: 22.4k × $5 × 12 = $1.34M.

New customers: 30k × $11 × 12 = $3.96M.

Minus the $0.94M monitoring fee: $4.36M a year. The $1.3M launch cost pays back in about 4 months.

So-what: new customers drive most of the value. If you'd counted upgraders' full premium margin you'd get $5.98M, overstating by $1.61M.

questions.q: How sensitive is this to the forecast of 30,000 new customers?
questions.answer:
Each new customer is worth $132 a year. Without any new customers, profit would be $0.40M a year, and the launch cost would take 3.2 years to recover.

New customers needed just to cover the monitoring fee, given the upgrades: none: upgrades alone cover it.

So-what: the plan pays even if new-customer demand disappoints, because upgrades are profitable on their own.

questions.q: What could go wrong after launch?
questions.answer:
• False alarms raising monitoring costs above $7 a month
  • Service quality: slow response would damage the brand
  • Contract terms: the $0.94M minimum fee is owed even if take-up is low
  • Regulatory checks for monitored alarm services

reco: Launch the premium plan. It adds about $4.36M a year: $1.34M from upgraders (counting only their extra margin) and $3.96M from new customers, after the $0.94M monitoring fee, and repays the $1.3M launch cost in about 4 months. It remains profitable even with no new customers. Risk: false alarms push monitoring costs up, so track cost per customer monthly. Next step: agree a monitoring contract with a lower minimum fee for the first year.
great: Counts upgraders' extra margin only
Separates one-off and recurring costs
Tests the most uncertain forecast
Flags service and cost risks

title: Velisse Skin
sub: A refill pouch: greener, but will it eat our bottle sales?
skills: Cannibalisation · channel incentives
prompt: Velisse Skin sells a premium face serum in French pharmacies at $48 a bottle. It plans to launch a refill pouch at $40 that customers pour into their existing bottle. The sales team worries that refills will cannibalise bottle sales. The CEO asks for the full economics.

clarify.a: A bottle costs $18 to make, including $7 of glass and pump. A refill pouch costs $11.
Pharmacies keep about 35% of the retail price, on bottles and refills alike.
280,000 regular customers buying about 3 bottles a year.
22% of customers would switch to refills; they'd buy slightly more often (3.4 times a year) because refills are cheaper. 32,000 new, sustainability-minded customers would join.
$1.35M a year for refill displays and marketing.

structure.root: Is the refill worth launching?

branches.head: Switchers
items: Margin per refill vs per bottle

branches.head: Channel
items: Pharmacy earnings on refills vs bottles

hypothesis: Refills sell for less but cost much less to make, so Velisse Skin's margin per sale may be similar. If that's true, cannibalisation is not the real risk.

questions.q: Compare Velisse Skin's margin on a bottle and a refill. What happens to a customer who switches?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Retail price and Velisse Skin's margin per unit ($)

questions.answer:
Velisse Skin receives 65% of the retail price; the pharmacy keeps 35%.

Bottle: $48 × 65% = $31.20 − $18 = $13.20. Refill: $40 × 65% = $26.00 − $11 = $15.00. A refill earns Velisse Skin more than a bottle.

A switcher's annual margin: 3.4 × $15.00 = $51.00 vs 3 × $13.20 = $39.60 before: +$11.40 each.

So-what: cannibalisation doesn't hurt here; switching customers are worth more.

questions.q: Calculate the total annual impact.
questions.answer:
Switchers: 61.6k × $11.40 = $0.70M.

New customers: 32k × (1 bottle × $13.20 + 2.4 refills × $15.00) = $1.57M.

Minus $1.35M of costs: +$0.93M a year.

So-what: worthwhile, and most of the value comes from new customers, but the yearly costs eat most of the gross gain.

questions.q: How might pharmacies react, and what would you do?
questions.answer:
A pharmacy earns $16.80 on a bottle but $14.00 on a refill: they lose $2.80 each time a customer switches, so they may not stock or promote refills.

Matching their $16.80 on every refill needs a 42% share. That cuts Velisse Skin's refill margin to $12.20 and the total gain to about +$0.13M a year: almost nothing.

  • Raise the pharmacy's share on refills only partly, or tie it to refill volume
  • Refill-station displays that also bring traffic into the pharmacy
  • Sell refills online too, but avoid undercutting pharmacies on price

reco: Launch the refill. After the pharmacy's 35% share, Velisse Skin earns more on a refill ($15.00) than on a bottle ($13.20), so switching customers are worth more, and new customers add most of the value: about +$0.93M a year after launch costs. The real risk is pharmacies, which earn $2.80 less per refill. Raise their share on refills only partly (matching them fully would cut the gain to about $0.1M), or tie it to refill volume. Next step: test refill stations in 50 pharmacies for three months.
great: Works out the margin after the channel's share, not on retail price
Shows cannibalisation is harmless here
Quantifies the new-customer gain
Spots the channel partner's incentive problem and prices the fix

title: Kinloch Workspace
sub: Day passes could fill empty desks, or empty the membership
skills: Cannibalisation · price fences · product design
prompt: Kinloch runs three coworking spaces in Singapore with 900 monthly members paying $600 for a desk. Desks are often empty on Mondays and Fridays. The team wants to sell day passes at $45 to fill them. The CEO asks whether that's a good idea.

clarify.a: Freelancers and small teams. 25% come in 8 days a month or fewer: about 7 days on average.
About 40 passes a day from people who aren't members, on any weekday.
About $8 (coffee, cleaning, admin).
More monthly profit, without weakening the membership base.

structure.root: Will day passes increase profit?

branches.head: Cannibalisation
items: Light members who'd switch to passes
What they pay now vs with passes

hypothesis: Day passes look like pure upside, but a member who comes 7 days a month would pay $315 in passes instead of $600. If light members switch, the scheme could lose money.

questions.q: Calculate the monthly impact of open day passes at $45, if all light members switch.
questions.answer:
New revenue: 40 passes × 22 days × ($45 − $8) = $32,560 a month.

Light members: 225. Each would pay 7 × $45 = $315 instead of $600: $285 less. Loss: 225 × $285 = $64,125.

Net: −$31,565 a month.

So-what: as designed, day passes lose money. The problem isn't the passes, it's that they're a cheaper substitute for membership.

questions.q: Alternative: day passes only on Mondays and Fridays (about 9 days a month), at $60. Kinloch expects 30 passes on those days and only 15% of light members to switch. Recalculate.

rows: Contribution from non-members, after $8 a visit ($/month)
exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Day-pass options compared

questions.answer:
New revenue: 30 × 9 × ($60 − $8) = $14,040.

Cannibalisation: 33.75 members (on average) × ($600 − 7 × $60) = $6,075.

Net: +$7,965 a month.

So-what: fencing passes by day and price turns a loss into a gain: members who come midweek can't switch, and $60 makes switching less attractive.

questions.q: What else would protect the membership base?
questions.answer:
• A part-time membership offered only to light members who try to cancel (e.g. 8 days a month for about $500). Offered to everyone, each light member who downgrades from $600 costs $100 a month
  • Members-only perks: meeting-room credits, events, mail handling
  • A monthly cap on day passes per person
  • Use day passes as a trial: credit the first pass against a membership

reco: Don't launch open day passes: they'd lose about $31,565 a month because light members would switch from $600 memberships to cheaper passes. Instead, sell passes only on Mondays and Fridays at $60, which adds about $7,965 a month, and offer a part-time membership only to light members who try to cancel, since a general downgrade to a cheaper plan would cost more than the passes earn. Risk: the switching estimate is uncertain, so track membership cancellations weekly. Next step: pilot at one site for two months.
great: Sees the substitution risk before calculating
Calculates the loss per switching member
Designs fences (day, price) to protect the core product
Offers a product that keeps light users as members

title: Horizon Language
sub: An AI speaking coach: good product, risky costs
skills: Cannibalisation · variable AI costs · pricing design
prompt: Horizon is a language-learning app with 500,000 subscribers paying $10 a month. It wants to launch an AI speaking coach (voice conversations with instant feedback) as a new tier at $20 a month. AI costs are high and uncertain. The CEO asks whether the tier will make money.

clarify.a: $1.00 a month today. The AI coach adds about $4.50 of AI processing per user per month, so $5.50 in total.
17% of subscribers upgrade; 90,000 new subscribers join for the AI tier.
$3M a year for the AI team and content.
Early tests show 10% of users talk to the coach five times as much as the others.

structure.root: Will the AI tier make money?

hypothesis: The tier likely pays on average, but AI cost scales with usage. Heavy users on a flat fee could wipe out the margin, so I'd look at the cost distribution, not just the average.

questions.q: Calculate the annual profit impact, using $4.50 of AI cost for every AI user.
questions.answer:
Upgraders: 85k, each gaining ($20.00 − $5.50) − ($10.00 − $1.00) = $5.50 a month: 85k × $5.50 × 12 = $5.61M a year.

New: 90k × $14.50 × 12 = $15.66M.

Minus $3M fixed: $18.3M a year.

So-what: new subscribers drive most of the value; upgraders add less because they already paid $10.

questions.q: Now account for heavy users: 10% of AI users use five times the AI processing of the rest. The $4.50 was measured on typical users. What happens?
questions.answer:
A heavy user's total cost: $1.00 + 5 × $4.50 = $23.50 a month, above the $20 price: each loses $3.50 a month.

The $4.50 was measured on typical users, so the true average AI cost = 90% × $4.50 + 10% × $22.50 = $6.30. Across 175k AI users, annual profit falls by about $3.8M, to $14.5M.

So-what: still profitable, but heavy users must be managed.
questions.note: A good candidate asks how the $4.50 average was measured before using it.

questions.q: How would you design the tier to control AI costs?
questions.answer:
• Monthly minute allowance (e.g. 300 minutes), with a top-up pack beyond it
  • Cheaper AI models for simple drills; the best model for open conversation
  • Annual plan at a discount to lock in revenue
  • Monitor cost per user weekly during the first three months

reco: Launch the AI tier with a usage allowance. On average costs it adds about $18.3M a year, mostly from new subscribers, but a heavy user costs $23.50 a month against the $20 price, and heavy users cut profit to about $14.5M. I recommend a monthly minute allowance with paid top-ups and cheaper AI models for simple exercises. Risk: AI costs and engagement in the first months differ from tests. Next step: launch to 10% of users and measure cost per user weekly.
great: Separates upgraders from new subscribers
Questions the average AI cost
Spots the flat-fee risk from heavy users
Designs pricing to cap cost exposure

title: Riverbend Bottling
sub: Which machine is holding the line back?
skills: Bottleneck analysis · payback
prompt: Riverbend bottles sparkling water in Ohio for supermarket private labels. Customers want 400,000 cases a year but Riverbend can't keep up, and it's losing orders. The plant manager has proposed a $230k upgrade to the filling machine. The owner asks you to check whether that's the right investment.

clarify.a: Four stations in sequence: rinse bottles, fill and cap, label, pack into cases.
Two shifts, about 3,800 hours a year.
97% of cases pass final inspection.
Each extra case sold earns about $4 of contribution.

structure.root: Will the filler upgrade let Riverbend meet demand?

hypothesis: A line runs at the speed of its slowest station. I'd check that the filler really is the bottleneck, and what becomes the bottleneck after the upgrade.

questions.q: Here are the station speeds. How many good cases can the line produce today, and how many orders is Riverbend losing?
questions.answer:
The filler is slowest at 100 cases an hour: 100 × 3,800 = 380k cases a year. After 97% yield: 368.6k.

Demand is 400k, so Riverbend loses about 31.4k cases a year: $126k of contribution.

questions.q: The upgrade makes the filler 17% faster. What happens?
questions.answer:
Filler: 100 × 1.17 = 117 an hour. Now the packer (110/hour) is the bottleneck: 110 × 3,800 × 97% = 405.5k good cases, more than demand, so Riverbend can supply all 400k.

Extra cases: 31.4k × $4 = $126k a year. Payback: $230k ÷ $126k = 1.8 years.

So-what: a good investment, and the new bottleneck still leaves headroom above demand.

questions.q: Is there a cheaper way to get the same output?
questions.answer:
• Run the filler through breaks with a relief operator: a few more hours a day on the bottleneck only
  • Cut changeover time between bottle sizes on the filler
  • Weekend shift for the filler with a small buffer of filled bottles

These could close part of the gap within weeks; the upgrade is the durable fix.

reco: Approve the filler upgrade. The filler is the bottleneck today, limiting output to about 368.6k good cases against 400k demand. Making it 17% faster moves the bottleneck to the packer, which still has enough capacity to meet demand, adding about $126k of contribution a year and paying back in 1.8 years. Meanwhile, run the filler through breaks to recover some volume now. Risk: faster filling could raise reject rates. Next step: trial the upgrade's speed on one product before committing.
great: Finds the bottleneck from station speeds
Checks what becomes the bottleneck after the upgrade
Caps output at demand
Suggests quick wins on the bottleneck itself

title: Cascade Furniture
sub: Late deliveries at a furniture plant: fix one machine or two?
skills: Bottleneck shifts · sequencing investments
prompt: Cascade makes flat-pack modular shelving in Denmark and sells it across Europe. Customers want about 105,000 units a year, but shipments run late because work piles up in the lacquer finishing area. The COO wants to add a second lacquer booth for $450k. She asks whether that solves the problem.

clarify.a: Three steps: cutting panels, assembly, lacquer finishing.
One shift: about 1,820 hours a year.
95% of units pass inspection.
Each extra unit sold earns $24 of contribution.

structure.root: How should Cascade raise output to meet demand?

hypothesis: Finishing is where work piles up, so it's probably the bottleneck. But speeding up finishing may just move the bottleneck to the next-slowest step.

questions.q: How many good units can Cascade ship today?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Units per hour by step

questions.answer: Finishing is slowest: 49 × 1,820 = 89.2k units; after 95% yield, 84.7k, against demand of 105k.

questions.q: A second lacquer booth raises finishing speed by 22% for $450k. What does it deliver?
questions.answer:
Finishing: 59.8/hour, but cutting (58/hour) is now the bottleneck: 105.6k units, 100.3k good units.

Extra: 15.6k × $24 = $373k a year; payback 1.2 years. Still 4.7k short of demand.

questions.q: Cutting could be made 10% faster for $150k (a faster saw and better panel loading). What if Cascade does both?
questions.answer:
Cutting: 63.8/hour; finishing at 59.8 is the bottleneck again: 108.8k units, 103.4k good, just below demand.

The cutting upgrade adds a further 3.1k units: $74k a year for $150k, a payback of 2.0 years.

So-what: the two changes work as a pair. On its own, the booth leaves Cascade short; together they nearly close the gap for $600k, paying back in 1.3 years.

reco: Do both: add the second lacquer booth and speed up cutting. The booth alone moves the bottleneck to cutting and leaves Cascade about 4.7k units short; with a 10% faster saw, output reaches about 103.4k good units against demand of 105k, adding about $447k a year and paying back the $600k in 1.3 years. Risk: both projects must land together, so plan the installs in the same summer shutdown. Next step: get firm quotes and installation dates.
great: Checks the bottleneck after each change
Sequences investments by where capacity is limited
Compares output with demand at each step
Recommends the combination, with a payback

title: Glacier Meals
sub: The packing robot that wouldn't add a single meal
skills: Bottlenecks · wrong-fix trap
prompt: Glacier makes frozen ready meals in Ontario for Canadian grocers. Demand is 440,000 trays a year and growing, and Glacier is turning down orders. The operations director proposes a $600k automated packing line, because packing is the most labour-intensive step. The CEO asks you to evaluate it.

clarify.a: Prep ingredients, cook, blast-freeze, pack. Trays move in sequence.
Two shifts, 3,200 hours a year.
96% of trays pass inspection.
Each extra tray sold earns about $4 of contribution.

structure.root: How should Glacier increase output?

branches.head: Capacity
items: Trays per hour at each step

hypothesis: Labour-intensive doesn't mean bottleneck. If packing is already faster than cooking, a robot will save labour but won't add any meals.

questions.q: Here are the step speeds. What would the packing robot (+25% packing speed) do to output?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Trays per hour by step

questions.answer:
Cooking is the bottleneck at 118 trays an hour: 377.6k trays, 362.5k good, against demand of 440k.

Packing is already the fastest step (145/hour). Making it faster changes nothing: output stays at 362.5k. Zero extra meals.

So-what: the robot can only be justified on labour savings, not on growth.

questions.q: Alternatives: an extra kettle to make cooking 18% faster ($180k), and a second blast-freezer to add 15% freezing capacity ($220k). Evaluate.
questions.answer:
Cooking only: 139/hour, but the blast freezer (124/hour) becomes the bottleneck: 380.9k good trays, +18.4k, $74k a year, payback 2.4 years.

Cooking and freezer: both are now above 130/hour, so prep becomes the bottleneck: 399.4k good trays, +36.9k, $147k a year for $400k: payback 2.7 years.
