So-what: this line is nearly balanced, so each fix only moves the limit to the next step. Even with both, Glacier is 40.6k trays short. Prep is manual, so the cheap next step is an extra prep worker per shift (to 150/hour). Cooking is then the limit again at about 427.7k good trays; the last 12.3k need around 90 hours of weekend overtime a year.

questions.q: The operations director says the robot also saves four packers' wages. How do you handle that?
questions.answer: Fair point: it's a cost-saving project, not a growth project, and should be judged on its own payback (four packers' wages vs $600k). It may still be worth doing later. But growth depends on cooking, freezing and prep, so those come first.

reco: Don't buy the packing robot to grow: packing isn't the bottleneck, so it adds no meals. Instead add a kettle and a second blast-freezer: output rises from 362.5k to 399.4k good trays, adding about $147k a year and paying back in 2.7 years. Prep then becomes the limit: an extra prep worker per shift takes output to about 427.7k, and weekend overtime covers the rest. Evaluate the robot separately as a labour-saving project. Risk: freezer temperature compliance can't be compromised for speed. Next step: confirm the freezer supplier's lead time.
great: Rejects the proposal with numbers, not opinion
Sees the line is nearly balanced: each fix moves the bottleneck to the next step
Separates growth projects from cost projects
Handles the director's objection respectfully

title: Axion Electronics
sub: Shortages at a circuit-board plant: the hidden bottleneck
skills: Hidden bottlenecks · yield and rework · capacity
prompt: Axion assembles circuit boards in Penang for industrial customers. It can't meet demand of 320,000 boards a year, and customers are threatening to dual-source. Engineering wants a $950k upgrade to make the pick-and-place machine 27% faster. The plant director asks you to test the proposal.

clarify.a: Print solder paste, pick-and-place components, reflow oven, automated test.
Pick-and-place 180 boards/hour; tester 175 tests/hour. Printing and reflow are faster than both.
91% of boards pass test first time. Failed boards are reworked and retested once; 60% of those then pass.
Hours: 1,920 a year. Each extra good board earns $42.

structure.root: How can Axion meet demand?

hypothesis: The tester is nominally only a little slower than pick-and-place, but every failed board is tested twice. With 9% failing, the tester is probably the real bottleneck, so a faster pick-and-place wouldn't help.

questions.q: How many boards per hour can the line actually start, and how many good boards a year does it produce?
questions.answer:
Each started board uses 1 + 9% = 1.09 tests. The tester can handle 175 ÷ 1.09 = 160.6 boards started per hour, below pick-and-place's 180. The tester is the bottleneck.

Good boards per board started: 91% + 9% × 60% = 96.4%.

Annual output: 160.6 × 1,920 × 96.4% = 297.2k good boards, against demand of 320k.
questions.note: This is the crux. Retests silently eat tester capacity.

questions.q: What would engineering's $950k pick-and-place upgrade deliver?
questions.answer: Nothing: the tester still limits the line to 160.6 starts an hour. Output stays at 297.2k. $950k for zero extra boards.

questions.q: Two alternatives: solder-paste inspection that raises first-pass yield to 96% ($400k), or a second tester ($600k). Compare them.
questions.answer:
Better yield: tests per board 1.04, so the tester handles 168.3 starts an hour; good per start 98.4%: output 317.9k (+20.7k), worth $871k a year: payback 0.5 years.

Second tester: pick-and-place becomes the bottleneck at 180/hour: output 320.0k (capped at demand) (+22.8k), worth $959k a year: payback 0.6 years.

So-what: the second tester meets demand; better yield gets most of the way for less and also cuts rework labour.

questions.q: Which would you recommend, and why?
questions.answer:
Start with solder-paste inspection: for $400k, less than half of engineering's proposal, it lifts output to 317.9k (99% of demand), cuts rework labour and improves quality for customers. Cover the last 2.1k boards with tester overtime.

Buy the second tester ($600k) when demand grows beyond today's 320k, or sooner if a tester breakdown would put key customers at risk.

reco: Don't approve the $950k pick-and-place upgrade: the real bottleneck is the tester, because every failed board is tested twice, so faster placement adds no output. Today the line makes about 297.2k good boards against 320k demand. I recommend solder-paste inspection to raise first-pass yield to 96% (about 317.9k boards, payback 0.5 years), with tester overtime for the remaining 2.1k; add a second tester once demand grows. Risk: yield gains take time to stabilise. Next step: install inspection on one line and measure first-pass yield for a month.
great: Accounts for retests when computing tester capacity
Proves the proposed upgrade adds nothing
Compares a quality fix with a capacity fix
Recommends the cheaper fix first, and the capacity fix when demand needs it

title: Heatherfield Hotels
sub: Should a hotel group run its own laundry?
skills: Make vs buy · payback · break-even volume
prompt: Heatherfield Hotels owns six hotels in Scotland with 900 rooms between them. All sheets and towels go to an outside laundry. The operations director wants to build a central laundry for $1.8M to cut costs. The CEO asks you whether it's worth it.

clarify.a: About 4 kg per occupied room per night. Occupancy averages 75% all year.

clarify.q: What does the outside laundry charge?
clarify.a: $0.95 per kg, including collection and delivery.
About $0.48 per kg for staff, energy, chemicals and vans, plus $250k a year of fixed costs: a manager, maintenance and insurance.
Five years. The equipment lasts about ten.

structure.root: Should Heatherfield build its own laundry?

branches.head: Non-financial
items: Risk if the plant breaks down

hypothesis: In-house laundries pay off at scale. With only six hotels the fixed costs may eat most of the saving, so volume will decide it.

questions.q: How much does Heatherfield spend on laundry today, and what would it cost in-house?
questions.answer:
Volume: 900 × 365 × 75% × 4 kg = 986 tonnes a year.

Outsourced: 986k kg × $0.95 = $936k. In-house: 986k × $0.48 + $250k = $723k.

Saving: $213k a year.

questions.q: Does it meet the five-year payback target?
questions.answer:
Payback = $1,800k ÷ $213k = 8.4 years, well beyond five, though inside the equipment's ten-year life.

A five-year payback needs a saving of $1,800k ÷ 5 = $360k a year. Adding back the $250k of fixed costs, the margin over outsourcing must reach $610k; at $0.47 a kg that takes 1,300 tonnes a year, 32% more than today.

So-what: on today's six hotels, no.
questions.note: Each kg saves $0.95 − $0.48 = $0.47 before fixed costs.

questions.q: The CEO mentions plans to open three more hotels (450 rooms) within two years. Does that change your answer?
questions.answer:
Volume rises to 1,478 tonnes. Saving: 1,478k × $0.47 − $250k = $445k. Payback: 4.0 years, within target.

So-what: the decision depends on the expansion. Build only if the new hotels are committed, and size the plant for them. This assumes the $1.8M plant can handle the larger volume and the new hotels are open from the start: if the plant ran on today's volume for two years first, payback would be about 5.1 years, so time the build to the openings.

questions.q: What else would you check before deciding?
questions.answer:
• Quality and speed: does the outside laundry cause complaints or stock-outs?
  • Risk: one plant serving all hotels needs a backup contract
  • Contract: could Heatherfield negotiate a lower outside price with its larger volume, which may beat building?
  • Site and staff: land, permits, hiring

reco: Don't build the laundry on today's six hotels: it saves about $213k a year, a payback of 8.4 years against a five-year target. If the three new hotels are committed, the saving rises to about $445k and payback falls to 4.0 years, so build when they open (two years at today's volume first would push payback to about 5.1 years), sized for 1,350 rooms. Meanwhile, use the coming volume to negotiate a lower price with the outside laundry. Risk: a single plant is a single point of failure, so keep a backup contract.
great: Computes volume from rooms and occupancy
Separates variable from fixed costs
Works out the volume needed to hit the target
Ties the answer to the expansion plan

title: Quantum API
sub: Leave the cloud? Only partly.
skills: Make vs buy · total cost of ownership · peak vs average load
prompt: Quantum runs payment APIs for online shops. Its cloud bill is $14M a year and growing 25% a year with the business. The CTO proposes moving everything onto servers Quantum owns, in rented data-centre space, saying it would halve the bill. The CFO asks you to test it over the next four years.

clarify.a: About 60% is steady traffic that runs all day. 40% is spiky: big sales days and batch jobs, sometimes 5× normal load for a few hours.
$12M of servers, sized for year-4 volume and lasting four years, plus $2M to migrate. Then $1.8M a year for space and power, and 8 engineers at $180k each.

clarify.q: Cost to move spiky work too?
clarify.a: Owned servers would have to be sized for year-4 peaks: another $24M of servers, $1M to migrate, $1.6M a year of space and power, 4 more engineers.
Ignore resale value of servers after four years.

structure.root: Should Quantum move off the cloud, and how much of it?

hypothesis: Owning servers is cheap for steady load but expensive for peaks, because you pay for peak capacity all year. I expect moving only the steady part to win.

questions.q: Here is the projected cloud bill. What would it cost over four years to stay on the cloud?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Cloud bill at 25% growth a year

questions.answer: Four-year cloud bill: $80.7M.

questions.q: Compare: move only the steady work (hybrid), or move everything.
questions.answer:
Hybrid: servers $12M + migration $2M + running $3.24M × 4 = $27.0M, plus the spiky cloud bill $32.3M = $59.2M. Saving: $21.5M.

Everything: hybrid's own costs plus $24M + $1M + $2.32M × 4 for the spiky part = $61.2M. Saving: $19.5M.

So-what: moving the spiky work costs $34.3M against $32.3M of cloud bill: it loses money. The cloud is cheapest exactly where load is uneven.

questions.q: The CTO says the full move 'halves the bill'. Where does that come from, and what is it missing?
questions.answer: It probably compares the yearly running cost of owned servers with the cloud bill, ignoring the upfront servers, migration and, most of all, the extra capacity needed for peaks. Other risks: reliability (Quantum now runs its own hardware), hiring 12 specialist engineers, and the team's attention moving away from the product.

reco: Move only the steady 60% of workloads onto owned servers and keep the spiky work on the cloud. Over four years that costs about $59.2M against $80.7M for staying on the cloud, saving about $21.5M. Moving everything saves less ($19.5M), because servers sized for rare peaks sit idle most of the time. Risk: reliability and hiring, so migrate in stages with a fallback to the cloud. Next step: confirm how steady the 60% really is with three months of usage data.
great: Splits steady from spiky load
Includes upfront, migration and running costs over the full period
Spots that peak capacity makes owning expensive
Challenges the 'halves the bill' claim with numbers

title: Marble Auto Parts
sub: Outsource a part to save money, or to free the factory?
skills: Make vs buy · relevant costs · opportunity cost
prompt: Marble makes brake systems in Monterrey for car makers. A supplier has offered to make Marble's caliper housings for $36 each. Marble's cost accounts show they cost $42 to make in-house, so the finance team wants to outsource all 500,000 a year. The COO asks whether that's right.

clarify.a: Materials $18, direct labour $9, variable overhead $5, and $10 of factory overhead allocated per unit.

clarify.q: What happens to the overhead if we outsource?
clarify.a: Only about 20% would go: the rest is rent, depreciation and management, which stay.

clarify.q: Would the freed machines sit idle?
clarify.a: Not necessarily. Marble buys 400,000 brackets a year at $28 each; it could make them on the freed line for $21 each in variable cost, after $0.8M of one-off tooling.
Reputable, with a two-year price guarantee.

structure.root: Should Marble outsource caliper housings?

hypothesis: The $42 includes allocated overhead that won't disappear, so the real saving may be smaller than it looks. But what the freed capacity can do may matter more.

questions.q: Finance says outsourcing saves $3M a year. Is that right?
questions.answer:
Finance compares the full cost ($42) with the quote ($36): ($42 − $36) × 500k = $3.0M.

But only 20% of the $10 overhead goes away. Cost that actually disappears: $18 + $9 + $5 + $2 = $34, which is less than the $36 quote.

Outsourcing on its own would cost $1.0M more a year, not save $3M.
questions.note: The classic trap: allocated fixed costs are not saved by outsourcing.

questions.q: Now consider the freed line. What is the full picture?
questions.answer:
Making brackets in-house saves ($28 − $21) × 400k = $2.8M a year.

Net effect of outsourcing housings and insourcing brackets: −$1.0M + $2.8M = +$1.8M a year, after one-off tooling of $0.8M (paid back in under a year).

So-what: outsource the housings, but because of what the line can make instead, not because of the accounting cost.

questions.q: What would make you hesitate?
questions.answer:
• Safety: brake parts are safety-critical; audit the supplier's quality system and run a dual-source period
  • Price after two years: negotiate a longer guarantee or an index-linked price
  • Know-how: is caliper casting a skill Marble wants to keep?
  • Bracket quality: Marble must prove it can make brackets to spec

reco: Outsource the caliper housings and use the freed line to make brackets in-house, which nets about $1.8M a year. Finance's $3M saving is wrong: most of the $10 overhead stays, so outsourcing alone would cost about $1.0M more. The gain comes from making brackets for $21 instead of buying at $28. Risk: brake parts are safety-critical, so audit the supplier and keep a dual-source period. Next step: trial 10% of housing volume with the supplier while tooling up for brackets.
great: Separates avoidable from allocated costs
Overturns the finance team's number
Values the freed capacity (opportunity cost)
Raises safety and supplier risk for a brake part

title: BlueTide Seafood
sub: Own the trucks, or keep paying a logistics firm?
skills: Make vs buy · utilisation · hidden costs and benefits
prompt: BlueTide distributes frozen seafood to restaurants and grocers along the US East Coast. A logistics company (a 3PL) does all its refrigerated trucking for $2.40 a loaded mile. The COO wants to buy BlueTide's own fleet of 40 refrigerated trucks. The CEO asks you whether owning is cheaper, and whether it's the right move.

clarify.a: About 4.4 million loaded miles a year.
Trucks cost $180k each and last six years. Drivers cost $95k per truck a year. Fuel and maintenance $0.95 a mile. Insurance and admin $0.6M a year.
Trucks come back mostly empty: empty miles add about 35% to the loaded miles. The 3PL charges only for loaded miles because it fills return trips with other customers' freight.

clarify.q: Could BlueTide sell its empty return capacity?
clarify.a: Probably about half of it, to other shippers, at about $1.60 a mile.
About 1.2% of cargo value spoils in transit with the 3PL, through temperature failures. BlueTide ships $150M of product a year.

structure.root: Should BlueTide run its own fleet?

branches.head: Own-fleet cost
items: Fuel and maintenance, including empty miles

branches.head: Risks
items: Running a fleet is not our core skill

hypothesis: On loaded miles alone owning looks cheaper, but empty return trips could wipe that out. Spoilage could be the deciding factor, since seafood is valuable.

questions.q: Compare yearly cost: 3PL vs own fleet, counting only loaded miles.
questions.answer:
3PL: 4.4M × $2.40 = $10.56M.

Own fleet: depreciation $7,200k ÷ 6 = $1.2M; drivers 40 × $95k = $3.8M; fuel and maintenance 4.4M × $0.95 = $4.18M; admin $0.6M. Total $9.78M.

Owning looks $0.78M a year cheaper.

questions.q: Now include the empty return miles.

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · From 3PL cost to own-fleet cost ($M a year)

questions.answer:
Empty miles: 35% × 4.4M = 1.54M, costing $1.46M. Own fleet: $11.24M, now $0.68M more than the 3PL.

If BlueTide sells half its return capacity to other shippers at $1.60 a mile, it earns $1.23M: net cost $10.01M, $0.55M cheaper than the 3PL.

So-what: on transport cost alone, owning saves only about 5%, and only if half the return trips are filled. That is a thin, fragile margin.

questions.q: BlueTide's own trucks would carry temperature sensors with live alerts, cutting spoilage to about 0.5%. What does that change?
questions.answer:
Spoilage saving: $150M × (1.2% − 0.5%) = $1.05M a year, more than any difference in transport cost.

Total yearly gain from owning: $1.60M. Cash payback on the $7.2M fleet: $7.2M ÷ ($1.60M gain + $1.2M non-cash depreciation) = 2.6 years.

So-what: the case for owning is about product quality, not trucking cost. That raises a question: could the 3PL fit the same sensors for less?

questions.q: What would you recommend, and what would you check first?
questions.answer:
• Ask the 3PL to commit to sensor monitoring and a spoilage penalty in its contract. If it agrees, most of the gain comes without owning trucks.
  • If not, build a fleet for the core, predictable routes and keep the 3PL for peaks and long-haul.
  • Check: the 1.2% spoilage figure, how reliably return loads can be sold, and driver availability.

reco: On trucking cost alone, owning a fleet saves only about 5% once empty return trips are counted, and only if BlueTide can sell half its return capacity. The real prize is spoilage: better temperature control saves about $1.05M a year. First, ask the 3PL to fit sensors and accept a spoilage penalty, which captures most of that gain without $7.2M of trucks. If it won't, buy a fleet for the core routes and keep the 3PL for peaks (a full 40-truck fleet would gain about $1.60M a year, cash payback 2.6 years; a smaller fleet scales this down). Risk: running a fleet is a new skill. Next step: verify spoilage by route.
great: Builds the own-fleet cost line by line
Catches the empty-return-mile trap
Finds that spoilage outweighs trucking cost
Looks for a way to get the benefit without the asset

title: Tessera Analytics
sub: Growing 20% a year, but leaking customers
skills: SaaS metrics · churn and net revenue retention · prioritisation
prompt: Tessera sells analytics software to retailers on annual subscriptions. It has $30M of annual recurring revenue (ARR) and grew about 20% last year. The board wants 30% growth next year. The CEO wants to double the sales team. The COO thinks the problem is customers leaving. You have $3M of extra budget to allocate.

clarify.a: The yearly value of all active subscriptions.
About $9M of new ARR a year from new customers.
Besides those who leave, existing customers downgrade about 3% of ARR a year and upgrade about 8%.
Every extra $1 of sales and marketing brings about $0.80 of new ARR.

structure.root: How can Tessera reach 30% ARR growth?

hypothesis: ARR growth = new ARR − ARR lost + upgrades. If a big share of ARR leaves every year, adding salespeople just refills a leaking bucket. I'd find where churn is concentrated first.

questions.q: Here is churn by segment. Walk me through next year's ARR and the gap to target.

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Churn by segment, last year

questions.answer:
Lost to churn: $4.56M (15.2% of ARR). Next year: $30M − $4.56M − $0.9M downgrades + $2.4M upgrades + $9M new = $35.9M, 20% growth.

Net revenue retention (what existing customers are worth a year later) is 90%. Target: $39.0M, a gap of $3.1M.

So-what: small businesses are only 20% of ARR but 53% of the ARR lost.

questions.q: Three ideas: (A) automated onboarding for small businesses, $0.5M, cutting their churn from 40% to 25%; (B) customer-success managers for mid-market, $1.0M, cutting churn from 12% to 7%; (C) more sales spend, $1.5M. Compare them.
questions.answer:
A saves $0.90M of ARR: $1.8 per $1. B saves $0.60M: $0.6 per $1. C adds $1.2M: $0.8 per $1.

Kept ARR is worth as much as new ARR: both recur next year. So A is by far the best use of money, then C, then B.

questions.q: Can Tessera hit 30% next year?
questions.answer:
With A and C: $38.0M (27% growth). Adding B too: $38.6M (29%). All three fall short of $39.0M.

So-what: tell the board 30% is a stretch. To close the last gap, look at upgrades: 8% expansion is low for analytics software; a paid add-on for existing customers could help.

reco: Prioritise retention before doubling the sales team. Small businesses make up 20% of ARR but 53% of the ARR lost, so automated onboarding for them is the best use of money: about $1.8 of ARR kept per $1, against $0.8 for extra sales spend. Fund onboarding ($0.5M) and $1.5M of extra sales spend; that gets growth to about 27%. Customer-success managers for mid-market ($1.0M) lift it to about 29%, still short of 30%; the rest has to come from selling more to existing customers. Risk: automated onboarding may not cut churn as much as planned, so pilot it on new sign-ups first.
great: Builds next year's ARR from churn, downgrades, upgrades and new sales
Finds where churn is concentrated in dollars, not customers
Compares options on ARR per dollar
Tells the board the target is a stretch, with numbers

title: Tallyline Payroll
sub: A discount that would lose money on its best customers
skills: Customer lifetime value · selection bias · pricing
prompt: Tallyline sells payroll software to small businesses for $100 a month, billed monthly. Its 20,000 customers can cancel any month. The marketing team wants to offer a 15% discount to anyone who switches to a yearly plan, arguing that yearly customers stay much longer. The CFO asks whether this makes money.

clarify.a: On monthly plans, about 3% cancel each month. Yearly-plan customers at a similar firm renew 80% of the time.
Surveys suggest about 30% of current customers would take the yearly plan. They are mostly long-standing customers, who cancel only about 1.5% a month.
About 8,000 sign up a year; around 40% would choose a yearly plan if offered.

structure.root: Should Tallyline offer a 15% discount for yearly plans?

branches.head: Existing customers who switch
items: Revenue now vs on a yearly plan

branches.head: New customers
items: Do yearly plans keep them longer?

hypothesis: Yearly plans do keep customers longer, but the customers who choose them are often the loyal ones who would have stayed anyway. Then the discount is just a price cut.

questions.q: Compare the expected lifetime revenue of a customer on each plan, using the averages marketing quotes.
questions.answer:
Monthly: at 3% a month, an average customer stays 1 ÷ 3% = 33.3 months: $3,330.

Yearly: $85 a month; at 20% cancelling each year, an average customer stays 1 ÷ 20% = 5 years: 60 × $85 = $5,100. Yearly plans look 53% better.
questions.note: Average lifetime = 1 ÷ churn rate, for a constant churn rate.

questions.q: But the customers who would switch cancel only 1.5% a month. Redo the comparison for them.

rows: Typical new customer (3% a month), if the yearly plan keeps them 5 years
exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Lifetime revenue per customer

questions.answer:
These customers already stay about 1 ÷ 1.5% = 66.7 months on a monthly plan: $6,670. A yearly plan doesn't make them stay longer; they were staying anyway.

So for them the discount is simply a 15% price cut: 66.7 months × $85 = $5,670, $1,000 less each. For 6,000 switchers that is about $6.0M of lifetime revenue lost.

So-what: the people most likely to take the offer are the ones who need it least. Marketing's comparison mixes up "yearly plans cause loyalty" with "loyal customers choose yearly plans".

questions.q: Is there a version of the offer that works?
questions.answer:
• Offer it to new customers only, at sign-up. If yearly plans keep them closer to 5 years, each is worth up to $1,770 more: up to $5.7M a year for 3,200 yearly sign-ups. But test it: some will be loyal types who would have stayed anyway.
  • Smaller discount (for example 1 month free on a yearly plan, about 8% off) only for customers showing signs of leaving.
  • Don't offer it to the existing base, or only to those whose usage is falling.

reco: Don't offer the 15% yearly-plan discount to existing customers: the 30% who would switch are loyal customers who cancel only 1.5% a month, and would stay just as long anyway, so the discount is a pure price cut: about $1,000 less each over their lifetime, around $6.0M in total. Offer yearly plans to new customers at sign-up and test whether they really stay longer, and use targeted offers for existing customers who look likely to leave. Risk: competitors may push yearly discounts anyway. Next step: run a sign-up test for two months.
great: Uses 1 ÷ churn for average lifetime
Spots that switchers are the loyal customers
Values the offer separately for existing and new customers
Redesigns the offer instead of just rejecting it

title: Brushline Studio
sub: Sign-ups are up 60%. Why isn't revenue?
skills: Cohort analysis · LTV vs CAC · channel economics
prompt: Brushline makes a design app for small online sellers, at $12 a month. Last year it started buying ads on social media, and paying sign-ups rose 60%. But revenue grew much less than that, and cash is tight. The founder asks what's going on and what to do.

clarify.a: Before the ads, almost all came through word of mouth, search and referrals. Now half come from social ads.
About $40 per paying user through organic and referral marketing; about $90 through social ads.
About 80% gross margin.

structure.root: Is Brushline's growth profitable?

hypothesis: Paid ads often bring users who try the app and leave. If they leave fast enough, each one costs more to acquire than they ever pay.

questions.q: Here is retention by channel. What do you see?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · % of users still paying, by month since sign-up

questions.answer: Ad users drop off fast: only 45% are still paying in month 3 against 70% for organic users, and they keep cancelling faster after that (9% a month against 4%). By month 12, 48% of organic users remain vs 19% of ad users.

questions.q: Work out a user's lifetime value against the cost to acquire them, for each channel.
questions.answer:
Expected months paid = the first three months, then each later month at the channel's cancel rate: organic about 19.3 months, ads about 6.6 months.

Lifetime gross profit = months × $12 × 80%: organic $185, ads $64.

Against acquisition cost: organic 4.6× its $40 cost; ads 0.71× its $90. Each ad user loses about $26.
questions.note: A common rule of thumb: value should be at least 3× the cost to acquire.

questions.q: What should the founder do?
questions.answer:
• Cut social ad spend sharply; keep only ad sets whose users retain like organic users
  • Fix the first 3 months for all users: onboarding templates, a first sale tracked in the app
  • Put money into referrals, the channel that works: a free month for both sides
  • Track value ÷ cost by channel every month, not total sign-ups

reco: Brushline's ad-driven growth destroys value: ad users stay about 7 months against 19 for organic users, so each is worth about $64 of gross profit but costs $90 to acquire. I recommend cutting most social ad spend, investing in referrals (4.6× return), and improving the first three months to lift retention for every channel. Risk: sign-up growth will slow, so explain to investors why that is healthy. Next step: report retention and value ÷ cost by channel monthly.
great: Reads cohort retention curves by channel
Turns retention into lifetime value
Compares lifetime value with acquisition cost
Recommends cutting a growth channel, with reasons

title: Flowkeep
sub: Switching to usage pricing: who wins and who walks?
skills: Pricing model change · winners and losers · break-even churn
prompt: Flowkeep sells workflow-automation software to mid-sized companies at $40 per user (seat) a month. The new head of product wants to switch everyone to usage pricing: $0.02 per automation run, because 'heavy users get far more value than they pay for'. The CEO asks you what it would do to revenue.

clarify.a: 1,000 customers: 600 light (10 seats, 500 runs per seat a month), 300 medium (25 seats, 2,000 runs), 100 heavy (80 seats, 6,000 runs).
Monthly, so customers can leave quickly.
Two rivals charge per seat; one charges per run.
Grow revenue without losing the biggest accounts.

structure.root: What happens if Flowkeep switches to usage pricing?

hypothesis: Usage pricing moves money from light users to heavy users. Revenue could jump on paper, but heavy users would see their bills rise sharply and might leave. I'd check how many heavy customers we can afford to lose.

questions.q: Calculate each segment's monthly bill now and under usage pricing.
questions.answer:
Light: $400 → $100. Medium: $1,000 → $1,000. Heavy: $3,200 → $9,600, 3× today.

Total monthly revenue: $860k → $1,320k (+53%) if nobody leaves.

questions.q: How many heavy customers could leave before Flowkeep is worse off?
questions.answer:
The gain is $460k a month. Each heavy customer who leaves takes $9,600. Flowkeep breaks even if 48 of 100 heavy customers leave: 48%.

So-what: a 3× price rise on monthly contracts, with seat-priced rivals available, could well push half of them out. The upside is real but fragile.

questions.q: Light customers' bills fall by 75%. Is that a problem or an opportunity?
questions.answer: It costs $180k a month in revenue immediately. But a $100 starting bill makes Flowkeep easier to try, which could bring in more new customers who grow over time. That benefit is uncertain and takes time; the revenue loss is certain and immediate.

questions.q: Design a better pricing change.
questions.answer:
• Platform fee + usage, with a minimum so light customers pay at least close to today
  • Cap heavy bills (for example $6,000 a month): revenue still rises to about $960k (+12%) if all stay, with much less risk of losing them
  • New customers first; move existing ones at renewal with 6 to 12 months' notice and annual-contract options
  • Talk to the 20 largest heavy customers before announcing anything

reco: Don't switch everyone to pure usage pricing. Revenue would rise 53% on paper, but heavy customers' bills would rise 3× and Flowkeep is worse off if 48% of them leave, while light customers would immediately pay 75% less. I recommend a platform fee plus usage with a minimum and a cap, applied first to new customers and then to existing ones at renewal. With a $6,000 cap, revenue still rises about 12% if customers stay. Next step: test reactions with the 20 largest accounts.
great: Models the bill change for each segment
Finds the break-even share of heavy customers who can leave
Sees both sides: heavy users pay more, light users pay less
Designs a transition for the existing base

title: Stonebridge Tiles
sub: Sell through distributors or build a sales team?
skills: Channel strategy · unit economics by segment
prompt: Stonebridge makes ceramic floor tiles and is entering Texas. It can either hire its own sales reps to sell directly to builders, or sign up local building-supply distributors, who buy at a discount and resell. The commercial director asks which route to take.

clarify.a: 150 large contractors spending about $200k a year on tiles, and 1,500 small builders spending about $20k.
Stonebridge earns 35% gross margin at list price. Distributors buy at 20% off list.
Each costs $150k a year. A rep can look after 25 large accounts or about 30 small ones.
Assume Stonebridge wins about 20% of accounts either way.

structure.root: Which route to market should Stonebridge use in Texas?

branches.head: Reach and speed
items: How many accounts each route covers

hypothesis: Big accounts can carry the cost of a rep; small ones probably can't. I expect a split: direct for large contractors, distributors for small builders.

questions.q: Work out the yearly profit per account for each route and segment.

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Profit per account by route

questions.answer:
Large: direct 35% × $200k − $150k ÷ 25 = $64k; distributor (35% − 20%) × $200k = $30k.

Small: direct 35% × $20k − $150k ÷ 30 = $2.0k; distributor 15% × $20k = $3.0k.

So-what: direct wins for large accounts; distributors win for small ones, where a rep's time costs more than the margin given away.

questions.q: What is the total profit of each approach, at 20% of accounts won?
questions.answer:
Accounts won: 30 large, 300 small.

  • All direct: $2.52M before rounding reps; it needs 11.2 reps' worth of accounts, so 12 reps: about $2.40M
  • All distributor: $1.80M
  • Split (direct large, distributor small): $2.82M

The split needs 1.2 reps' worth of accounts. In practice Stonebridge hires 2, which costs $120k more than the per-account figures assume: about $2.70M, still the best option.

questions.q: What would worry you about the split?
questions.answer:
• Channel conflict: distributors may want the large accounts too; agree clear account lists
  • Price consistency: a builder could see different prices; set a price list both use
  • Dependence: pick two distributors, not one

reco: Use both routes: a small direct team for the 150 large contractors and distributors for the 1,500 small builders. A large account earns $64k a year sold direct versus $30k through a distributor, while a small account earns more through a distributor because a rep's time costs more than the margin given away. The split earns about $2.70M a year at a 20% win rate with two reps, more than either route alone. Risk: channel conflict, so agree account lists with distributors upfront.
great: Computes profit per account, not just revenue
Includes rep cost per account
Sees the answer differs by segment
Raises channel conflict

title: Arcline Aligners
sub: Direct to patients, or through orthodontists?
skills: Channel choice · unit economics · hidden costs
prompt: Arcline makes clear teeth-straightening aligners. Its founders want to sell directly to patients online, at $1,900 a treatment with remote check-ins by contracted dentists. A board member argues it should instead sell through orthodontists, who would buy aligners and treat patients in their own clinics. Which route should Arcline launch with?

clarify.a: Aligners cost $600 to make; the remote dentist review costs $250 a patient; marketing costs about $450 per patient won.
In direct sales about 15% of patients are found unsuitable or unhappy and get a full refund, but the aligners and review are already paid for.
Orthodontists pay $1,100 per treatment; Arcline's sales team costs about $100 per case.
About 20,000 patients a year direct; about 30,000 cases a year through orthodontists once 1,500 clinics are signed.

structure.root: Which route gives Arcline the better business?

hypothesis: Direct looks better per case because Arcline keeps the full price. But refunds and marketing costs eat into it, and orthodontists bring volume and clinical oversight.

questions.q: Compare profit per case for the two routes.
questions.answer:
Direct, as the founders see it: $1,900 − $600 − $250 − $450 = $600.

Direct, with refunds: only 85% of patients pay, but every patient costs the aligners, review and marketing: 85% × $1,900 − $1,300 = $315.

Orthodontists: $1,100 − $600 − $100 = $400.

questions.q: What about total profit?
questions.answer:
Direct: 20k × $315 = $6.3M. Orthodontists: 30k × $400 = $12.0M.

So-what: the orthodontist route wins on both profit per case and volume, once refunds are counted.

questions.q: Beyond the numbers, what else favours one route?
questions.answer:
• Clinical risk: remote-only treatment has a higher risk of poor outcomes and complaints; in-clinic care lowers refunds and protects the brand
  • Regulation: dental boards in several states restrict remote treatment
  • Direct's advantage: Arcline owns the patient relationship and can sell retainers and whitening later

reco: Launch through orthodontists. Once the 15% refund rate is counted, a direct case earns about $315 against $400 through an orthodontist, and orthodontists bring more volume: about $12.0M a year against $6.3M. They also lower clinical and regulatory risk. Keep direct sales as a later option for retainers and follow-up products. Risk: orthodontists may push their existing brands, so offer training and marketing support. Next step: sign 50 pilot clinics.
great: Includes refunds, where costs are incurred but revenue is lost
Compares profit per case and total profit
Raises clinical and regulatory risk
Keeps an option open for the direct route

title: Vivid Career Courses
sub: Sell to learners or sell to employers?
skills: B2C vs B2B · customer lifetime value · renewals
prompt: Vivid sells online courses in data and digital skills to individual learners for $400 each, mostly through online ads. Growth has stalled as ad costs rise. Its head of sales wants to start selling seats to employers for staff training. The CEO asks whether the employer route is worth building.

clarify.a: Each costs about $220 in ads to win. Delivery (platform, tutors, certificates) costs $40 a learner. About 10% buy a second course later, at a $30 marketing cost.
Vivid would charge $250 a seat. A typical deal is 200 seats and costs about $15,000 of sales effort.
Similar providers see about 70% of employers renew each year, at a small account-management cost of about $10 a seat.

structure.root: Should Vivid build an employer (B2B) business?

hypothesis: Per seat, employer deals look worse because the price is lower. But employers renew, so the cost to win is paid once and the profit repeats. I'd compare over three years.

questions.q: Compare first-year profit per learner or seat.
questions.answer:
Individual: $400 − $220 − $40 = $140. Employer seat: $250 − $15,000 ÷ 200 − $40 = $135.

About the same in year 1, despite the lower price, because winning a seat costs far less than winning an individual.

questions.q: Now compare over three years.

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Three-year profit per learner or seat ($)

questions.answer:
Employer seat: year 1 $135; year 2: 70% renew × ($250 − $40 − $10) = $140; year 3: 49% × $200 = $98. Total $373.

Individual: $140 + 10% buy again × ($400 − $40 − $30) = $173.

So-what: over three years an employer seat earns 2.2× as much, because renewals don't need new marketing.

questions.q: What would it take to make the employer route work?
questions.answer:
• A small sales team targeting HR and learning heads at mid-sized firms
  • Employer features: progress reports, cohort scheduling, invoicing
  • Proof of results: completion rates and skills tests, since employers buy outcomes
  • Check the 70% renewal assumption with a pilot of 10 employers

reco: Build the employer route. A seat earns about the same as an individual learner in year 1 ($135 vs $140), but because employers renew, a seat earns about $373 over three years against $173 for an individual, 2.2× as much. Start with a small sales team and the reporting features employers need, while keeping the individual business. Risk: the 70% renewal rate is borrowed from other providers. Next step: pilot with 10 employers and measure completion and renewal intent.
great: Compares profit after the cost to win, not price
Looks beyond year 1 to renewals
Quantifies the three-year difference
Lists what the new channel needs to work

title: Ironvale Plant Hire
sub: An online rental platform: scale it up or shut it down?
skills: Channel economics · cannibalisation · break-even vs market size
prompt: Ironvale rents construction equipment to builders from 12 depots around Brisbane. A year ago it launched an online booking platform with delivery to site, aimed at small builders. Online orders are growing, but the platform loses money. The board must decide whether to invest more or close it. The CEO asks for your view.

clarify.a: The average online rental is $380 with a 55% contribution margin before delivery. Delivery and collection cost $95 an order, free to the customer.
About $60 to win a new online customer, who then places about 4 orders a year.
$1.2M a year for the platform, support and marketing team.
About 30% of online orders come from builders who used to walk into a depot.
About 9,000 small builders in the delivery area, each renting about 6 times a year.
About 4,000 online orders a year, from roughly 1,000 online customers.

structure.root: Should Ironvale scale or close the online platform?

branches.head: Cannibalisation
items: Orders that would have come to a depot anyway

hypothesis: Free delivery takes a big bite out of each order, and some online orders are depot customers switching, which adds nothing. The break-even could be out of reach unless delivery is charged.

questions.q: What does a new online order earn, and how many orders would break even?
questions.answer:
Contribution: 55% × $380 = $209. Less delivery $95 and marketing $60 ÷ 4 orders = $15: $99 per order.

Break-even: $1,200k ÷ $99 = 12.1k orders a year, against 4k today.

questions.q: Now account for the 30% of orders that come from depot customers.

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · What an online order is really worth ($)

questions.answer:
A depot customer moving online already earned $209 at the depot. Online, Ironvale now also pays $95 delivery: that order is worth −$95 extra.

Blended value per online order: 70% × $99 + 30% × (−$95) = $41. Break-even: $1,200k ÷ $41 = 29.4k orders.

The whole small-builder market is about 54k rentals a year, so break-even needs about 54% of every rental in the area. Not realistic.

Today, at 4k orders, the platform loses about $1.04M a year.

questions.q: What if Ironvale charged a $60 delivery fee, as most rivals do?
questions.answer:
Each order gains $60: $101 per order, before any benefit from click-and-collect. Break-even falls to 11.9k orders, about 22% of the market. Ambitious, but possible over a few years.

Some customers will drop off, and depot customers who don't want delivery should be offered free click-and-collect, which removes the cannibalisation cost.

reco: Don't scale the platform in its current form: free delivery and 30% cannibalisation leave each order worth about $41, so break-even needs about 54% of all small-builder rentals. Keep it, but change the model: charge a $60 delivery fee and offer free click-and-collect, which brings break-even to about 11.9k orders a year (22% of the market). Set a 12-month target and close the platform if order growth stalls below the break-even path. Risk: the fee may slow growth. Next step: test the fee in two postcodes.
great: Builds profit per order including delivery and marketing
Accounts for cannibalisation of depot orders
Checks break-even against the size of the market
Finds a lever that changes the answer and sets a kill date

title: Tidewell Foods
sub: A healthy-snack brand: worth $110M to us?
skills: M&A valuation · synergies · deal structure
prompt: Tidewell is a large US snack maker whose sales of crisps and crackers are flat. It wants to buy Greenleaf, a fast-growing healthy-snack brand, and the founders are asking $110M. Tidewell's CEO asks: should we buy, and is $110M the right price?

clarify.a: EBITDA (operating profit before depreciation) of $8M. Similar snack brands sell for about 10× EBITDA.
Tidewell could buy ingredients and packaging for Greenleaf more cheaply and share warehouses: about $2M a year.
Putting Greenleaf into Tidewell's 30,000 stores could add $15M of sales a year at a 25% margin. The sales team thinks it's a coin flip whether it fully happens.
About $6M one-off to combine systems and supply chains.

structure.root: Should Tidewell buy Greenleaf at $110M?

hypothesis: Greenleaf on its own is probably worth less than $110M, so the price depends on synergies. Cost savings are fairly certain; extra sales much less so.

questions.q: What is Greenleaf worth on its own, and what are the synergies worth?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · What Greenleaf is worth to Tidewell ($M)

questions.answer:
Standalone: $8M × 10 = $80M.

Cost synergies: $2M × 10 = $20M. Revenue synergies: $15M × 25% = $3.75M a year; at a 50% chance, $1.875M × 10 = $18.8M. Integration: −$6M.

Value to Tidewell: $112.8M, just above the $110M asking price.

questions.q: So should Tidewell pay $110M?
questions.answer:
At $110M Tidewell keeps only $2.8M of the value it creates, and that depends on the uncertain sales synergies. If they don't happen, the deal is worth $94M: Tidewell overpays by $16M.

So-what: buy, but pay up front only for what Tidewell controls (about $94M), and pay for the sales upside only if it arrives.

questions.q: How would you structure the offer?
questions.answer:
• Up front: about $94M, the standalone value plus cost savings less integration ($80M + $20M − $6M); open lower, around $88M, to leave room to negotiate
  • Earn-out: up to $16M more over three years if Greenleaf's sales through Tidewell's stores reach agreed targets. The sellers reach their $110M only if the sales synergy arrives
  • Keep the founders for two years, with part of the earn-out tied to their staying; the brand's appeal is in its founder story

reco: Buy Greenleaf, but not for $110M up front. On its own it is worth about $80M; certain cost savings add $20M and integration costs $6M, so Tidewell should pay about $94M up front. The extra-sales synergy is worth about $19M but is a coin flip, so pay for it through an earn-out tied to sales targets. Total value to Tidewell is about $113M, so offering $110M up front would hand almost all of it to the sellers. Risk: losing the founders, so tie part of the earn-out to their staying.
great: Values the target on its own first
Separates certain cost synergies from uncertain revenue synergies
Sets a walk-away price
Uses deal structure (earn-out) to share risk

title: Lattice Payments
sub: A bank wants a fintech. Is it worth the premium?
skills: M&A · premium vs synergies · build, partner or buy
prompt: A large UK bank wants to offer its small-business customers a modern payments app. Lattice, a fast-growing fintech, has agreed in principle to sell for $180M. The bank's strategy head asks you whether the price makes sense.

clarify.a: EBITDA of $6M, growing fast. Similar fintechs trade at about 15× EBITDA.
Offer the app to its 2 million small-business customers. Pilots suggest about 3% would adopt, each earning about $100 of profit a year.
About $1M a year from shared compliance and hosting.
About $10M one-off. Lattice's founders have said they may leave after a year.
Use 10× the yearly synergy, a little below Lattice's multiple because they are less certain.

structure.root: Should the bank buy Lattice for $180M?

hypothesis: Paying $180M for a company worth about $90M on its own means paying a $90M premium for synergies. I'd check whether the cross-selling can realistically earn that back.

questions.q: What is the bank paying for, beyond Lattice itself?
questions.answer:
Standalone value: $6M × 15 = $90M. The premium for synergies is $90M.

To justify it at 10×, the bank needs about $9M a year of synergies, plus enough to cover $10M of integration.

questions.q: Can the synergies deliver that?
questions.answer:
Cross-selling: 2 million × 3% = 60k users × $100 = $6M a year. Cost savings: $1M. Total $7M a year, worth $70M.

Maximum sensible price: $90M + $70M − $10M = $150M, $30M below the agreed price.

So-what: at $180M the bank would pay away more than all the value it creates, even if the 3% adoption is achieved.

questions.q: What alternatives would you put to the bank?
questions.answer:
• Partner (white-label): offer Lattice's app under the bank's brand and share revenue. If the bank keeps about 70% of the cross-sell profit, it earns ~$4.2M a year with no premium and no integration
  • Renegotiate: offer up to ~$150M, with part paid only if adoption passes 3%
  • Build: slower and risky for a bank; only if the app is truly strategic

reco: Don't buy Lattice at $180M. Lattice is worth about $90M on its own, and realistic synergies (about $7M a year from cross-selling and cost savings) justify at most about $150M. I recommend a white-label partnership, which gives the bank's customers the app and earns most of the cross-sell profit without paying a premium; or a revised offer of up to $150M with an earn-out. Risk: a rival bank may buy Lattice instead. Next step: test adoption with 20,000 customers through a partnership pilot.
great: Calculates the premium paid for synergies
Turns the premium into the synergies needed per year
Shows the deal destroys value even if the plan works
Offers partnership and renegotiation as alternatives

title: Corvane Medical
sub: A big orthopaedics deal, a competition regulator, and a debt limit
skills: M&A · antitrust remedies · leverage
prompt: Corvane makes hip and knee implants and has EBITDA of $240M. It wants to buy its rival Halden Ortho (EBITDA $60M) for $1.0B, paid with debt. The board asks you three things: is it worth it, will the competition regulator allow it, and can Corvane afford it?

clarify.a: Orthopaedic companies trade at about 14× EBITDA.
$45M a year of cost savings (closing two plants, shared overheads). About $10M a year of profit from cross-selling, judged 50% likely. $90M one-off integration.
In knee implants the combined company would hold about 55% of the market. Halden's knee business earns $20M EBITDA, and $12M of the plant savings depend on it.
Corvane has $300M of net debt today. Its lenders cap net debt at 3.5× EBITDA.

structure.root: Should Corvane buy Halden for $1.0B?

hypothesis: The synergies look large, so the deal is probably worth it on paper. The real questions are whether regulators force Corvane to sell the knee business, and whether the debt fits.

questions.q: What is Halden worth to Corvane?
questions.answer:
Standalone: $60M × 14 = $840M. Cost synergies: $45M × 14 = $630M. Revenue synergies: 50% × $10M × 14 = $70M. Integration −$90M.

Total: $1,450M against a $1,000M price. Strongly positive.

questions.q: At 55% of knee implants, the regulator will likely make Corvane sell Halden's knee business, probably at about 12× EBITDA. What is the deal worth then?
questions.answer:
Lose the knee business's value ($20M × 14 = $280M), gain sale proceeds ($20M × 12 = $240M), and lose $12M of plant savings (× 14 = $168M).

Value: $1,450M − $280M + $240M − $168M = $1,242M, still well above $1.0B.

So-what: the deal survives the likely remedy, so Corvane can offer it to the regulator up front and speed approval.

questions.q: Can Corvane fund it with debt?
questions.answer:
Debt after the deal: $300M + $1,000M = $1,300M. EBITDA: $240M + $60M = $300M (before synergies). Leverage 4.3×, above the 3.5× limit by $250M of debt.

Using the $240M from selling the knee business: ($1,300M − $240M) ÷ $280M = 3.8×, still slightly above the limit before synergies arrive.

The remaining gap is ($1,060M − 3.5 × $280M) = $80M. Options: pay about $80M of the price in Corvane shares, a small equity raise, or a temporary higher limit with lenders until synergies arrive in year 2.

reco: Buy Halden. It is worth about $1,450M to Corvane against a $1.0B price, and still about $1,242M after the likely forced sale of Halden's knee business, so offer that sale to the regulator up front. Debt would reach 4.3× EBITDA against a 3.5× limit; use the knee-sale proceeds and pay about $80M of the price in shares to stay within it. Risks: plant closures could disrupt supply to hospitals, and the regulator may ask for more. Next step: early talks with the regulator and lenders.
great: Values the deal with risk-weighted synergies
Checks the competition-law remedy and re-values the deal
Tests whether the financing fits the lenders' limit
Uses the remedy proceeds to solve the financing gap

title: Haulmark
sub: A trucking company wants to buy a freight app its rivals use
skills: M&A · channel conflict · partner vs buy
prompt: Redline is a large US trucking company. Its trucks often drive back empty. It wants to buy Haulmark, an app that matches shippers' loads with trucking firms, for $150M, to fill its empty return trips. The CEO asks whether the deal makes sense.

clarify.a: Revenue of $30M a year from fees on loads matched. Freight apps like it sell for about 4× revenue.
Priority access to loads on its return routes: about $8M a year of extra profit, which Redline values at 8×.
About 60% of Haulmark's fees come from trucking firms that compete with Redline.
In interviews, about half of those rivals say they would move to another app if Redline owned Haulmark.

structure.root: Should Redline buy Haulmark for $150M?

hypothesis: Haulmark is valuable because it is neutral. If Redline owns it, Redline's rivals may leave, and the app could lose much of its value.

questions.q: What is Haulmark worth to Redline, assuming nothing else changes?
questions.answer: Standalone: $30M × 4 = $120M. Benefit to Redline: $8M × 8 = $64M. Total $184M, above the $150M price.

questions.q: Now factor in rival carriers leaving.

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Value to Redline vs price ($M)

questions.answer:
60% of fees come from rivals and half of them leave: Haulmark loses 30% of its revenue. Standalone value falls to $84M.

Total value: $84M + $64M = $148M, below the $150M price. With fewer carriers, the app may also attract fewer shippers, so it could fall further.

So-what: buying Haulmark damages the very thing that makes it valuable: its neutrality.

questions.q: How else could Redline fill its empty return trips?
questions.answer:
• Commercial partnership with Haulmark: guaranteed volume on Redline's routes in return for first look at return loads. If it captures 75% of the benefit, that's ~$6M a year, worth about $48M at 8×, for no money up front. Buying is worth about −$2M after the price
  • Use several freight apps at once
  • Sign direct contracts with shippers on its main return lanes

reco: Don't buy Haulmark. On paper it is worth $184M to Redline, but about 60% of its fees come from Redline's rivals, and if half of them leave, the value falls to about $148M, below the $150M price. Instead, agree a partnership that gives Redline first access to return loads on its routes, which captures most of the ~$8M a year benefit without the purchase. Risk: a rival could buy Haulmark, so include a right to bid in the partnership. Next step: approach Haulmark with a volume-for-priority proposal.
great: Values the deal before and after customer reactions
Spots that neutrality is the asset
Shows the deal flips from positive to negative
Finds a way to get the benefit without buying

title: Crescent Dental Labs
sub: Can a fund triple its money on dental labs?
skills: Private equity returns · buy-and-build · value-creation bridge
prompt: A private equity fund is looking at Crescent, which makes crowns and dentures for dentists across the Midwest. Crescent has $10M of EBITDA and the owners want 8×: $80M. The fund needs at least 2.5× its money in five years. The deal partner's plan is to buy small local labs and fold them into Crescent. Does the deal work?

clarify.a: Half debt, half fund equity: $40M each.
About 4% a year from more procedures and an ageing population.
There are hundreds of small labs. The fund expects to buy 10 over five years, each with about $1M of EBITDA, at about 5×, funded with extra debt.
Crescent's cash flow can repay about $20M of debt over five years. Lab groups of Crescent's size or larger sell for about 9× EBITDA.

structure.root: Will the fund make 2.5× in five years?

hypothesis: Organic growth of 4% alone won't get to 2.5×. The returns probably depend on buying small labs cheaply and selling them as part of a bigger group at a higher multiple.

questions.q: First, what return would Crescent deliver without any add-ons?
questions.answer:
EBITDA in year 5: $10M × 1.04⁵ = $12.2M. Exit value at 9×: $109M. Debt: $40M − $20M = $20M. Equity: $89M.

Return: $89M ÷ $40M = 2.24× (about 17% a year), below the 2.5× target.

questions.q: Now add the buy-and-build plan.

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Where the fund's return comes from ($M)

questions.answer:
Ten labs × $1M × 5 = $50M of extra debt. EBITDA in year 5: $12.2M + $10M = $22.2M. Exit value at 9×: $199M.

Debt at exit: $40M + $50M − $20M = $70M. Equity: $129M. Return: 3.2× (about 26% a year).

So-what: buying labs at 5× and selling them as part of a group at 9× is what makes the deal work.
questions.note: Each add-on lab is bought for $5M but is worth $9M inside the group at exit.

questions.q: What if exit multiples don't rise and the group still sells at 8×?
questions.answer:
Exit value: $22.2M × 8 = $177M; equity $107M; return 2.7×. Still above target.

The bigger risk is execution: buying and integrating 10 labs in five years, and keeping their dentist customers.

reco: Invest, with the buy-and-build plan as the core of the case. On its own, Crescent returns only about 2.2× in five years. Adding 10 small labs at 5× EBITDA lifts EBITDA to about $22M and the return to about 3.2× (26% a year), and still 2.7× if the exit multiple stays at 8×. Risks: integrating labs and keeping their dentists, and paying more for add-ons as rivals copy the strategy. Next step: build a pipeline of 20 target labs before signing.
great: Computes entry equity, exit equity and the money multiple
Shows the business alone misses the target
Explains multiple arbitrage in buy-and-build
Stress-tests the exit multiple

title: Beacon Field Services
sub: One customer is a third of the business
skills: Private equity · customer concentration · returns and pricing
prompt: Beacon maintains heating, air-conditioning and electrical systems in offices and warehouses. A PE fund is considering buying it for 10× its $25M EBITDA: $250M. The fund needs 2.5× its money in five years. In due diligence you find that one property group provides 35% of Beacon's revenue, and its contract is up for renewal in year 2.

clarify.a: Debt of 5× EBITDA ($125M); the rest is fund equity.
Market growing about 8% a year; Beacon has kept pace.
Debt falls to about $75M by year 5 in the base case; to about $105M if the big client leaves, as cash flow drops.
Management says the relationship is strong. Industry data suggests about 30% of contracts this size are re-tendered and lost.
Assume the exit multiple stays at 10×.

structure.root: Should the fund buy Beacon at $250M?

hypothesis: Even the base case may be tight at 10×. The client concentration is the key risk: losing 35% of revenue in a leveraged deal hurts the equity a lot.

questions.q: What is the return in the base case, where the client renews?
questions.answer:
Equity in: $250M − $125M = $125M. Year-5 EBITDA: $25M × 1.08⁵ = $36.7M; exit at 10× = $367M; less $75M debt = $292M.

Return: 2.34× (19% a year). Already below the 2.5× target.

questions.q: And if the client leaves in year 2?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Returns by scenario at a $250M price

questions.answer:
EBITDA falls by 35% (assuming its margin is average): $23.9M in year 5. Exit $239M less $105M debt = $134M. Return: 1.1×.

Weighted by a 30% chance: 70% × $292M + 30% × $134M = $245M expected, 2.0×.

questions.q: At what price would the fund expect 2.5×?
questions.answer:
The fund needs equity in of $245M ÷ 2.5 = $98M. With $125M of debt, the price is $223M: about 8.9× EBITDA.

Other ways to protect the fund: make the deal conditional on the client renewing first, or defer part of the price until it does.

reco: Don't pay $250M. Even if the big client renews, the fund makes only about 2.3×; if it leaves (about a 30% chance), the return falls to about 1.1×, giving an expected 2.0×. Offer about 8.9× EBITDA (around $223M), or keep the $250M headline but defer part of it until the contract is renewed. Risk: another bidder may pay more. Next step: meet the client and test how likely it is to re-tender.
great: Computes base-case returns before worrying about risk
Quantifies the downside and the probability-weighted return
Works backwards to the right entry price
Uses deal structure to protect against a known risk

title: Banyan Language Schools
sub: Where will the value come from?
skills: Private equity value creation · operating leverage · EBITDA bridge
prompt: A PE fund is buying Banyan, which runs 40 English-language schools for children in Vietnam. The price is 9× EBITDA, with debt of 4× EBITDA. The partner asks you to build the value-creation plan: how much could EBITDA grow in five years, from which levers, and what return would that give?

clarify.a: Each school has 600 places and is 70% full. Families pay $3,000 a year. Teaching materials and part-time tutors cost $600 per student; rent and core staff $700k per school a year.
Management believes better marketing and timetabling can fill schools to 80%, fees can rise 5% with new digital homework tools, and 10 new schools can open in under-served cities.
Each costs about $2M to open, paid from cash flow, and within three years reaches the same economics as an existing school after the improvements (80% full, fees 5% higher).
About $30M.

structure.root: How much value can the fund create at Banyan?

branches.head: Returns
items: Exit value − debt vs equity in

hypothesis: Schools have high fixed costs, so each extra student is very profitable. I expect filling empty seats to be the biggest lever.

questions.q: What does one school earn today, and what is Banyan's EBITDA?
questions.answer:
Students: 600 × 70% = 420. Each contributes $3,000 − $600 = $2,400: $1,008k. Less $700k fixed: $308k per school.

Across 40 schools: $12.3M EBITDA.

questions.q: Build the EBITDA bridge to year 5.
questions.answer:
Fill to 80%: +60 students × $2,400 = +$144k per school; × 40 = +$5.76M.

Fees +5%: $150 more × 480 students = +$72k per school; × 40 = +$2.88M.

10 new schools at mature economics ($524k each): +$5.24M, needing $20M of capital.

Year-5 EBITDA: $26.2M, about 2.1× today.
questions.note: Fixed costs mean a 14% rise in students lifts school profit by 47%.

questions.q: What return would the fund make?
questions.answer:
Entry: 9 × $12.3M = $111M; debt $49M; equity $62M.

Exit at 9×: $236M; less $30M debt: $206M. Return: 3.3× (about 27% a year).

questions.q: Which lever would you trust least, and why?
questions.answer: New schools: they take time to fill, need good sites and teachers, and use cash. The plan assumes they're mature by year 5. Fees are the easiest to deliver but must be backed by visible quality, or families will switch. Filling schools is the biggest lever and fully in management's control, so start there.

reco: Back the deal. Banyan earns $12.3M EBITDA today; filling schools from 70% to 80% adds $5.8M, a 5% fee rise adds $2.9M, and 10 new schools add $5.2M, taking EBITDA to about $26M in five years and the fund's return to about 3.3×. Filling existing schools is the biggest and most controllable lever, so put the first 100 days there. Risk: new schools may fill more slowly than planned. Next step: rank schools by utilisation and test marketing in the five emptiest.
great: Builds school-level economics before company totals
Separates the levers in an EBITDA bridge
Explains operating leverage from fixed costs
Judges which lever is most reliable

title: Fjord Chemicals
sub: A record year, a record price: is it a trap?
skills: Private equity · cyclical earnings · leverage risk
prompt: Fjord makes specialty coatings for ships and offshore platforms. It just had its best year ever: $80M of EBITDA. The owners want 8× that, $640M, and banks will lend 5× this year's EBITDA. A PE fund asks you whether to bid, needing 2.5× its money in five years.

clarify.a: Demand follows shipbuilding and offshore investment, which move in cycles of roughly 5–7 years.
Order books for new ships are falling from their peak.
Similar businesses sell for about 7× EBITDA mid-cycle.
About $100M over five years in a normal cycle.

structure.root: Should the fund bid $640M for Fjord?

branches.head: Earnings
items: Peak vs average through the cycle

hypothesis: The price is set on a peak year. If earnings return to their average, the fund pays far too much, and debt set on peak earnings could become dangerous in a downturn.

questions.q: Look at Fjord's EBITDA history. What do you notice?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Fjord EBITDA ($M)

questions.answer: EBITDA swings between $38M and $80M. The nine-year average is about $58.2M, so this year is about 37% above average, near the top of the cycle.

questions.q: If the fund pays $640M and EBITDA returns to its average by exit, what return does it make?
questions.answer:
Equity in: $640M − $400M debt = $240M. Exit: $58.2M × 7 = $408M; less $300M debt = $108M.

Return: 0.45×. The fund loses money, even though Fjord stays profitable.

questions.q: What happens to the debt in a downturn like the last one?
questions.answer: At the last trough EBITDA was $38M. With $400M of debt, leverage would be 10.5×, far above the 4–6× where lenders usually step in. The fund could lose control of the company.

questions.q: What would you bid?
questions.answer:
Start from mid-cycle earnings and debt the business can survive: about 3.5× $58.2M = $204M.

Even 8× mid-cycle ($466M) returns only about 1.2× when the exit is at 7×. For 2.5×: exit equity $58.2M × 7 − ($204M − $100M repaid) = $304M, so equity in can be at most $122M and the price at most about $325M (5.6× mid-cycle EBITDA).

Even that debt would be about 5.4× EBITDA at a trough like the last one, at the edge of what lenders accept, so treat $325M as a ceiling, not a target.

That is half the asking price, so the owners will refuse. Be ready to walk away, or wait and bid in the downturn.

reco: Don't bid $640M. This year's $80M of EBITDA is near the top of the cycle; the nine-year average is about $58.2M. Paying 8× peak earnings and exiting at average earnings returns about 0.45× the fund's money, and $400M of debt would reach 10.5× EBITDA in a downturn like the last one. To reach 2.5× with safe debt, the fund could pay at most about $325M, half the asking price, so walk away now and look again in the downturn. Next step: model the next three years from the ship order book.
great: Recognises a cyclical business and normalises earnings
Shows that buying at the peak destroys returns
Stress-tests leverage at the trough
Works back to a maximum price and is willing to walk away

title: Patchwork
sub: Charge freelancers more, or lose them?
skills: Marketplace take rate · break-even · disintermediation
prompt: Patchwork is a marketplace that connects small businesses with freelance designers and developers. It takes 10% of every job paid through the platform: $20M of revenue on $200M of jobs a year. The CFO wants to raise the fee to 15%. The head of community says freelancers will leave. The CEO asks you to settle it.

clarify.a: Freelancers: it's deducted from what the client pays them.
About 60% of the value of jobs comes from clients rehiring a freelancer they met on Patchwork.
Two large platforms charge 10–20%; many freelancers use several.
Once a client and freelancer know each other, they can easily agree to work directly.

structure.root: Should Patchwork raise its fee to 15%?

branches.head: Revenue maths
items: How much job value can we lose?

branches.head: Better designs
items: Different fees by type of job

hypothesis: A higher fee only works if the value of jobs doesn't fall by a third. The risk is concentrated in repeat work, which is easy to take off the platform.

questions.q: How much job value could Patchwork lose before the fee rise stops paying?
questions.answer: Revenue stays at $20M if 15% × job value = $20M: job value of $133M, a fall of 33%.

questions.q: Where would the losses come from?
questions.answer:
Repeat work is 60% of job value. A freelancer and client who already know each other save 15% by working directly; for a $10,000 project that's $1,500, a strong reason to leave. New matches are safer: the client needs Patchwork to find someone.

So-what: the fee rise hits hardest exactly where Patchwork adds least value.

questions.q: Design a better fee structure.
questions.answer:
15% on new matches, 10% on repeat work: revenue = 40% × $200M × 15% + 60% × $200M × 10% = $24M: up to +$4M if new-match volume holds, while protecting repeat pairs. New-match revenue rises from $8M to $12M, so the change still breaks even if new-match job value falls by a third.

  • Add value for repeat work: payment protection, invoicing, tax forms, so staying on the platform is worth the fee
  • Charge clients a small fee too, rather than only freelancers

reco: Don't raise the fee to 15% across the board. It needs job value to fall less than a third to pay off, and most risk sits in repeat work (60% of job value), where pairs can easily go direct. Instead charge 15% on new matches and keep 10% on repeat work, which adds up to about $4M a year, and add invoicing and payment protection to make repeat work worth keeping on the platform. Risk: freelancers may still see it as a price rise. Next step: test the new fees in one category.
great: Calculates the break-even fall in volume
Spots the risk of repeat pairs going direct
Designs fees by type of job
Adds value to justify the fee

title: LeafCart
sub: Every grocery order earns 86 cents
skills: Unit economics · marketplace levers · break-even
prompt: LeafCart delivers groceries from local supermarkets in Toronto in under an hour. It handles 1.2 million orders a year but loses money overall. Investors ask whether it can ever be profitable, and what it would take.

clarify.a: 18% commission from the supermarket on each basket, plus a $3.99 delivery fee from the customer.
Courier pay $7.50, card fees 2.5% of the basket, customer support $0.60, and promotions (discount codes) averaging $2.00.
About $6M a year for technology, marketing staff and the office.

structure.root: How can LeafCart become profitable?

hypothesis: Per order, the margin is tiny, so more volume alone won't fix this. Courier cost is the biggest item, so batching orders and bigger baskets are likely the main levers.

questions.q: What does LeafCart earn on an average order?
questions.answer:
Revenue: 18% × $45 = $8.10 + $3.99 fee = $12.09. Costs: $7.50 + $1.13 + $0.60 + $2.00 = $11.23. Contribution: $0.86 an order.

On 1.2M orders that is $1.0M, far below $6M of fixed costs. Break-even would need 7.0M orders, about 5.8× today.

questions.q: Management has three ideas. Size each.
questions.answer:
• Batch orders (two orders per courier trip, cutting courier cost 30%): +$2.25 → $3.11
  • Bigger baskets ($45 → $55 via a minimum order and suggestions): +$1.55 → $4.66
  • Cut promotions to $0.80 by targeting them at new customers only: +$1.20 → $5.86

With all three: $5.86 × 1.2M = $7.0M, above the $6M of fixed costs.

questions.q: What could stop this working?
questions.answer:
• Batching may slow deliveries, LeafCart's main selling point; offer a cheaper 'within 2 hours' option
  • A minimum basket may push away small top-up orders
  • Cutting promotions could slow growth; measure repeat rates by cohort

reco: LeafCart can become profitable, but not through volume: it earns only $0.86 an order, so it would need about 5.8× today's orders to cover fixed costs. Batching deliveries, raising the average basket to $55 and targeting promotions at new customers would lift contribution to about $5.86 an order, about $7.0M a year against $6M of fixed costs. Risk: slower or less convenient delivery. Next step: trial batching and a minimum basket in two neighbourhoods.
great: Builds contribution per order line by line
Shows that volume alone can't fix it
Sizes each lever in dollars per order
Checks the result against fixed costs

title: Palletpoint
sub: A freight marketplace in a new region: which side do we pay?
skills: Two-sided markets · liquidity · subsidy design
prompt: Palletpoint is an online marketplace where shippers post loads and independent truckers bid to carry them. It earns $60 on each load moved. It launched in the Southeast six months ago, and it is struggling: only 55% of posted loads find a carrier, against 85% in its mature regions. The regional head has $1M to spend and asks whether to subsidise carriers or shippers.

clarify.a: 400 active shippers, each posting about 5 loads a month. About 20 new shippers join a month.
When fewer than 70% of their loads are filled, about 25% of shippers stop using Palletpoint each month. In regions with 80% fill, it's about 5%.
Pay carriers a $40 bonus per load moved in the region for a year. Pilots suggest this lifts fill to about 80%.
Give shippers $30 off each load moved. More shippers would join (about 30 a month), but with the same carriers, fill would slip to about 50% and churn rise to about 28%.

structure.root: Which side of the marketplace should Palletpoint subsidise?

hypothesis: The problem is on the carrier side: shippers post loads that nobody picks up, so they leave. Subsidising shippers would add loads to a market that can't fill the ones it has.

questions.q: Diagnose the problem. Which side is scarce?
questions.answer: Shippers are posting loads, but 45% go unfilled, so carriers are scarce. Unfilled loads make shippers leave: at 25% a month, the region loses most of its shippers within a few months, faster than 20 new ones a month can replace them.

questions.q: Model both options over 12 months. Use revenue minus subsidy.
questions.answer:
Each month: loads filled = shippers × 5 × fill rate; revenue $60 a load; shippers next month = shippers × (1 − churn) + new shippers.

Do nothing: shippers fall to 90; 12-month revenue $363k.

Pay carriers: shippers hold at about 400; revenue $1,152k, subsidy $768k, net $384k.

Discount shippers: shippers fall to 113; revenue $347k, discount $173k, net $173k, worse than doing nothing.

So-what: over the 12 months the carrier bonus only just beats doing nothing, but it leaves a region earning about $96k a month instead of $15k. The value is in the base it builds.
questions.note: Candidates can approximate; the interviewer wants the direction and rough size, not exact compounding.

questions.q: What happens after the carrier subsidy ends?
questions.answer: The subsidy keeps a base of about 400 shippers, posting about 2,000 loads a month. That steady flow of loads is what keeps carriers in the region once the bonus stops. Taper it over months 9–12, and track fill weekly; reintroduce a smaller bonus on lanes where fill drops below 75%.

reco: Subsidise carriers, not shippers. The Southeast's problem is too few carriers: 45% of loads go unfilled, so shippers leave at 25% a month. A $40-a-load carrier bonus lifts fill to about 80%, keeps the shipper base at about 400 instead of shrinking to 90, pays for itself within the year, and leaves the region earning about $96k a month against $15k if Palletpoint does nothing. Discounting shippers adds more loads that can't be filled and does worse than nothing. Taper the bonus once load volume can keep carriers busy. Risk: carriers may leave when it ends. Next step: launch on the 10 busiest lanes first.
great: Identifies the scarce side of the marketplace
Links fill rate to churn on the other side
Models both options month by month
Plans how to remove the subsidy

title: Hearthstay
sub: Biggest city or best city? Choosing the next launch
skills: Marketplace expansion · supply acquisition · payback
prompt: Hearthstay is a holiday-rental marketplace with a strong position in northern Spain. It wants to launch one new city next year and is choosing between Lisbon, Porto and Seville. The CEO's instinct is Lisbon, the biggest tourist market. The board wants the city that pays back fastest.

clarify.a: It takes 15% of each booking. It must recruit hosts (property owners) before guests can book.
An active host is booked about 12 nights a month on average.
About $150k per city for a local team and legal set-up, plus the cost of recruiting each host.
Strong in Lisbon (two big platforms), weaker in Porto and Seville.

Lisbon: 18,000 guest-nights a month, we could win 12%, $120 a night, guest marketing 8% of bookings, $600 to recruit each host; Porto: 8,000 guest-nights a month, we could win 35%, $95 a night, guest marketing 4% of bookings, $250 to recruit each host; Seville: 12,000 guest-nights a month, we could win 20%, $110 a night, guest marketing 5% of bookings, $350 to recruit each host.

structure.root: Which city should Hearthstay launch next?

hypothesis: Lisbon is biggest, but with strong competitors Hearthstay would win a small share at a high cost. A smaller city with weak competition may pay back faster.

questions.q: For each city, work out nights booked, hosts needed and monthly contribution.
questions.answer: Nights = demand × share we can win. Hosts needed = nights ÷ 12. Contribution = nights × nightly rate × (15% take − guest marketing %).
questions.note: Launch cost = hosts × cost per host + $150k.

questions.q: Which city would you choose, and why not Lisbon?
questions.answer:
Porto pays back in about 7 months: weaker competition means a large share, hosts are cheap to recruit, and guest marketing is low.

Lisbon has the most demand, but Hearthstay would win only 12%, hosts cost $600 each to win from rivals, and 8% of each booking goes on marketing, leaving 7% of the booking as contribution. Payback: about 14 months.

So-what: in marketplaces, the best city is where you can become the leader, not the biggest market.

questions.q: What would you check before committing to Porto?
questions.answer:
• Seasonality: is demand spread through the year, or concentrated in summer?
  • Regulation: local short-let licence rules and caps
  • Network effect: guests from Spain may book Porto, so cross-promotion could lower guest marketing further
  • Whether Lisbon could follow once Porto proves the model

reco: Launch in Porto first. It pays back in about 7 months, against about 14 for Lisbon, because weak competition lets Hearthstay win a large share with cheap hosts and little guest marketing. Lisbon is the biggest market, but strong rivals would keep Hearthstay's share small and its costs high. Risks: seasonality and short-let licensing in Porto. Next step: recruit 50 hosts as a pilot before full launch, then reconsider Lisbon once the region is established.
great: Builds supply needs from demand (hosts per night booked)
Compares payback, not market size
Explains why share matters more than size in marketplaces
Checks seasonality and regulation

title: Cedarline Home
sub: The chatbot says it handles 35% of customers. Does it?
skills: AI business case · containment vs resolution · cost per contact
prompt: Cedarline is a home-furnishings retailer whose service centre handles 2 million customer contacts a year. A vendor proposes an AI chatbot and claims it would save about $3M a year. The head of customer service asks you to check the claim before signing.

clarify.a: About $6 for an agent to handle a call or chat.
The chatbot fully handles 35% of conversations without passing them to an agent.
$0.40 per conversation (every contact would start with the bot) plus $500k a year for the platform.
