In a one-month pilot, 20% of customers the bot 'handled' contacted Cedarline again within a week about the same issue.

structure.root: Will the chatbot save Cedarline money, and how much?

hypothesis: 'Handled by the bot' isn't the same as 'resolved'. If some customers come back, the saving is smaller than the vendor says.

questions.q: Recreate the vendor's $3M estimate.
questions.answer: 2M × 35% = 700k contacts avoided × $6 = $4.2M. Less bot costs: 2M × $0.40 + $0.5M = $1.3M. Net: $2.9M.

questions.q: Now use the pilot data on customers who come back.
questions.answer:
Only 80% of 'handled' contacts are truly resolved: 2M × 35% × 80% = 560k × $6 = $3.36M. Net: $2.06M, about 29% below the vendor's figure.

So-what: still worth doing, but judge the vendor on resolution (no repeat contact), not containment.

questions.q: How would you roll it out?
questions.answer:
• Start with simple, high-volume questions: order tracking, delivery slots, returns policy
  • Hand over to an agent quickly for damaged goods and complaints, with the chat history
  • Pay the vendor partly on resolution rate, measured as no repeat contact within 7 days
  • Track customer satisfaction for bot and agent contacts separately

reco: Go ahead, but expect about $2.1M a year of savings, not $3M. The vendor counts every conversation the bot doesn't pass on as a saving, but 20% of those customers come back, so the real saving is about 29% lower. Start with simple order and delivery questions, hand complaints to agents quickly, and tie the vendor's fees to resolution rather than containment. Risk: customer frustration if the bot blocks access to an agent.
great: Rebuilds the vendor's number
Distinguishes containment from resolution
Revises the saving with pilot data
Designs the rollout around simple contacts

title: Northpeak Insurance
sub: AI for claims: faster payouts and less fraud?
skills: AI business case · automation · false positives
prompt: Northpeak is a home and car insurer handling 120,000 claims a year. It's considering an AI system that would automatically approve simple claims and flag suspected fraud. Build cost: $4M; running cost: $1M a year. The COO asks whether it pays off, and what could go wrong.

clarify.a: About $180 of adjuster time per claim. An auto-approved claim costs about $20 to check.
About 30%: simple claims like broken windscreens and small water leaks.
Northpeak pays out about $900M a year. Industry studies suggest about 3% of payouts are fraudulent; the AI is expected to catch an extra 10% of that.
In testing, about 2% of genuine claims were wrongly flagged as suspicious, which delays them. Each costs about $150 in extra handling and goodwill gestures.

structure.root: Should Northpeak invest in AI claims triage?

hypothesis: Automating simple claims should save a lot of handling cost. Fraud savings depend on an estimate, and wrongly flagged genuine customers are a real cost.

questions.q: Size the yearly savings and costs.
questions.answer:
Automation: 120k × 30% = 36k claims × ($180 − $20) = $5.76M.

Fraud: $900M × 3% × 10% = $2.7M.

Wrongly flagged claims: 120k × 2% × $150 = −$0.36M. Running cost: −$1M.

Net: $7.10M a year; payback on $4M: 0.6 years.

questions.q: Which number would you trust least?
questions.answer: The fraud saving: both the 3% fraud rate and the extra 10% caught are estimates. Even if fraud savings were zero, the system would still pay back in 0.9 years on automation alone.

questions.q: What safeguards would you build in?
questions.answer:
• A human reviews every claim the AI wants to reject or flag; the AI never refuses a claim on its own
  • Fast-track wrongly flagged customers once cleared
  • Test regularly whether some customer groups are flagged more than others
  • Keep the reasons for each flag, so decisions can be explained to customers and regulators

reco: Invest. Automating simple claims saves about $5.8M a year and catching more fraud about $2.7M; after running costs and wrongly flagged claims, the net benefit is about $7.1M, paying back the $4M in about 0.6 years, and within a year on automation alone. Keep a human in the loop for every flag or rejection, fast-track wrongly flagged customers, and test for unfair patterns. Next step: pilot on windscreen claims, where decisions are simplest.
great: Sizes each benefit separately
Counts the cost of false positives
Tests the case without the least certain benefit
Designs safeguards for fairness and explainability

title: Larchwood Bank
sub: Will AI coding assistants make 2,000 developers 55% faster?
skills: AI productivity · realistic benefit sizing · capacity vs headcount
prompt: Larchwood Bank employs 2,000 software developers at about $150k a year each, fully loaded. A vendor's study says developers complete tasks 55% faster with its AI coding assistant, which costs $40 per developer a month. The CTO asks what it's really worth, and whether the bank can cancel some of the 150 new hires planned for next year.

clarify.q: How do developers spend their time?
clarify.a: About 40% writing and changing code; the rest on design, meetings, reviews, testing and support.
Measured on well-defined coding tasks only.
Developers who used it regularly spent about 25% less time on coding tasks; about 70% kept using it after a month.
About $0.5M for training and security review.

structure.root: What is the AI assistant worth to Larchwood?

hypothesis: A 55% speed-up on coding tasks doesn't mean 55% more output, because developers spend most of their time on other things, and not everyone will use the tool.

questions.q: What would the vendor's claim imply, and what is a realistic estimate?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · From headcount to real capacity gained

questions.answer:
Read literally, 55% faster across 2,000 developers sounds like 1,100 extra developers of capacity. But it only applies to coding time.

Realistic: 2,000 × 40% coding × 25% less time × 70% using it = 140 developers' worth of time, about $21M a year.

Cost: 2,000 × $480 = $0.96M a year plus $0.5M once. Worth roughly 22× its cost.

questions.q: Can the bank cancel the 150 planned hires?
questions.answer:
Not all of them: the realistic gain is about 140 developers' worth, and it is spread across 2,000 people in small slices, not 140 free people.

A prudent plan: hire about 80 instead of 150 (bank half the gain), and use the rest to clear the backlog. Review after six months of measured data.

questions.q: What could go wrong?
questions.answer:
• Quality: AI-written code can contain bugs or security flaws; keep code review and automated security scanning
  • Data: make sure code and customer data don't leave the bank's control
  • Measuring: track delivery speed and defect rates, not just how often the tool is used

reco: Buy the assistant for all developers: it costs about $1.0M a year and is realistically worth about $21M of developer time (140 developers' worth), about 22× its cost. But the vendor's 55% applies only to coding, which is 40% of a developer's time, and not everyone uses the tool. So trim next year's hiring modestly, to about 80 rather than 150, and use the rest to clear the backlog. Keep code review and security scanning in place. Next step: measure delivery speed and defects for six months.
great: Breaks the vendor's claim into time share × speed-up × adoption
Compares value with cost
Is cautious about turning time saved into fewer hires
Raises quality, security and measurement

title: Brinewater Ports
sub: Predictive maintenance: a $3.5M promise
skills: AI business case · bottleneck value · peak vs off-peak
prompt: Brinewater runs a container terminal with 12 ship-to-shore cranes. A vendor offers AI that predicts crane breakdowns from sensor data, claiming it would cut unplanned downtime from 8% to 5% and add about $3.5M a year of container moves. It costs $1.2M to install and $0.4M a year to run. The terminal director asks for your view.

clarify.a: Each crane is available about 8,000 hours a year and moves about 30 containers an hour; each move earns about $40 of margin.
For about four months a year (the peak season) ships queue and every crane hour is used. The rest of the year, cranes are often idle.
Fewer emergency repairs and overtime would save about $0.6M a year.
None during peak; berths and yard have spare capacity.

structure.root: Is predictive maintenance worth it for Brinewater?

branches.head: Are those hours valuable?
items: Only when cranes are the bottleneck

hypothesis: Extra crane hours are only valuable when ships are waiting. Most of the year cranes are idle, so the vendor is probably overstating the value.

questions.q: Recreate the vendor's claim.
Which of those hours actually add moves?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Net yearly benefit, including maintenance savings and running costs ($M)

questions.answer:
Only during peak season, when ships are queuing: one-third of the year. Off-peak, a crane that would have broken down is simply replaced by an idle one.

Valuable hours: 2,880 × 1/3 = 960; × 30 × $40 = $1.15M. Plus maintenance savings $0.6M, less $0.4M running: $1.35M a year.

Payback on $1.2M: 0.9 years. Still a good investment, but the extra moves are worth only a third of what the vendor claims ($1.15M vs $3.46M). On the same net basis as ours (adding maintenance savings, less running costs), the vendor's case would be $3.7M.

questions.q: How could Brinewater get more value from it?
questions.answer:
• Plan maintenance for the quiet months, using the predictions to do repairs off-peak so cranes are fully available in peak season
  • Negotiate the vendor's fee as a share of peak-season availability gains
  • Extend later to yard equipment if that becomes a bottleneck

reco: Invest, but expect about $1.4M of net yearly benefit, not the $3.7M the vendor's figures imply. Extra crane hours only add moves in the four-month peak, when ships queue; for the rest of the year cranes have spare time. Including $0.6M of maintenance savings, the system pays back in about 0.9 years. Use the predictions to shift maintenance into quiet months, and tie part of the vendor's fee to peak-season availability. Risk: sensor data quality on older cranes. Next step: pilot on the four busiest cranes.
great: Rebuilds the vendor's figure
Values capacity only where it is the bottleneck
Includes maintenance savings and running costs
Finds a way to raise the value (shift maintenance off-peak)

title: Westmoor Clinic
sub: Patients wait three weeks. Build more rooms?
skills: Capacity · bottleneck · task shifting
prompt: Westmoor is a private outpatient clinic. Patients wait about three weeks for an appointment, and some go elsewhere. The practice manager wants to convert storage space into four more consultation rooms for $600k. The owners ask whether that will cut waiting times.

clarify.a: 10 consultation rooms, open 9 hours a day. Each appointment holds a room for about 30 minutes, including cleaning and set-up.
6 doctors, each seeing patients for about 7 hours a day. Each appointment takes about 20 minutes of doctor time, much of it taking history and measurements.
About 160 appointment requests a working day.

structure.root: How can Westmoor see more patients?

branches.head: Doctor capacity
items: Doctors × hours ÷ doctor time per appointment

hypothesis: More rooms only help if rooms are the constraint. I'd compare room capacity with doctor capacity first.

questions.q: How many patients a day can the rooms handle, and how many can the doctors see?
questions.answer:
Rooms: 10 × 9 hours × 2 an hour = 180. Doctors: 6 × 7 hours × 3 an hour = 126.

Demand is 160 a day. Doctors are the bottleneck; rooms already have spare capacity. Four more rooms would add nothing.

questions.q: How could Westmoor raise doctor capacity without hiring doctors?
questions.answer:
Give history-taking and measurements to intake nurses before the doctor comes in: if doctor time falls from 20 to 15 minutes, capacity rises to 6 × 7 × 4 = 168, above demand.

Cost: two nurses at about $70k = $140k a year, against $600k for rooms that wouldn't help. Rooms still fit: 168 patients need 84 room-hours, against 90 available.

questions.q: What else could help?
questions.answer:
• Video appointments for follow-ups, which need no room
  • Reminders to cut no-shows, so doctor time isn't wasted
  • Longer doctor sessions on the busiest days

reco: Don't build the rooms: doctors, not rooms, limit Westmoor to about 126 patients a day against 160 requests, and the rooms can already handle 180. Hire two intake nurses to take histories and measurements, cutting doctor time to 15 minutes and lifting capacity to about 168 a day for about $140k a year. Risk: doctors must trust the nurses' notes. Next step: trial with two doctors for a month and measure appointment length.
great: Computes capacity for both rooms and doctors
Identifies the real constraint
Rejects a fix aimed at the wrong constraint
Finds a cheaper fix that shifts work off the bottleneck

title: Willow Physio
sub: One appointment in seven is a no-show
skills: Capacity utilisation · no-shows · option comparison
prompt: Willow runs 40 physiotherapists across Sydney, each with 16 half-hour appointments a day, 250 days a year, at $90 an appointment. About 15% of patients don't turn up and don't cancel. The CEO asks how much no-shows cost and what to do about them.

clarify.a: None today. In a trial, an SMS reminder the day before cut no-shows to 9%. Each SMS costs about $0.10.
Taking a card deposit at booking cut no-shows to 5% in another clinic group, but about 5% of patients chose not to book at all.
Some clinics book one extra patient a day per therapist, expecting at least one no-show.
Most clinics have a short waiting list that can fill the odd late cancellation, but it could not replace a lasting fall in bookings.

structure.root: How should Willow reduce the cost of no-shows?

hypothesis: No-shows waste a fixed cost: the physio is paid anyway. Reminders are cheap; deposits work but may put patients off.

questions.q: How much do no-shows cost Willow?
questions.answer: Appointments: 40 × 16 × 250 = 160,000. No-shows: 15% = 24,000. Lost revenue: $2.16M a year, and the physios are paid anyway.

questions.q: Compare reminders and deposits.
questions.answer:
SMS reminders: no-shows fall to 9%: 9,600 more appointments × $90 = $0.86M, less SMS costs $0.02M: +$0.85M.

Deposits: 5% fewer bookings, but only 5% no-shows: attended appointments = 95% × 95% = 90.25% of today's slots, against 85% now: +$0.76M.

So-what: reminders gain more, cost almost nothing and don't put patients off.

questions.q: Should Willow also overbook?
questions.answer: With reminders, about 9% still don't come, so a physio with 16 bookings expects about 1.4 no-shows a day. One extra booking a day would usually be seen in a no-show gap, adding up to about $0.8M a year. But on days when everyone turns up, a patient waits or the physio works late. Use it only for therapists and times with high no-show rates, and use the waiting list to fill late cancellations first.

reco: No-shows cost Willow about $2.2M a year in lost revenue. Start with SMS reminders the day before: they cut no-shows from 15% to about 9% and add about $0.85M a year for almost no cost, more than deposits ($0.76M), which also put some patients off. Then fill late gaps from the waiting list, and overbook only where no-show rates stay high. Risk: overbooking can make patients wait. Next step: roll out reminders to all clinics this month.
great: Sizes the problem in dollars
Compares options including their side effects
Counts lost bookings from deposits
Treats overbooking carefully

title: Summit Dialysis
sub: 25 patients waiting for a dialysis slot
skills: Capacity planning · shifts vs assets · healthcare operations
prompt: Summit runs a dialysis centre with 20 chairs. Patients with kidney failure need three 4-hour sessions a week, so slots are fixed for months at a time. The centre is full and 25 patients are on a waiting list, travelling to a centre an hour away. The director asks how to make room for them.

clarify.a: Two shifts a day (morning and afternoon), Monday to Saturday. Patients come either Mon/Wed/Fri or Tue/Thu/Sat.
One nurse per four chairs plus one technician per shift. A staff shift costs about $400.
Insurers pay about $300 per session. Supplies and drugs cost about $90.
(A) An evening shift on Mon/Wed/Fri. (B) Six more chairs in an unused room, for about $660k of chairs and works.

structure.root: How can Summit treat the 25 waiting patients?

hypothesis: The chairs are idle in the evenings, so an extra shift uses existing equipment. It may not fit all 25 patients, though.

questions.q: How many patients can Summit treat today?
questions.answer: 20 chairs × 2 shifts × 6 days = 240 sessions a week ÷ 3 per patient = 80 patients.

questions.q: Compare the two options.
questions.answer:
A: evening shift Mon/Wed/Fri: 20 chairs × 3 evenings = 60 sessions = 20 patients. Staff: 5 nurses + 1 technician = 6 shifts × 3 evenings × 52 weeks × $400 = $374k. Yearly gain: 60 × 52 × ($300 − $90) − $374k = $281k, with no investment.

B: six more chairs: 6 × 2 × 6 ÷ 3 = 24 patients. Investment $660k; extra nurses (1.5 per shift) $374k a year; the existing technician covers the room. Yearly gain: $412k; payback 1.6 years.

questions.q: What would you do?
questions.answer:
Start the Mon/Wed/Fri evening shift now: it treats 20 patients within weeks, needs no investment and suits patients who work.

For the other 5, a small Tue/Thu/Sat evening shift on 8 chairs (2 nurses and a technician) adds 8 places and about $75k a year. Together that's 28 places, enough for all 25, without spending $660k on chairs.

Keep the six chairs as the next step if the waiting list grows again. Check first that enough nurses will work evenings.

reco: Treat the waiting patients in two steps. First, open an evening shift on Mon/Wed/Fri, which uses idle chairs and adds 20 places with no investment and about $281k a year of margin. Then run a smaller evening shift on Tue/Thu/Sat with 8 chairs for another 8 places, so all 25 waiting patients can be treated locally without spending $660k on new chairs; keep that investment for when the list grows again. Risk: recruiting nurses for evenings. Next step: survey waiting patients on evening slots and start recruiting.
great: Computes capacity in patients, not sessions
Uses idle hours before buying equipment
Compares options on patients added and economics
Meets the full need without over-building

title: Lantern Vaccination Centre
sub: From 120 to 200 people an hour
skills: Process throughput · moving bottlenecks · public services
prompt: A city health department runs a mass vaccination centre in a sports hall during a flu-and-COVID campaign. It vaccinates about 120 people an hour; the target is 200. The centre manager wants to hire more nurses. The deputy health officer asks you how to reach 200 an hour at the lowest cost.

clarify.a: Check-in desk, then a screening interview (health questions, consent), then vaccination, then 15 minutes' observation in a chair.
Check-in: 4 desks, 1.5 minutes each. Screening: 6 nurses, 3 minutes each. Vaccination: 8 vaccinators, 2 minutes each. Observation: 60 chairs.
If people complete health questions online before they arrive, screening takes about 1 minute. About 70% would do so if asked when booking.

structure.root: How can the centre reach 200 people an hour?

hypothesis: Throughput is set by the slowest step. Screening looks slowest; but after fixing it, another step will probably limit the flow.

questions.q: Work out the capacity of each station per hour. Where is the bottleneck?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · People per hour by station

questions.answer:
Check-in: 4 × 60 ÷ 1.5 = 160. Screening: 6 × 60 ÷ 3 = 120. Vaccination: 8 × 30 = 240. Observation: 60 chairs × 4 an hour = 240.

Screening is the bottleneck at 120 an hour.

questions.q: The manager wants more screening nurses. How many would be needed, and is there a cheaper way?
questions.answer:
For 200 an hour at 3 minutes each: 200 × 3 ÷ 60 = 10 nurses, 4 more.

Cheaper: ask people to complete health questions online. Average screening time: 70% × 1 + 30% × 3 = 1.6 minutes, so 6 nurses screen 225 an hour.

But now check-in (160 an hour) is the bottleneck.

questions.q: How do you get to 200?
questions.answer:
Add one check-in desk (5 desks: 200 an hour). Now every station handles at least 200: the slowest is check-in at 200.

Total change: online forms plus one desk clerk, instead of four extra nurses. Check observation: at 200 an hour, 200 × 15 ÷ 60 = 50 people seated at once, within 60 chairs.

reco: Reach 200 an hour by removing work rather than adding nurses. Screening limits the centre to 120 an hour; asking people to complete health questions online cuts screening time to about 1.6 minutes, lifting it to 225 an hour, and one extra check-in desk clears the next bottleneck, taking every station to at least 200. That needs one clerk instead of four extra nurses. Risk: fewer people complete forms online than expected, so keep two nurses on call. Next step: add the online form to the booking confirmation.
great: Computes capacity for every station, including observation chairs
Finds the bottleneck and the next one
Prefers removing work to adding staff
Checks that every station meets the target

title: Vega Logistics
sub: Solar on the warehouse roof: buy the panels or buy the power?
skills: NPV · own vs lease · energy economics
prompt: Vega runs a large distribution warehouse in Arizona. It can put solar panels on the roof for $1.5M, or let a solar developer install them for free and buy the power under a 25-year contract (a power purchase agreement, PPA). The CFO asks which is better, using Vega's 8% cost of capital.

clarify.a: About 1,800 MWh a year for 25 years.

clarify.q: How much would Vega use itself?
clarify.a: About 70%; the rest would be exported to the grid when the warehouse is quiet.
Vega pays $120 per MWh for grid power. Exported power earns $40 per MWh. Maintenance costs about $20k a year if Vega owns the panels.
The developer would sell Vega the power it uses at $90 per MWh, and keep any exports.

structure.root: Should Vega own the panels or sign a PPA?

branches.head: Other factors
items: Risk of the roof or the business changing

hypothesis: Owning gives the full saving but ties up capital; a PPA gives a smaller saving with no investment. At an 8% cost of capital, the PPA could well win.

questions.q: What is owning worth, in NPV and payback?
questions.note: Present value of $1 a year for 25 years at 8% = 10.67.

questions.q: What is the PPA worth?
questions.answer:
Vega saves $120 − $90 = $30 on each MWh it uses: 1,800 × 70% × $30 = $37.8k a year, with no investment.

NPV: $37.8k × 10.67 = $404k, about 3× the NPV of owning.

questions.q: Owning only just pays. Why, and what could change that?
questions.answer:
Thirty percent of the power is exported at $40, a third of the grid price, and Vega's 8% cost of capital is high for a 25-year asset. If Vega charged its electric forklifts in daytime and used 85% on site, owning would be worth $362k, still below the PPA.

The developer can own panels more cheaply because its cost of capital is lower. Vega's capital is better spent on its core business.

reco: Sign the PPA. Owning the panels has an NPV of only about $131k at Vega's 8% cost of capital, because 30% of the power is exported cheaply, while the PPA saves about $38k a year with no investment, an NPV of about $404k. Even using 85% of the power on site, owning stays behind. Negotiate the PPA price, a price-escalation cap and what happens if Vega leaves the building. Next step: get two more developer quotes.
great: Values both options with the same discount rate and life
Values export and self-used power differently
Sees how cost of capital favours the PPA
Checks whether more self-use changes the answer

title: Northwind Hotels
sub: Replace the old boilers with heat pumps?
skills: NPV · incremental analysis · sensitivity
prompt: Northwind owns 20 mid-size hotels in Ontario. Their gas boilers are reaching the end of their lives. The sustainability lead wants to replace them with electric heat pumps instead of new boilers. The CFO asks whether the extra cost pays off, using a 7% discount rate over a 15-year life.

clarify.a: Heat pump system: $400k. A new gas boiler system: $120k.
Gas: about $60k a year, plus about $8k of carbon charges. A heat pump would use about $38k of electricity a year. Maintenance is similar.
A provincial programme may cover 20% of heat-pump costs; the application takes three months.
About $8k a year today. They could double to about $16k a year from next year, but that isn't certain.

structure.root: Should Northwind install heat pumps instead of new boilers?

hypothesis: The right comparison is heat pump vs new boiler, since the boilers must be replaced anyway. The savings look close to the extra cost, so the grant and carbon charges may decide it.

questions.q: Compare the heat pump with a new boiler for one hotel.
questions.answer:
Extra cost: $400k − $120k = $280k. Yearly saving: $60k + $8k − $38k = $30k.

Discount factor for 15 years at 7%: 9.11. NPV = −$280k + $30k × 9.11 = −$7k. Roughly break-even.
questions.note: Comparing with 'do nothing' would be wrong: the boilers must be replaced anyway.

questions.q: How do the grant and higher carbon charges change it?

rows: Carbon charges double to $16k from next year, no grant
exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · NPV of heat pump vs new boiler

questions.answer:
Grant (20% of $400k = $80k): NPV +$73k per hotel.

Carbon charges doubling to $16k from next year (no grant): NPV +$66k.

Across 20 hotels with the grant: about +$1.5M.

questions.q: What would you recommend, and what are the risks?
questions.answer:
• Apply for the grant now and replace boilers hotel by hotel as they fail, starting with the oldest
  • Keep gas back-up in the coldest hotels for extreme cold snaps
  • Risks: electricity prices rising faster than gas; installation disruption to guests (do it off-season)

reco: Install heat pumps, with the provincial grant. Compared with new gas boilers, a heat pump costs $280k more per hotel and saves about $30k a year, which is roughly break-even over 15 years at 7% (−$7k). The 20% grant makes it clearly positive (about +$73k per hotel, +$1.5M across 20), and rising carbon charges would add more. Replace boilers as they reach end of life, oldest first, and install in the off-season. Risk: electricity prices. Next step: submit the grant application.
great: Compares against the real alternative (new boiler), not doing nothing
Discounts savings over the asset's life
Tests the grant and carbon price
Phases the rollout with the replacement cycle

title: Fenland Biogas
sub: A digester that runs on other people's waste
skills: NPV · sensitivity · revenue risk
prompt: A farming co-operative in eastern England wants to build a $15M anaerobic digester, which turns food waste and manure into biogas for electricity. It would earn money from three sources: selling electricity, charging food companies to take their waste (gate fees), and selling the leftover material as fertiliser. The co-op's chair asks whether it's a sound investment.

clarify.a: Electricity about $1.6M; gate fees about $1.2M; fertiliser about $0.2M.
About $1.3M a year for staff, maintenance and transport.
20 years; the co-op's lender uses 8%.
Three new digesters are planned within 30 miles. Gate fees elsewhere fell by about half when new digesters opened nearby. No long-term waste contracts are signed yet.

structure.root: Should the co-op build the digester?

hypothesis: Gate fees are a large share of income and could fall as competitors open. I'd test the NPV if they halve.

questions.q: What is the NPV in the base case?
What if gate fees halve as new digesters open?
questions.answer:
Cash flow falls to $1.1M a year. NPV = −$15M + $1.1M × 9.82 = −$4.2M.

Break-even: gate fees can fall to about 86% of today's level before the project stops paying.

So-what: the project's value depends on gate fees, which are not contracted and face new competition.

questions.q: What would you need before saying yes?
questions.answer:
• Long-term waste contracts (10+ years) for most of the gate-fee income, at fees above 86% of today's
  • Use more of the co-op's own manure and crop waste, so less depends on outside food waste
  • A fixed electricity price contract if available

reco: Build the digester only once most of its waste is under long-term contract. The base case NPV is about +$1.7M, but gate fees are 40% of income, uncontracted, and likely to fall as three new digesters open nearby; if they halve, the NPV becomes −$4.2M. The project breaks even if gate fees stay above about 86% of today's level. Sign 10-year waste contracts and use more of the co-op's own manure before committing. Next step: approach the three largest food processors.
great: Computes NPV with the lender's rate
Identifies the riskiest income stream
Finds the break-even gate fee
Makes the decision conditional on contracts

title: Arbor Wind
sub: Sell the power at market prices, or lock in a lower price?
skills: NPV · risk and discount rates · contracting
prompt: Arbor is developing a 100 MW wind farm in Texas, costing about $110M after federal tax credits. It can sell its power on the wholesale market at whatever the price is, or sign a 25-year power purchase agreement (PPA) with a technology company at a fixed $48 per MWh. Market forecasts average about $55. The investment committee asks which route to take.

clarify.a: Wind farms here run at about 35% of full capacity over a year (capacity factor).
About $4M a year to operate and maintain.
Investors want about 9% for projects selling at market prices, and about 6.5% for projects with a fixed-price contract, because the income is more certain.
In a scenario with lots of new solar, average prices could fall to about $40.
About 25 years, the same as the PPA term.

structure.root: Should Arbor sign the PPA or sell at market prices?

hypothesis: The market route earns more per MWh on average, but the income is riskier, so investors discount it more. The fixed price may be worth more once risk is priced in.

questions.q: How much power will the farm produce a year?
Compare the NPV of the two routes.
questions.answer:
Market: 0.307M MWh × $55 − $4M = $12.9M a year; 25 years at 9% (factor 9.82): NPV = −$110M + $12.9M × 9.82 = +$16.3M.

PPA: 0.307M × $48 − $4M = $10.7M a year; at 6.5% (factor 12.20): NPV = +$20.7M.

So-what: the PPA earns less each year but is worth more, because certain income is discounted less.

questions.q: What happens to the market route if prices average $40?
questions.answer: Cash flow: 0.307M × $40 − $4M = $8.3M; NPV = −$28.8M. The project would lose money. The PPA is unaffected.

questions.q: Any reason to keep some market exposure?
questions.answer: Yes: a PPA for most of the output (say 70–80%) secures financing, while selling the rest at market prices keeps some upside if prices rise. Also check the buyer's credit quality, since a 25-year PPA is only as good as the company paying it.

reco: Sign the PPA, at least for most of the output. Although $48 is below the expected $55 market price, the fixed price makes the income far more certain: its NPV is about +$20.7M at 6.5%, against +$16.3M for selling at market prices at 9%, and the market route loses money if prices average $40. Consider keeping 20–30% of output on the market for upside. Risk: the buyer's credit over 25 years. Next step: credit check on the buyer and negotiate an inflation clause.
great: Computes output from capacity and capacity factor
Uses different discount rates for different risks
Shows a lower price can be worth more
Stress-tests the market route

title: CraneParcel
sub: One parcel in eight needs a second trip
skills: Last-mile economics · option comparison
prompt: CraneParcel delivers 30 million parcels a year for online retailers in the Northeast. About 12% of first delivery attempts fail because nobody is home, and each redelivery costs about $6. The operations director has two ideas: text customers a one-hour delivery window, or install parcel lockers. Which should come first?

clarify.a: Customers get a text with a one-hour window and can redirect the parcel. In a trial, failures fell to 7%. Texts and tracking cost about $0.05 a parcel.

1,500 lockers at $8k each to install and $1.2k a year to run. About 8% of parcels would go to lockers. Only 1% of locker deliveries fail, and dropping many parcels at one locker saves about $1.20 a parcel.
Yes; budget is the constraint this year.

structure.root: How should CraneParcel cut failed deliveries?

hypothesis: Windows apply to every parcel at almost no cost, so they probably save the most quickly. Lockers need investment and only reach a small share of parcels.

questions.q: How much do failed deliveries cost today?
questions.answer: 30M × 12% = 3.6M redeliveries × $6 = $21.6M a year.

questions.q: Compare the two ideas.
questions.answer:
Windows: failures fall 5 points: 30M × 5% × $6 = $9.0M, less 30M × $0.05 = $1.5M: $7.5M a year, no investment.

Lockers: 8% of parcels = 2.4M; each avoids 11 points of failures (× $6 = $0.66) and saves $1.20 = $1.86 per parcel: $4.46M, less $1.8M running: $2.7M a year, for $12M upfront (payback 4.5 years).

questions.q: What would you do?
questions.answer:
Launch delivery windows across the network now: bigger saving, no investment. Then add lockers in dense areas with the highest failure rates (apartment blocks, offices), where they fill fastest and pay back soonest.

Careful: the two savings overlap. Once windows have cut failures to 7%, each locker parcel avoids only 6 points of failure, not 11: 2.4M × (6% × $6 + $1.20) − $1.8M ≈ $1.9M a year, a payback of about 6 years. So put lockers only where failure rates stay high after windows.

reco: Start with one-hour delivery windows: they cut failures from 12% to about 7% across all 30 million parcels and save about $7.5M a year with no investment. Then roll out lockers in the densest, highest-failure areas: once windows are live, 1,500 lockers would save about $1.9M a year (about $2.7M on their own) for $12M upfront, paying back in about 6 years, so put them first where failures stay highest. Risk: customers ignoring texts. Next step: switch on windows region by region and track failures weekly.
great: Sizes the problem first
Compares savings and investment for each option
Prioritises the option that reaches every parcel
Targets lockers where they pay back fastest

title: Coral Pharmacy
sub: Four warehouses into one?
skills: Network design · risk pooling · trade-offs
prompt: Coral runs 600 pharmacies across eastern Australia, supplied from four regional warehouses. The supply chain director proposes closing three and serving every store from one large warehouse near Sydney. The CFO asks whether it would save money without hurting service.

clarify.a: Each warehouse holds safety stock to cover unexpected demand: $20M in total across the four.
About 25% of stock value a year (capital, storage, expiry, insurance).
Each warehouse costs about $1.5M a year to run, beyond the work of handling goods.
Longer journeys from one site would add about $3M a year. About 15% of stores are more than 12 hours' drive from Sydney.

structure.root: Should Coral consolidate to one warehouse?

branches.head: Inventory
items: Safety stock needed in one place vs four

hypothesis: Pooling stock in one place needs less safety stock, because highs in one region offset lows in another. That saving, plus fewer sites, might outweigh extra transport, but distant stores could suffer.

questions.q: How much safety stock would one warehouse need?
questions.answer:
A common rule of thumb (the square-root law): if demand in each region is similar and independent, safety stock falls with the square root of the number of sites. Four sites into one: $20M ÷ √4 = $10M.

Saving: $10M × 25% = $2.5M a year.
questions.note: Demand in different regions partly cancels out when pooled.

questions.q: What is the net saving?
questions.answer: Inventory $2.5M + fixed costs of three warehouses (3 × $1.5M = $4.5M) = $7.0M gross saving, less extra transport $3.0M = $4.0M a year.

questions.q: What would worry you?
questions.answer:
• Service: the 15% of stores more than 12 hours away would lose next-day delivery; prescriptions can't wait. Keep a small cross-dock or use overnight carriers there.
  • Resilience: one site means one point of failure (fire, flood, strike)
  • Transition: moving stock without gaps on shelves

reco: Consolidate, but keep a small hub for distant stores. One warehouse needs about half the safety stock ($10M instead of $20M), saving about $2.5M a year, and closing three sites saves $4.5M; after $3M of extra transport, the net saving is about $4.0M a year. The 15% of stores more than 12 hours from Sydney would lose next-day delivery, so serve them through a cross-dock or overnight carrier. Risk: one site is a single point of failure, so agree a backup site. Next step: model delivery times store by store.
great: Applies risk pooling (square-root law) with its assumptions
Nets inventory and fixed savings against transport
Protects service for distant stores
Raises resilience

title: Vista Fresh
sub: Fly it or ship it?
skills: Logistics trade-offs · spoilage · segmentation
prompt: Vista imports fresh produce from Peru and sells it to US supermarkets. It flies everything today. Air freight prices have risen, and the CEO wants to switch everything to refrigerated sea containers, which are five times cheaper. The head of quality is worried. You're asked to settle it.

clarify.a: Vista sells at about $6 a kg and buys at about $2.50. Air freight costs $3.20 a kg; sea $0.60.
Air: 2 days. Sea: about 18 days.
By air about 3% is lost. By sea about 15% of avocados (which ripen slowly) but about 60% of blueberries.
Sea-freighted fruit arrives with less shelf life; supermarkets pay about 10% less for it.

structure.root: Should Vista switch from air to sea freight?

hypothesis: Sea is much cheaper per kg shipped, but what matters is cost per kg sold. For fragile fruit, spoilage could wipe out the saving.

questions.q: Compare margin per kg sold for avocados by air and by sea.
questions.answer:
Air: cost per kg sold = ($2.50 + $3.20) ÷ 97% = $5.88; margin $6.00 − $5.88 = $0.12.

Sea: ($2.50 + $0.60) ÷ 85% = $3.65; price $5.40 after the shelf-life discount: margin $1.75.

Sea is far better for avocados.

questions.q: And blueberries?
questions.answer:
Sea: ($2.50 + $0.60) ÷ 40% = $7.75 per kg sold, above the $5.40 price: margin −$2.35. By air: $0.12.

Air margins are thin, but sea loses money. Blueberries must stay on air, and Vista should review their price.

questions.q: What would you recommend?
questions.answer:
• Split by product: ship robust fruit (avocados, citrus) by sea; keep fragile fruit (berries) on air
  • For berries: renegotiate air rates with volume commitments, or raise prices; margins by air are too thin
  • Test controlled-atmosphere containers, which may cut sea spoilage further

reco: Don't switch everything to sea. Avocados should move to sea freight: margin rises from about $0.12 to $1.75 a kg. But 60% of blueberries would spoil on an 18-day voyage, making each kg sold cost more than it sells for, so they must stay on air, where margins are thin and prices need review. Decide product by product on margin per kg sold, not freight cost per kg shipped. Next step: trial two sea containers of avocados and measure spoilage and supermarket feedback.
great: Converts cost per kg shipped into cost per kg sold
Includes the shelf-life discount
Splits the decision by product
Flags thin margins on the air product

title: Boreal Parts
sub: A broken truck costs $20k an hour. Which parts should sit next to it?
skills: Inventory placement · service level vs cost · risk pooling
prompt: Boreal provides maintenance for haul trucks at six mines in northern Canada. When a truck breaks down, the mine loses about $20k an hour of output. Parts come from a central store 36 hours away. The client asks Boreal to stock parts at every mine to cut that to 4 hours. Stocking everything everywhere would be very expensive. Which parts should be stocked where?

clarify.a: Three groups: cheap parts that fail often (about $2k each, 4 failures a year per site), mid-price pumps ($40k, 0.5 failures), and expensive gearboxes ($600k, about one failure every five years per site).
About 25% of a part's value a year.
A regional depot could serve all six mines within about 10 hours.

structure.root: Which spare parts should be stocked at each mine?

branches.head: Benefit of local stock
items: Failures × hours saved × cost per hour

branches.head: Cost of local stock
items: Value × holding cost × number of sites

hypothesis: Cheap parts that fail often are an easy yes. Expensive parts that rarely fail probably don't justify a copy at every mine, but a shared regional spare might.

questions.q: For each part group, compare the yearly benefit of stocking at all six mines with the cost.

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Stocking at all six mines

questions.answer:
Benefit = failures × 6 sites × 32 hours saved × $20k. Cost = 6 × part value × 25%.

  • A: benefit $15.36M vs cost $3k
  • B: benefit $1.92M vs cost $60k
  • C: benefit $0.77M vs cost $0.90M: not worth it

questions.q: What about one shared gearbox at a regional depot?
questions.answer:
Lead time falls from 36 to 10 hours: 0.2 × 6 × 26 hours × $20k = $0.62M a year, against $0.15M to hold one gearbox: clearly worth it.

So-what: match stocking to how critical and how expensive a part is: local for cheap and frequent, regional for expensive and rare.

questions.q: What else could reduce downtime?
questions.answer:
• Monitor gearbox condition to predict failures and order ahead
  • Agree with the manufacturer to hold consigned stock (paid for only when used)
  • Share expensive spares with other operators in the region

reco: Don't stock everything at every mine. Cheap, frequently failing parts and mid-price pumps should be held at each mine: they save far more downtime than they cost to hold. Gearboxes should not: a copy at each mine costs about $0.90M a year to save about $0.77M of downtime. Instead keep one at a regional depot within 10 hours, which pays for itself, and add condition monitoring. Next step: classify all parts by cost of downtime and holding cost.
great: Values downtime avoided against holding cost
Splits parts by criticality and value
Finds a middle option (regional pooling)
Suggests ways to cut lead time without stock

title: Riverside City
sub: $10M to reduce homelessness: where should it go?
skills: Public sector · cost-effectiveness · budget allocation
prompt: Riverside, a mid-sized US city, has $10M of new funding to reduce homelessness this year. The council is choosing between programmes. Most of the money has traditionally gone to emergency shelters. The mayor's office asks you how to get the most people into stable housing.

clarify.a: (1) Emergency shelter beds. (2) Rapid rehousing: help with a deposit and a year of rent support, about $9,000 per household. (3) Prevention: one-off grants to households about to be evicted, about $2,500 each.

Shelters give a bed but few people move on to stable housing from them alone. 75% of rapid-rehousing households are still housed after a year. Prevention grants keep about 40% of households from becoming homeless who otherwise would have.
Caseworkers can identify about 1,500 households at real risk of eviction this year.
Number of households in stable housing a year from now.

structure.root: How should Riverside spend $10M to maximise households in stable housing?

branches.head: Define the outcome
items: Households stably housed after a year

branches.head: Allocation
items: Cheapest per outcome first, up to its limit

hypothesis: Prevention is usually cheapest per household kept housed, but only works for people we can find in time. I'd rank programmes on cost per outcome and fill the cheapest first.

questions.q: What is the cost per household stably housed for prevention and rehousing?
questions.answer:
Prevention: $2,500 ÷ 40% = $6,250 per household kept housed. Rapid rehousing: $9,000 ÷ 75% = $12,000.

Shelters provide safety tonight but, on their own, produce few stable outcomes, so they are a different goal: keep enough beds for emergencies, but they shouldn't get the new money.
questions.note: The key move: measure cost per outcome, not cost per person served.

questions.q: How would you allocate the $10M?
questions.answer:
Fund prevention first, up to its limit: 1,500 × $2,500 = $3.75M, keeping about 600 households housed.

The remaining $6.25M funds 694 rapid-rehousing places, housing about 521. Total: about 1,121 households.

All $10M on rehousing would house about 833.

questions.q: What might the council push back on, and how would you respond?
questions.answer:
• "People sleeping rough need beds tonight." True: protect existing shelter funding; this new money is for lasting exits.
  • "How do we know prevention worked?" Track households for 12 months; the 40% figure must be tested locally.
  • "Will landlords take rehousing tenants?" Build a landlord partnership with guarantees for damage.

reco: Put the new $10M into prevention first, then rapid rehousing. Prevention costs about $6,250 per household kept housed, against $12,000 for rehousing; funding all 1,500 at-risk households ($3.75M) and putting the rest into rehousing would leave about 1,121 households stably housed, against about 833 if everything went to rehousing. Keep existing shelter funding for emergencies. Risk: the 40% prevention rate is an estimate, so track outcomes for a year. Next step: set up eviction referral links with courts and landlords.
great: Defines a clear outcome
Compares cost per outcome, not per person served
Funds the cheapest programme up to its limit
Handles political objections respectfully

title: Ministry of Health
sub: Screen everyone over 40, or only people at high risk?
skills: Public health · cost per outcome · targeting vs coverage
prompt: A national health ministry wants to find people with undiagnosed type 2 diabetes earlier, before complications. It has 1.2 million adults over 40. One proposal is to offer a blood test to all of them; another is to test only those at high risk, using a short questionnaire at GP visits. You're asked which is better value.

clarify.a: About 6% of adults over 40 have undiagnosed diabetes. Among the 30% classed as high risk (weight, family history, age), it's about 14%.
About $30 per test including the nurse's time; the questionnaire is free.
About 60% of people invited usually come for a test.

structure.root: Which screening approach gives the best value?

hypothesis: Targeting tests people more likely to have diabetes, so each case found should cost much less. The question is how many cases targeting misses.

questions.q: Compare the two approaches on cases found and cost per case found (ignore uptake for now).
questions.answer:
Everyone: 1.2M × $30 = $36M; cases found 1.2M × 6% = 72k: $500 per case.

High risk only: 360k × $30 = $10.8M; cases 360k × 14% = 50.4k: $214 per case.

Targeting finds 70% of the cases for 30% of the cost.

questions.q: Does uptake change the comparison?
questions.answer: At 60% uptake both approaches find 60% as many cases at 60% of the cost, so cost per case is unchanged. But targeting through GP visits may get higher uptake, because a doctor is recommending it.

questions.q: Who would targeting miss, and what would you do about it?
questions.answer: About 30% of cases are in people not classed as high risk, and groups that rarely visit a GP would be missed. Add community testing in areas with high rates of diabetes and low GP use, and review the risk questionnaire every year.

reco: Test people at high risk first. Targeting finds about 70% of undiagnosed cases for 30% of the cost: about $214 per case found against $500 for testing everyone over 40. Use the money saved for community testing where GP visits are rare, so targeting doesn't miss the groups most at risk of complications. Next step: build the questionnaire into GP systems and pilot in two regions.
great: Computes cost per case found for both options
Shows how much targeting misses
Checks whether uptake changes the answer
Addresses equity for people who don't see a GP

title: Kestrel Metro
sub: Free buses, or more buses?
skills: Public sector · policy options · cost per outcome
prompt: A city transport authority wants more people to take the bus instead of driving, to cut congestion and emissions. A popular proposal is to make buses free, costing $30M a year in lost fares. The authority could instead spend the same $30M running buses more often. You're asked which gets more new riders.

clarify.a: 60 million trips a year; fares bring in $30M.
Studies of similar cities suggest about 12% more trips, but much of the increase comes from people who used to walk or cycle, not drive.
$30M a year would raise frequency on the 20 busiest routes from every 12 minutes to every 6; similar changes elsewhere raised trips across the whole network by about 18%.
About 35% of riders are on low incomes.

structure.root: Which option attracts more new riders for $30M a year?

branches.head: Cost per new trip
items: Lost fares vs extra operating cost

branches.head: Quality of new trips
items: From cars, or from walking and cycling?

hypothesis: Free fares spend most of the money on trips people already make. More frequent service attracts people who currently find the bus too slow, often drivers.

questions.q: Compare new trips and cost per new trip.

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · New trips a year (millions) for $30M

questions.answer:
Free fares: 60M × 12% = 7.2M new trips for $30M: $4.17 per new trip. And the $30M mostly subsidises the 60M trips already made.

More frequent buses: 60M × 18% = 10.8M new trips: $2.78 per new trip.

questions.q: Does it matter where the new riders come from?
questions.answer: Yes: the goal is fewer car trips. Evidence from cities with free fares is that many new trips replace walking and cycling. Frequency improvements mostly win people who found the bus too slow or unreliable, more of whom were driving. So the gap in car trips removed is likely even larger than the gap in new trips.

questions.q: Free fares are popular and help low-income riders. How would you address that?
questions.answer: Offer free or half-price fares only to low-income riders (about 35%), through existing benefit cards: half-price for them costs about $5.2M plus about $2M to administer, well under $30M. Combine that with frequency increases funded by the rest, if the budget allows.

reco: Spend the $30M on more frequent buses, not free fares. More frequent service would add about 10.8M trips a year at about $2.78 each, against 7.2M at $4.17 for free fares, and more of those new riders would otherwise drive. To help low-income riders, offer targeted discounts through benefit cards for a fraction of the cost. Risk: frequency gains take time to show, so publicise the new timetable. Next step: model frequency increases route by route.
great: Compares cost per new trip, not total riders
Asks where new riders come from (the real goal)
Keeps the equity aim with a cheaper targeted option
Phrases the answer for a political audience

title: Lakeside School District
sub: Tutoring or smaller classes?
skills: Public sector · cost-effectiveness · stakeholder management
prompt: Lakeside school district has 10,000 primary students; 40% are below the reading standard for their age. A $4.8M state grant must be used to raise reading results this year. Teachers' representatives want smaller classes. The superintendent has seen research on small-group tutoring. You're asked which plan would bring more students up to standard.

clarify.a: Three sessions a week in groups of three with trained tutors, for students below standard: about $1,200 per student a year. Local pilots: about 30% of tutored students reached the standard who otherwise wouldn't.
Cutting class sizes from 28 to 24 costs about $700 per student covered a year (more teachers and rooms). Research suggests about 6% more of the students covered reach the standard.
Tutors can be recruited within a term; extra classrooms aren't available in some schools.

structure.root: Which plan brings more students up to the reading standard?

branches.head: Outcome
items: Students reaching standard who otherwise wouldn't

hypothesis: Tutoring targets the students who need help, so each dollar should go further. Smaller classes spread money across all students, most of whom are already at standard.

questions.q: Compare cost per extra student reaching the standard.
questions.answer:
Tutoring: $1,200 ÷ 30% = $4,000 per student who reaches the standard.

Smaller classes: $700 ÷ 6% = $11,700.

Tutoring is about 2.9× as cost-effective.

questions.q: What would $4.8M achieve under each plan?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Extra students reaching the reading standard

questions.answer:
Tutoring: $4.8M ÷ $1,200 = 4,000 students tutored (all of them below standard; there are 4,000), of whom about 1,200 reach the standard.

Smaller classes: $4.8M ÷ $700 = 6,857 students covered; about 411 more reach the standard.

questions.q: Teachers argue smaller classes help every child, not just those behind. How do you respond?
questions.answer: They're right that smaller classes have wider benefits, like behaviour and teacher workload, that this measure doesn't capture. But this grant's goal is reading results, and tutoring delivers far more of them. Involve teachers: let them choose which students are tutored and align tutoring with classroom lessons. Revisit class sizes if longer-term funding comes.

reco: Fund small-group tutoring. It costs about $4,000 per extra student reaching the reading standard, against about $11,700 for smaller classes, so the $4.8M would bring about 1,200 students up to standard rather than about 411. Tutoring also targets the students who are behind and can start within a term, while extra classrooms aren't available everywhere. Involve teachers in choosing students and linking tutoring to lessons. Risk: tutor quality, so train and monitor them. Next step: recruit tutors and test students at the start and end of the year.
great: Defines the outcome precisely
Computes cost per outcome for both plans
Notes that one plan targets the students in need
Engages the teachers' argument rather than dismissing it

title: Harbourview Hotel
sub: Revenue per room is up. Profit is down.
skills: Yield management · RevPAR vs profit · break-even
prompt: Harbourview is a 200-room hotel in Hobart. In the 200-day off-season it is 55% full at $160 a night. The revenue manager proposes a 20% off-season discount, expecting occupancy to rise to 72%, and points out that revenue per available room (RevPAR, the industry's favourite measure) would go up. The general manager asks whether to do it.

clarify.a: About $40 a night for cleaning, laundry, amenities and booking fees.
About $5.5M a year for staff, building and overheads; these don't change with occupancy.
Unaffected: the discount applies only off-season.

structure.root: Should Harbourview cut off-season prices by 20%?

branches.head: Other effects
items: Guests who would have paid full price

hypothesis: RevPAR ignores the cost of each extra occupied room. If the discount fills rooms at a lower margin, profit could fall even as RevPAR rises.

questions.q: Compare RevPAR before and after.
Now compare off-season contribution (revenue minus the $40 per occupied room).
questions.answer:
Room-nights available: 200 × 200 = 40,000.

Before: 22,000 × ($160 − $40) = $2.64M. After: 28,800 × ($128 − $40) = $2.53M.

Profit falls by $106k, even though RevPAR rises. Fixed costs are the same either way, so they don't change the comparison.

To break even, the discount would need occupancy of 75%.

questions.q: Is there a better way to fill the off-season?
questions.answer:
• Discount only on nights forecast to be emptiest, not across the whole season
  • Packages (room + dinner, conference rooms) that raise spend rather than cut rate
  • Target groups the hotel doesn't currently reach (corporate retreats, events), so discounts don't go to guests who would have paid full price

reco: Don't cut off-season prices by 20%. RevPAR would rise from $88 to $92.16, but each extra room costs $40 to service, so off-season contribution would fall from $2.64M to $2.53M. The discount would need occupancy of 75% to break even. Use targeted discounts on the emptiest nights and packages that raise spend instead. Track profit per available room, not just RevPAR.
great: Computes RevPAR and contribution side by side
Explains why RevPAR can mislead
Finds the break-even occupancy
Suggests targeted alternatives

title: Cinder Theatre
sub: Sold out on Saturdays, half empty on Tuesdays
skills: Yield management · price by demand · capacity
prompt: Cinder is a 1,000-seat theatre in Chicago running a hit musical six nights a week, at $60 a ticket for every show. Friday and Saturday sell out weeks ahead; Tuesday and Wednesday are half empty. The theatre's fixed costs are about $6M a year. The director asks whether pricing by night would help.

clarify.a: At $60, about 1,400 people a night want Friday or Saturday seats, about 850 Thursday or Sunday, and about 500 Tuesday or Wednesday.
Past offers suggest each 10% price change moves ticket demand about 8% the other way (treat it as a constant elasticity of −0.8).
About 45 weeks a year.

structure.root: How should Cinder price its shows?

hypothesis: At $60 the weekend is underpriced (we turn people away) and midweek may be overpriced. Raising weekend prices should raise revenue; I'd check whether cutting midweek prices does too.

questions.q: What does a week earn today?
questions.answer: Fri/Sat: 2 × 1,000 (capped) × $60 = $120k. Thu/Sun: 2 × 850 × $60 = $102k. Tue/Wed: 2 × 500 × $60 = $60k. Total $282k a week, about $12.7M a season against $6M of fixed costs.

questions.q: Try $80 at weekends and $45 on Tuesday and Wednesday. What happens?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · The tested prices by night

questions.answer:
Fri/Sat at $80 (+33%): demand falls about 21% to about 1,110, still above 1,000: still sold out, now at $80. Revenue per show: $60k → $80k.

Tue/Wed at $45 (−25%): demand rises about 26% to about 629 a show. But revenue per show falls, from $30.0k to $28.3k: with a sensitivity below 1, a price cut loses more on price than it gains in seats.

Together: $318.6k a week (+13%). Raising weekends alone and keeping midweek at $60 does better: $322k a week, +14%, about $1.8M more a season, almost all profit because costs are fixed.

So-what: the gain is all in the weekend. A general midweek discount fills a few more seats but costs about $3.4k a week.
questions.note: Uses a constant price sensitivity of −0.8.

questions.q: What would you watch out for, and how would you fill midweek seats?
questions.answer:
• Fans may see higher weekend prices as unfair; keep a block of affordable seats and a lottery for each show
  • Weekends would still sell out at up to about $91, so $80 is cautious; raise in steps and watch how fast shows sell out
  • Fill midweek with targeted offers (student and rush tickets, groups, bar or dinner bundles) rather than a general discount, so full-price buyers don't trade down
  • Review prices every month as demand changes

reco: Price by night: raise Friday and Saturday to about $80 (they would still sell out) and keep Tuesday and Wednesday at $60, because a general midweek discount would lose revenue at this price sensitivity. Weekly revenue rises from $282k to about $322k, about $1.8M a season, nearly all profit since costs are fixed. Fill midweek seats with targeted offers such as student and rush tickets, and keep a block of affordable seats at every show for fairness. Next step: test new prices on next month's performances.
great: Spots unmet demand at the weekend
Uses price sensitivity to estimate new demand
Notices the midweek cut loses revenue when demand is not very price-sensitive
Balances revenue with fairness to fans

title: Gateway Parking
sub: A car park that's full by 8:30 and empty by 7pm
skills: Time-based pricing · capacity · segmentation
prompt: Gateway runs an 800-space car park in downtown Vancouver at a flat $20 a day. On weekdays it's full by 8:30am and turns away about 200 cars; after 6pm it's mostly empty. The owner asks how to earn more from the same spaces.

clarify.a: Mostly commuters who stay all day. Shoppers and visitors arrive after 10am and stay 2–4 hours, but find it full.
About 150 cars come in the evening for restaurants and events and pay the $20 day rate; that price puts others off.
Commuters would pay up to about $24 to guarantee a space. About 300 late-morning visitors a day would come at $16 for a stay of up to 4 hours. An $8 evening rate would bring about 400 evening cars.
Short-stay visitors free their space mid-afternoon, so two short stays can share a space.
Assume about 250 weekdays a year; ignore weekends.

structure.root: How should Gateway price its spaces?

hypothesis: A flat price ignores that the space is scarce in the morning and idle at night. Charging by time of day should raise revenue and serve more people.

questions.q: What does Gateway earn today?
questions.answer: (800 daytime + 150 evening cars) × $20 × 250 weekdays = $4.75M a year.

questions.q: Design a time-based price list and estimate revenue.
questions.answer:
Commuters (before 10am, all day): $24, about 650 spaces.

Short stays (after 10am, up to 4 hours): $16, about 300 cars; two can share a space, so they need about 150 spaces. 650 + 150 = 800.

Evening (after 6pm): $8, about 400 cars.

Revenue: (650 × $24 + 300 × $16 + 400 × $8) × 250 = $5.9M, +24%.

questions.q: What could go wrong?
questions.answer:
• Commuters may resent paying $24; offer monthly passes at a small discount for loyalty
  • Need space-availability signs and an app so short-stay visitors know there's room
  • Check local rules on evening charges and nearby residents' concerns

reco: Charge by time of day: $24 for all-day commuters, $16 for short stays after 10am, and $8 in the evening. Reserving about 150 spaces for short-stay visitors, who can share a space across the day, and filling the empty evenings raises revenue from $4.75M to about $5.9M a year (+24%). Offer monthly passes to keep regular commuters. Risk: commuters switching to rival car parks. Next step: install availability signs and test prices for three months.
great: Sees time as the scarce resource
Segments users by when and how long they park
Checks the plan fits capacity
Keeps loyal commuters with passes

title: Alder Grand Hotel
sub: How many extra bookings should a full hotel take?
skills: Overbooking · expected value · probability
prompt: The Alder Grand is a 300-room conference hotel in Washington, DC. On busy weeknights it sells out, but about 8% of guests with bookings don't show up, leaving rooms empty that could have been sold. The revenue manager wants to accept extra bookings beyond 300. The general manager worries about turning away guests who do arrive. How many extra bookings should the hotel take?

clarify.a: Rate about $250 a night; about $45 of costs per occupied room.
On busy weeknights, about 8% of booked guests don't arrive, independently of each other.
If more guests arrive than there are rooms, the hotel pays for a room at a nearby hotel plus transport and a goodwill voucher: about $400 per guest, plus reputational damage.
No-shows aren't charged on most corporate rates.

structure.root: How many bookings beyond 300 should the Alder Grand accept?

branches.head: Probability
items: How many no-shows on a given night

hypothesis: With 8% no-shows, about 24 rooms go empty on a sold-out night, but the number varies. Since walking a guest costs more than a room earns, the hotel should stop a little short of the bookings that would, on average, exactly fill the hotel.

questions.q: A simple answer would be to overbook by the expected number of no-shows. What is that, and what's wrong with it?
questions.answer:
To expect exactly 300 arrivals, book 300 ÷ 92% ≈ 326, i.e. 26 extra. But arrivals vary from night to night, so on about half of those nights more than 300 guests would turn up.

An extra booking that fills an empty room earns $205; one that arrives to a full hotel costs $400. Because the downside is bigger than the upside, the hotel should stop a little short of 26.

questions.q: Here is expected profit per night for different numbers of extra bookings. What do you recommend?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Expected profit by extra bookings accepted

questions.answer:
Expected profit peaks at about 24 extra bookings: $60,435 a night, against $56,580 with no overbooking: about $3,855 more a night.

At 24, the hotel expects to walk about 1.1 guests a night; at 26 it would walk about 1.9 and earn less ($60,330).
questions.note: Assumes each booked guest independently has a 92% chance of arriving.

questions.q: How would you make overbooking safer?
questions.answer:
• Overbook less on nights with many loyalty members or conference speakers, who must not be walked
  • Charge no-shows on more rates, which lowers the no-show rate itself
  • Agree a standing arrangement with a nearby hotel, and always walk guests to a better hotel with a clear apology
  • Update no-show estimates by day, season and booking source

reco: Accept about 24 bookings beyond the 300 rooms on busy weeknights. That's a little fewer than the 26 needed to expect a full house, because walking a guest ($400) costs nearly twice what a room earns ($205). It raises expected profit by about $3,855 a night, with about 1.1 guests a night walked on average. Protect loyalty members and VIPs from being walked, and keep an agreement with a nearby hotel. Next step: estimate no-show rates by booking source and day of week.
great: Explains why the best level is below the bookings that would fill the hotel on average
Weighs the margin of a filled room against the cost of walking a guest
Reads the expected-profit curve
Protects the most valuable guests

title: Granite Holdings
sub: $50M to spend, $80M of good projects
skills: Capital rationing · profitability index · NPV
prompt: Granite is an industrial manufacturer. Its divisions have proposed five projects needing $80M in total, all with a positive NPV. The board has capped next year's investment at $50M. The CFO asks which projects to fund.

clarify.a: No: each is all-or-nothing.
Yes: all use the same 9% discount rate and have been reviewed by finance.
None; projects are independent.
No.

structure.root: Which projects should Granite fund within $50M?

hypothesis: With limited capital, the best set isn't the projects with the biggest NPVs but those that create the most value per dollar invested.

questions.q: Here are the projects. If you fund the biggest NPVs first, what do you get?
questions.answer: A ($12M) then B ($9M): $45M used. D and C don't fit; E does. Set A, B, E: NPV $22.5M.

questions.q: Now rank by NPV per dollar invested. Which set is better?
questions.answer:
Ranking by NPV ÷ investment: B (0.60), C (0.50), A and D (0.40), E (0.30). Funding in that order: B, C, then A doesn't fit, D does, then E: B, C, D, E, using $50M.

NPV: $23.5M, $1.0M more than funding the biggest projects first. Checking every combination confirms it is the best set.

So-what: when capital is the constraint, rank by value per dollar.

questions.q: Is there anything that would make you fund A anyway?
questions.answer: Yes, if the plant is strategically necessary (for example, existing capacity runs out next year), if its NPV is more certain than the others', or if delaying it loses the opportunity. Also ask whether the $50M cap is truly fixed: if projects return well above the cost of capital, borrowing to fund A may create value.

reco: Fund B, C, D and E ($50M), which together create about $23.5M of NPV, more than the $22.5M from funding the biggest project, A, first. With capital capped, rank projects by NPV per dollar invested. Revisit A next year, or challenge the $50M cap if all projects are as solid as they look.
great: Ranks by NPV per dollar under a capital limit
Shows why ranking by NPV fails
Checks the full combination
Questions whether the cap itself is right

title: Copperleaf Retail
sub: $200M of cash: grow, buy, or give it back?
skills: Capital allocation · return vs cost of capital · buybacks
prompt: Copperleaf is a profitable home-goods retailer with $200M of spare cash. Management has three ideas, and some shareholders want a share buyback. The board asks how to use the money. Copperleaf's cost of capital is 10%.

clarify.a: $80M to refit 60 stores; expected return about 16% a year on the money invested.
$100M for 25 stores in new towns; expected return about 11%.
Buy a smaller rival for $150M; expected return about 8%, including savings.
Returns cash to shareholders, who can invest it elsewhere at about the cost of capital.

structure.root: How should Copperleaf use $200M?

hypothesis: Only projects returning more than the 10% cost of capital create value. Anything below that is better returned to shareholders.

questions.q: Which options create value, and how much?

exhibit.title: Exhibit 1 · Options vs 10% cost of capital

questions.answer:
Value created a year = money invested × (return − 10%).

  • Refit: $80M × 6% = +$4.8M a year
  • New stores: $100M × 1% = +$1.0M
  • Acquisition: $150M × −2% = −$3.0M: destroys value

questions.q: New stores return only 1% above the cost of capital. Would you do them?
questions.answer: Barely. A 1-point margin can vanish if a few stores underperform. I'd open them in stages, starting with the towns most like Copperleaf's best stores, and stop if early stores miss target.

questions.q: What's your recommendation for the $200M?
questions.answer: Refit stores ($80M), open new stores in stages (up to $100M), skip the acquisition, and return the remaining $20M, plus any new-store money not used, through a buyback.

reco: Refit the existing stores first: $80M at about 16% creates about $4.8M of value a year. Open new stores in stages, because their 11% return is only just above the 10% cost of capital. Don't buy the rival: an 8% return destroys about $3M of value a year. Return the remaining $20M, and any unused new-store money, to shareholders through a buyback.
great: Compares each return with the cost of capital
Computes value created, not just return
Treats a thin margin with caution
Returns cash that can't earn its cost

title: Osprey Group
sub: Four businesses, one budget: which to grow, fix or sell?
skills: Portfolio strategy · economic profit · divestment
prompt: Osprey is a listed group with four businesses. Each asks for more capital every year, and the CEO tends to share it out evenly. A new CFO asks you to recommend a portfolio strategy. Osprey's cost of capital is 9%.

clarify.a: Packaging: $400M invested, 15% return, market growing 6%. Specialty films: $150M, 22%, growing 12%. Industrial labels: $300M, 8%, growing 1%. Paper mills: $500M, 4%, shrinking 2% a year.
A paper company has offered $420M for the mills.
Little sharing between the businesses apart from head office.

structure.root: Where should Osprey invest, and what should it sell?

hypothesis: Sharing capital evenly feeds businesses that destroy value. Specialty films should get more; paper mills look like a candidate to sell.

questions.q: Which businesses create value, and which destroy it?
questions.answer:
Value created a year = capital × (return − 9%).

Films +$19.5M, packaging +$24.0M, labels −$3.0M, mills −$25.0M.

questions.q: Should Osprey accept $420M for the paper mills?
questions.answer:
The mills earn about 4% on $500M = $20M a year, in a shrinking market. Valued at the 9% cost of capital with no growth: $20M ÷ 9% = about $222M, and less if earnings keep falling.

An offer of $420M is worth more to Osprey than keeping them. The buyer may value them more because it can combine mills and cut costs.

questions.q: Lay out the portfolio strategy.
questions.answer:
• Grow specialty films: highest return in the fastest-growing market; give it first claim on capital
  • Maintain packaging: solid returns; invest where returns stay above 9%
  • Fix or exit labels: just below the cost of capital in a flat market; set a two-year target to reach 10%+, or sell
  • Sell the mills and use part of the $420M to fund films and part to reduce debt or return cash

reco: Stop sharing capital evenly. Specialty films earns 22% in a market growing 12% and should get first claim on capital; packaging should be maintained; labels needs a turnaround plan to beat the 9% cost of capital within two years or be sold. Sell the paper mills: they destroy about $25M of value a year, are worth only about $222M to Osprey, and a buyer is offering $420M. Risk: losing scale in purchasing and head-office costs. Next step: test the films growth plan.
great: Computes value created by each business
Values the business to sell against the offer
Assigns a clear role to each business
Links the sale proceeds to where capital goes

title: Saltire Telecom
sub: Where should $600M of fibre go first?
skills: Capital allocation · customer lifetime value · infrastructure rollout
prompt: Saltire is building a fibre broadband network in Scotland and has $600M for the next three years. The board wants to know which areas to build in, in what order. A rival has just announced fibre plans for the main cities.

clarify.a: Each customer pays about $50 a month at a 60% margin, and stays for 15 years on average. Discount rate 8%. Connecting a customer's home costs about $300, paid from the operating budget, not the $600M build budget.

clarify.q: Cost to pass a home with fibre?
clarify.a: Urban about $400; suburban about $700; rural about $1,800.
Expected share of homes passed that sign up: urban 40%, suburban 35%, rural 30%. Homes: 300k urban, 500k suburban, 400k rural.
The government pays $1,000 per rural home passed.
If the rival builds in a city first, Saltire's urban take-up could fall to about 25%.

structure.root: How should Saltire allocate $600M across regions?

branches.head: Value per home passed
items: Take-up × customer value − build cost + subsidy

hypothesis: Urban areas are cheapest to build and have the highest take-up, so they come first, especially with a rival coming. Rural only works with the subsidy.

questions.q: What is a customer worth today?
questions.answer: $50 × 12 × 60% = $360 a year for 15 years at 8% (factor 8.56): $3,081. Less $300 to connect: $2,781.

questions.q: What is each home passed worth in each region?
questions.answer:
Urban: 40% × $2,781 − $400 = +$713. Suburban: 35% × $2,781 − $700 = +$273. Rural: 30% × $2,781 − $1,800 + $1,000 subsidy = +$34, only just positive.

Value per dollar spent: urban 1.78, suburban 0.39, rural 0.04 (per dollar of Saltire's own money after the $1,000 subsidy; about 0.02 on the full $1,800).

questions.q: How would you spend the $600M, and in what order?
questions.answer:
Urban: $120M, about 300k homes, value about $214M.

Suburban: $350M, about 500k homes, value about $137M.

That uses $470M. Rural adds only about 4 cents of value per dollar, too thin to fund from a capped budget, so hold the remaining $130M back for cost overruns and to speed up the urban build.

Build urban first and fast: the rival's plans make it urgent. Even if the rival arrives and take-up falls to 25%, an urban home is still worth +$295.

questions.q: Should Saltire build rural areas at all?
questions.answer: With the subsidy each rural home is worth only about +$34: a small cost overrun or lower take-up would make it negative. Build rural only with a bigger subsidy, cheaper methods (using existing poles), or partners to share costs. Not from this budget.

reco: Spend about $470M on urban areas first, then suburban, and hold $130M back. An urban home passed is worth about +$713, a suburban one about +$273, and a rural one only about +$34 even with the $1,000 subsidy. Build cities first and quickly to get there before the rival; even at 25% take-up they stay valuable. Leave rural out of this budget unless subsidies rise or costs fall. Risk: build costs and take-up are estimates, so release funding in stages. Next step: start the two largest cities this quarter.
great: Values a customer over their lifetime
Converts customer value into value per home passed
Ranks regions by value per dollar and allocates the budget
Weighs timing and competition
